PHP and WordPress Development · Facilitator Guide

Part 1: Themes

Sessions 1 to 8. Modules 1 to 4: set up a WordPress 7.1 development site with Docker, WP-CLI, debugging and Mailpit, write PHP the WordPress way, learn the content model, the database and hooks, then build the Pages & Co. block theme with theme.json, templates, patterns and style variations, a child theme, and a classic/hybrid theme with the Loop, custom queries and functions.php. Runs on its own as a short course and ends with the Part 1 project and assessment.

Instructor Kit · Facilitator Guide

Session 1: WordPress for Developers and Your Local Environment

How to teach the first session of PHP and WordPress Development. Welcome a room of PHP and MySQL developers, find out which machines run the course's Docker project and what the room remembers from the Foundations courses, then show WordPress as a developer sees it (one request through core, the folder that is yours, an edited core file and an old tutorial caught) and make every laptop ready: an install clinic, WP-CLI and debugging on the real site, a site-report lab, and a health check learners can rerun all course.

2 lessons 3 hrs session Lessons 1.1–1.2 Session 1 of 18 · Part 1

How to Use This Guide

  • Same rhythm for both lessons: frame (the goal and one mental model) → live demo (you type, they type along) → guided lab (a kit lab, new practice on the lesson's ideas) → start the lesson's own project. The lesson exercises, quiz and journal are homework.
  • Type, do not paste. Every command below was run to produce the output printed under it, on WordPress 7.1.3, PHP 8.5.12, MySQL 9.7 and WP-CLI 2.12.0: a fresh course site, exactly what a learner has at the end of Lesson 1.2. Ask for a prediction before every run, and read every message from the left, out loud: the level, the message, the file, the line.
  • The lessons are the reference. Keep lesson_01.html and lesson_02.html open in browser tabs for the request diagram and the per-platform Docker sections. Labs live in labs/module-01/ (learners keep the folder in their project folder, next to compose.yaml): _starter files are handouts, _solution files and the store_hours_solution/ folder are yours.
  • Session 1 is different in two ways. It opens with 30 minutes of welcome, environment check and diagnostic instead of the usual 10-minute warm-up, and Lesson 1.2's room time is mostly an install clinic: setting up Docker and the course project is prework (the kit's setup guide follows Lesson 1.2), so the room fixes what went wrong instead of watching downloads.
  • Part 1, "Themes" (Sessions 1 to 8), can run on its own as a short course; nothing in this session depends on Part 2. Teal blocks are hands-on, amber blocks are watch-outs. Lesson codes (1.1, 1.2) match the course site.
The #1 risk of Session 1: the setup eats the session

Docker installs differently on every platform, and each path has its own trap: Windows needs WSL 2, Docker Desktop's WSL integration switched on, and the project in the Linux file system; Linux needs the docker group (and a new login) and the course's file-owner fix before the first start; every platform downloads about a gigabyte of images on the first docker compose up -d. Done together on venue Wi-Fi, setup fills three hours and nobody looks at WordPress. Before: send the setup guide a week ahead (Docker, the pagesco-dev project, the install commands, the labs/ folder in the project folder, then check_environment.sh) and ask every learner to reply with its last line. In the room: the check gets 12 minutes in the opening; a NOT READY machine gets a ready partner until the 25-minute install clinic at 1:40, not your attention during Lesson 1.1. After: whoever is still not ready leaves with a numbered plan and runs the check again before Session 2.

Before the Session

  • ☐ A week before: email the setup guide (install Docker following Lesson 1.2 for your platform, unpack pagesco-dev in the home folder, on Linux and WSL do the file-owner setup BEFORE the first start, docker compose up -d, the two install commands, the Mailpit plugin, copy the kit's labs/ folder into pagesco-dev, then bash labs/module-01/l1_0-orientation/check_environment.sh). Ask learners to reply with the last line it prints. No reply means a setup risk: chase it.
  • ☐ Files to hand out (shared folder or USB stick, in case the network fails): the whole labs/ folder without the *_solution.* files and the store_hours_solution/ folder; pagesco-dev.zip from the course site; the workbook. If you can, put the course images on the stick too: on your machine, docker save -o pagesco-images.tar wordpress:7.1-php8.5-apache mysql:9.7 axllent/mailpit:latest wordpress:cli-php8.5, and learners run docker load -i pagesco-images.tar (it saves the gigabyte download; the wpcli image is then built from the local base).
  • ☐ Run the kit check once: python3 labs/check_labs.py module-01 from this kit's folder (every line PASS; 15 results in about two minutes, a third of it the environment check's own throwaway project). With your own course project: WP_LABS_COMPOSE=~/pagesco-dev python3 labs/check_labs.py module-01 (labs/README.md). Then run check_environment.sh on the projector machine so you can show what READY looks like.
  • ☐ Projector machine: the course project running (docker compose up -d) with the wp shortcut defined, VS Code open on pagesco-dev at a large font, two terminals in the project folder at 18 pt or larger (one for commands, one for tail -f wordpress/wp-content/debug.log), a browser with http://localhost:8080, http://localhost:8080/wp-admin/ (admin / password) and http://localhost:8025 in tabs, plus lesson_01.html and lesson_02.html.
  • ☐ Board, before learners arrive: the request path (index.php → wp-blog-header.php → wp-load.php → wp-config.php → wp-settings.php → wp() → template-loader.php → HTML); the triage line "docker not found = install · Cannot connect to the Docker daemon = start Docker Desktop · no configuration file = wrong folder · Permission denied in wordpress/ = the Linux fix"; and a box labeled wp-content = yours.
  • ☐ Print or share: the workbook (its Start Here page has the environment checklist and the diagnostic), sticky notes for help flags and the exit ticket.
Known environment traps
SymptomCauseFix
docker: command not found, or Cannot connect to the Docker daemonDocker not installed, or Docker Desktop not startedInstall it (Lesson 1.2) or start Docker Desktop and wait for "running"; Linux: sudo systemctl start docker.
Windows: docker works in PowerShell but not in UbuntuDocker Desktop's WSL integration is off for that distributionDocker Desktop > Settings > Resources > WSL integration: switch on Ubuntu, then a new Ubuntu terminal.
Linux: permission denied while trying to connect to the Docker daemon socketThe user is not in the docker group yet, or has not logged in againsudo usermod -aG docker "$USER", then log out and back in (a new terminal is not enough).
mkdir: cannot create directory ... Permission denied in wordpress/ (Linux, WSL)The containers created the files as uid 33 (www-data)Lesson 1.2's repair box: docker compose run --rm --user root wpcli chown ..., the .env and compose.override.yaml, docker compose up -d.
required variable PAGESCO_UID is missing a valuecompose.override.yaml copied, .env not madeThe printf ... > .env line of Lesson 1.2, in the project folder.
tar: ./index.php: Cannot open: Permission denied in docker compose logs wordpressDocker created wordpress/ as root before the first startStop, docker compose run --rm --user root wpcli chown -R "$(id -u):$(id -g)" /var/www/html, or delete the empty folder and mkdir wordpress as yourself, then up -d.
Bind for 0.0.0.0:8080 failed: port is already allocatedAnother project, an old container or a local server uses 8080 (or 8025)docker ps (PORTS column), stop the other one. Changing the course port means three edits and lessons that no longer match: free the port.
no configuration file provided: not foundThe terminal is not in the project foldercd ~/pagesco-dev; add the wp alias to ~/.bashrc or ~/.zshrc.
Error establishing a database connection after editing compose.yamlThe database password was changed after the first startPut the old password back and docker compose up -d (Common Mistakes 4).
wp_mail() prints bool(false); the check says FIX for Mailpitmailpit-smtp.php is not in wordpress/wp-content/mu-plugins/cp config/mailpit-smtp.php wordpress/wp-content/mu-plugins/.
Pages load in several seconds (Windows)The project is on the Windows drive (/mnt/c/...)Move it to the Linux home folder inside WSL (the check says CHECK for this).
The first docker compose up -d takes foreverAbout a gigabyte of images over venue Wi-Fidocker load -i pagesco-images.tar from the USB stick, or pair today and finish at home.

In the room. The lesson pages estimate 100 + 150 = 250 minutes for a learner working alone, and after the 30-minute opening, the break and the wrap-up the room has 130. Lesson 1.1 keeps its full shape (model, demo, lab, project start). Lesson 1.2's Docker installation sections are prework from the setup guide: the room uses its time for an install clinic, a WP-CLI-and-debugging demo, a short lab and the start of the health check. The lesson's alternatives section (wp-env, Playground) is reading at home.

Goes home (about 2 to 3 hours). The Pages & Co. plan (Playground Steps 1 and 2, and the rest of Step 4) and the health check Step 4 (break it, read it, clean up); each lesson's Hands-on Exercises; both Quick Quizzes; both journal entries; Lesson 1.2's "Before the Next Lesson" list. Anyone still NOT READY finishes the setup with the numbered plan from the clinic.

Protect, in this order: the environment check result for every learner (nobody leaves without knowing whether their machine is ready and what to do next); the install clinic; the 1.1 demo through Mistake 1 (core is not yours: the rule the whole course leans on); the 1.2 debug demo (every later lesson assumes learners read debug.log). Cut first: the 1.1 demo's last step (the Link header) and the 1.2 Mailpit step (learners see it in the health check), then the 1.1 project start (send the whole plan home), then the 1.2 project start (the demo already showed the pieces; learners type the script at home).

Opening Segment

0:00

Welcome, Environment Check and Diagnostic

30 min
Timing
5mWelcome and introductions
5mHow the course runs: 18 sessions in two parts, one or two lessons a session, the room and home split, the journal
12mEnvironment check: check_environment.sh ends with READY on every machine, or the machine gets a partner and a clinic slot
8mDiagnostic: six readiness questions, not graded
Sequence and talking points
  • Welcome (5m). One minute on yourself, including a WordPress site you once had to fix (the plugin that broke on an update, the theme someone edited by hand). Then a quick round: name, what they want to build with WordPress (client sites, a plugin to sell, the site at work), and which PHP and MySQL they already know. Write three or four goals on the board; they come back in the 1.1 journal prompt. Housekeeping in one breath: break at 1:20, where the lab files are, and "if you are stuck, put a sticky note on your laptop lid and keep trying while I get to you."
  • How the course runs (5m). Show the course home page. Say: "Eighteen sessions of three hours in two parts. Part 1, Themes, the first eight sessions, takes you from a local site to the Pages & Co. block theme, a child theme and a classic theme; Part 2, Plugins to Launch, builds the pagesco-books plugin, custom blocks, REST endpoints, tests and a deployment, and ends with the whole site launched." Then the deal: "Each lesson was written for someone working alone for 100 to 150 minutes, so two do not fit in three hours. In this room we do what is hard alone: the mental model, a live demo, a guided lab, and the first steps of each project. At home you finish the projects and do the exercises, quiz and journal: plan on two to three hours a week." Scroll once through lesson_01.html: objectives, sections with real output, common mistakes made on purpose, a project in steps, exercises with hidden solutions, a quiz, a journal prompt.
  • Environment check (12m). Say: "Before any new ideas, we find out which machines are ready." On the projector, then theirs: 1 open a terminal in the project folder (cd ~/pagesco-dev, the folder with compose.yaml and labs/); 2 docker compose up -d if the site is not running; 3 bash labs/module-01/l1_0-orientation/check_environment.sh. Done = the last line says READY for PHP and WordPress Development (READY WITH NOTES on PHP 8.4 or a project on the Windows drive is fine for today). Anyone who saw READY at home runs it again and becomes a helper. NOT READY falls into three piles: Docker not running or not reachable (often one minute: start Docker Desktop, fix the WSL integration), FIX lines on a running site (the site is not installed, the Mailpit plugin is missing, the Linux owner fix: two to five minutes, fix now), no Docker or no project at all (do not start a download now: pair with a ready neighbor; install clinic at 1:40). Write the third pile's names on a sticky note.
  • Diagnostic (8m). Say: "Six quick questions on what WordPress development builds on: PHP arrays, escaping, SQL, the terminal, HTTP and callbacks. Not a test, nobody collects it. It tells you what to brush up and tells me what to slow down for." Learners answer D1 to D6 on the workbook's Start Here page (about four minutes), then show fingers (1 to 4 for A to D) as you reveal each. Keep a tally of wrong answers per question on a sticky note.
Diagnostic answers and how to read the tally

Answers: D1 A) 3 Dune; D2 B) Hello, &lt;b&gt;Maya&lt;/b&gt;; D3 C) SELECT title FROM books WHERE price < 10 ORDER BY price;; D4 D) cd pagesco-dev, then docker compose up -d; D5 A) 404 Not Found; D6 B) DUNE! EMMA!.

  • D1 (arrays) and D6 (callbacks) predict the next two sessions: Lesson 1.3 is arrays of arguments and callbacks in every form, Lesson 2.3 hooks your functions into core by name. Two or more misses on D6: say "core calls YOUR function" every time a callback appears in Sessions 2 and 3.
  • D2 (escaping) comes back in Lesson 1.3 (esc_html() and friends) and Lesson 5.3 (security). A miss here is the most important one to follow up: escaping is non-negotiable in WordPress code.
  • D3 (SQL) comes back in Lesson 2.2 (WordPress's own tables) and 5.5 ($wpdb). Learners who miss it are usually rusty, not lost: point them to MySQL Foundations' SELECT lessons before Session 3.
  • D4 (folders) predicts trouble in the next hour: no configuration file provided is almost always it. Learners who missed it get the typing role in the lab pair, with you nearby for the first command.
  • D5 (HTTP) matters from Module 3 on (the 404 template, redirects). Misses are rare.
  • Three or more wrong: not a problem to announce. Pair them with a strong neighbor today, and at the wrap-up hand them labs/module-01/l1_0-orientation/diagnostic_starter.php: D1, D2 and D6 done by PHP on their own site, one small gap each (diagnostic_solution.php is your reference). The workbook's Start Here page says where each skill comes back; PHP Foundations and MySQL Foundations are the review.
Watch-outs
  • Do not debug one machine in front of the room. Two minutes per machine during the check, then pair and move on: the install clinic at 1:40 exists so that you can say "we will fix that at 1:40" with a straight face.
  • Mixed backgrounds. Some learners have built WordPress sites in the dashboard and never written a plugin; some write PHP daily and have never used WordPress. The diagnostic and the check are for both groups; say so.
  • "I use Local / XAMPP / MAMP." Those work for WordPress, but the course's outputs, paths, port, mail catcher and WP-CLI fixes are tested on the Docker project (Lesson 1.2 FAQ). Ask them to run the course project alongside for the labs; nothing needs uninstalling.
  • "I already know WordPress." Welcome them and give them a job: helper during the check and the clinic, and the stretch tasks in each lab. Old habits (editing a theme's functions.php from the dashboard, FTP to the live site, tutorials from before blocks) are exactly what Module 1 replaces.

Lesson Plans

1.1

WordPress for Developers

50 min
Objectives (from the lesson page)
  • Describe WordPress 7.1 as a developer sees it: a PHP and MySQL application with themes, plugins, blocks and APIs as extension points
  • Explain the difference between WordPress.org (the software) and WordPress.com (a hosting service), and pick the right one for a project
  • Trace a front-end request from index.php to the finished HTML, naming the core files on the way
  • Say where your code belongs (themes, plugins, must-use plugins in wp-content/) and why you never edit core files
  • Map what you know from PHP Foundations and MySQL Foundations to the way WordPress does the same jobs
  • Describe the Pages & Co. project and plan how you will work through this course
Timing in the room
10mFrame: the apartment building; the extension points; WordPress.org and WordPress.com; load, query, template
15mLive demo: the front door in core, curl, where code lives, two mistakes caught
15mGuided lab: core_tour_starter.sh in pairs
10mStart the lesson project: the Pages & Co. plan, Steps 3 and 4
Mental model to say

Tell it while you draw it: "WordPress core is an apartment building. The owner, the WordPress project, maintains the structure, the wiring and the plumbing, and renovates a few times a year. You are a tenant. You paint and furnish your rooms (themes), plug appliances into the sockets the building provides (plugins and hooks), and you can add a doorbell that rings in the lobby (the REST API). You never knock down a wall of the building: the next renovation would put it back."

Then the extension points as a list on the board: hooks (Lesson 2.3), themes (Modules 3 and 4), plugins (Module 5), blocks (Module 6), APIs (Module 7). "Almost everything a WordPress developer does is one of these five. Each has its module." Then WordPress.org and WordPress.com in two sentences: "WordPress.org is the free software and its community; WordPress.com is one company's hosting of it, where your own plugins depend on the plan. This course is self-hosted: your own site from Lesson 1.2."

Then the trip, one box at a time, on the drawing from the board: "Every front-end address goes to index.php. WordPress loads itself, settings first, then core, must-use plugins, plugins and the theme, and fires init. Then wp() turns the address into a query and runs it. Then the template loader picks the theme's template and draws the page. Load, then query, then template." Write inversion of control: core runs the program and calls you under it.

Live demo (you type, they follow)

The lesson's own commands, typed live on the projector in the WP-CLI container shell (docker compose run --rm wpcli sh; the prompt changes to /var/www/html $). Ready learners type along; the others watch and get their turn after the clinic. Ask for a prediction before every run.

  1. The front door (3m). "In PHP Foundations one file answered one address. Here almost every address goes to ONE file. Let us read it." Open a shell in the WP-CLI container (docker compose run --rm wpcli sh) and grep the two front-door files. Ask first: how many lines of real code does index.php have? 
    grep -n "WP_USE_THEMES\|require" index.php
grep -n "require\|wp();" wp-blog-header.php
    14:define( 'WP_USE_THEMES', true );
17:require __DIR__ . '/wp-blog-header.php';
13:	require_once __DIR__ . '/wp-load.php';
16:	wp();
19:	require_once ABSPATH . WPINC . '/template-loader.php';
    Two: one constant and one require. Then wp-blog-header.php does three things in order: load WordPress, wp(), the template loader. Draw them on the board as three boxes: load, query, template.
  2. The end of the trip (2m). "Now from the outside, the way a browser asks." curl runs inside the container, where http://localhost:8080 is the site. 
    curl -s http://localhost:8080/hello-world/ | grep -o '<title>.*</title>'
    <title>Hello world! &#8211; Pages &amp; Co.</title>
    "Hello world!" came from the main query, "Pages & Co." from the options table, the dash is an HTML entity. None of it is in a file: it is the database plus the theme.
  3. Where code lives (3m). "Everything in the root belongs to WordPress, except two things." List the root, then the one folder that is yours. 
    ls
ls -d wp-content/*/
ls wp-content/themes wp-content/plugins
    index.php             wp-activate.php       wp-comments-post.php  wp-config.php         wp-includes           wp-login.php          wp-signup.php
license.txt           wp-admin              wp-config-docker.php  wp-content            wp-links-opml.php     wp-mail.php           wp-trackback.php
readme.html           wp-blog-header.php    wp-config-sample.php  wp-cron.php           wp-load.php           wp-settings.php       xmlrpc.php
wp-content/mu-plugins/  wp-content/plugins/     wp-content/themes/      wp-content/uploads/
wp-content/plugins:
akismet    hello.php  index.php

wp-content/themes:
index.php          twentytwentyfive   twentytwentyfour   twentytwentythree
    Point at wp-config.php (your settings) and wp-content/ (your themes, plugins, must-use plugins, uploads). Ask: "who updates each folder?" Core: WordPress. Twenty Twenty-Five: its own updates. pagesco: you.
  4. Mistake 1: a quick fix in core (3m). "A tutorial says: add a line to wp-includes/functions.php. Watch WordPress notice." The lesson's block makes a backup, appends a harmless comment, then compares every core file with the official checksums. 
    cp wp-includes/functions.php wp-content/functions.php.bak
echo '// my quick fix' >> wp-includes/functions.php
wp core verify-checksums
    Warning: File doesn't verify against checksum: wp-includes/functions.php
Warning: File should not exist: wp-config-docker.php
Error: WordPress installation doesn't verify against checksums.
    Read it from the top: the edited file fails; the second warning is the Docker image's own extra file (expected on every Docker site); the verdict is an Error. Restore and check again: 
    mv wp-content/functions.php.bak wp-includes/functions.php
wp core verify-checksums
    Warning: File should not exist: wp-config-docker.php
Success: WordPress installation verifies against checksums.
    "The next update would have removed your line without asking, at night, and a security scanner would have reported a hack."
  5. Mistake 2: an old tutorial (2m). "This one still works. Listen to what WordPress says about it." 
    wp eval 'get_currentuserinfo();'
    Deprecated: Function get_currentuserinfo is <strong>deprecated</strong> since version 4.5.0! Use wp_get_current_user() instead. in /var/www/html/wp-includes/functions.php on line 6260
    The message names the version that deprecated it (4.5.0, years ago) and the replacement. You only see it because debugging is on: that is why the course site always runs with WP_DEBUG (Lesson 1.2).
  6. What gives WordPress away (2m). "Every WordPress site announces itself." Ask for the response headers only: 
    curl -sI http://localhost:8080/ | grep -i '^link'
    Link: <http://localhost:8080/wp-json/>; rel="https://api.w.org/"
    The REST API's address in a header (Module 7). Learners try the Bonus Challenge on a site they admire at home; hiding these clues is not security (Lesson 2.3). Type exit to leave the container shell.
Three mistakes to expect, and how to coach each
  • "Just edit the file." A learner finds the line in core (or in Twenty Twenty-Five) that does what they want and changes it. Coach with the drawing and one question: "Who updates this folder?" If the answer is not "me", the change goes in a plugin or theme, on a hook. (Self-check Q1 and Q4.)
  • Thinking in pages, not in requests. "Where is the file for /about/?" Coach: "There is none. index.php answers, wp() finds the page in the database, the theme draws it." (Self-check Q5, the lesson's Exercise 2.)
  • Trusting an old tutorial. Classic-only code, get_currentuserinfo(), query_posts(), editing functions.php from the dashboard. Coach: "Which version was it written for? What does debug.log say when you run it?" (Mistake 2, the debug handout.)
Guided lab

File: learners copy labs/module-01/l1_1-wordpress-for-developers/core_tour_starter.sh into wordpress/ and run it in the WP-CLI container; your reference is labs/module-01/l1_1-wordpress-for-developers/core_tour_solution.sh. It practices the lesson's central picture on core itself: each TODO is one grep that finds the line that does a step of the trip, so learners leave knowing the trip is real code they can read.

  • Run it as shipped first (3m). On the projector, from the project folder: cp labs/module-01/l1_1-wordpress-for-developers/core_tour_starter.sh wordpress/ then docker compose run --rm wpcli sh core_tour_starter.sh. Step 1 prints its line (50: of wp-load.php); every other step prints TODO.
  • TODOs 2 to 5 in pairs (10m). Each is one grep (or a find and a count). Circulate for quoting: a pattern with ' inside needs double quotes around it, and do_action( 'init' ) has spaces inside the parentheses (core's coding standard, Lesson 1.3). TODO 4's plain grep template_include also finds a comment: ask what makes a pattern exact.
  • Expected (WordPress 7.1.3): must-use plugins at line 506 of wp-settings.php, plugins_loaded at 630, init at 779, 1059 PHP files in wp-includes (the lesson says "more than a thousand").
  • Debrief (2m): "Must-use plugins load at line 506, plugins after them, init at 779: what does that tell you about where a plugin can register a post type?" (On init or later: the lesson's Exercise 2.)
  • Fast finishers: labs/module-01/l1_1-wordpress-for-developers/wp_paths_starter.php (where code lives, asked of WordPress itself with constants and two functions), then labs/module-01/l1_1-wordpress-for-developers/debug_old_tutorial.php (three deprecated calls from an old tutorial, fixed one at a time).
Start the lesson project

The lesson project is Meet WordPress and Plan Pages & Co.: a test drive in WordPress Playground (Steps 1 and 2) and the plan the course builds from (Steps 3 and 4, pagesco-plan.txt). In the room, start the plan: it is the part that benefits from discussion (10 minutes).

  • Step 3: learners create pagesco-plan.txt in a course folder and copy the lesson's seven addresses, then add three of their own (a staff picks page? a gift card page?).
  • Step 4: the feature list, each feature marked content, theme or plugin with a reason. In the room: the first four of the lesson's eight required features. Use the lesson's test aloud: "What should happen if Pages & Co. switches to a different design next year?"
  • Done in the room = ten addresses and four features with a reason. Take two answers for "the store notice bar" from the room: theme or plugin? (The course puts it in a must-use plugin in Lesson 2.3, and the arguments for both are good.)
  • Goes home: Playground Steps 1 and 2 (their own dev site works for Step 2 too: the Code editor shows the same block markup) and the rest of Step 4. Keep the file: Lesson 5.1 asks for it again.
Checks for understanding

Ask these out loud during the demo and the lab (cold-call gently, or think-pair-share):

  • Which folder of the WordPress root is yours? Answer: wp-content/ (and your settings in wp-config.php); everything else is core.
  • In which order: init, the main query, the template? Answer: init (end of loading), then wp() runs the main query, then the template loader draws the page.
  • A client is on WordPress.com and wants your plugin. What do you ask first? Answer: which plan they are on: only some allow your own plugins.
  • Why does get_currentuserinfo() still work if it is deprecated? Answer: WordPress keeps old functions so old sites keep running; the message says what replaced it and since which version.

Workbook self-check, items Q1 to Q6 (learners do them at the end of the block or at home).

Answers: Q1 C) wp-includes/; Q2 <title>Pages &amp; Co.</title>; Q3 C) the init action fires, after plugins and the theme are loaded; Q4 D) Someone edited a core file: restore it and put the change in a plugin or theme, on a hook; Q5 B) index.php in the WordPress root; Q6 esc_html(). Full set with explanations in the Answer Key.

Differentiation

Support: learners whose machines are not ready do the lab with a ready neighbor (one keyboard, two heads, the NOT READY learner reads the core lines aloud and says what each does). For learners new to grep, write grep -n "text" file on the board and leave it there; Step 1 of the starter is the model.

Stretch: wp_paths_starter.php and debug_old_tutorial.php; then the lesson's Exercise 4 (read the front door yourself, including where wp() is defined) and the Bonus Challenge (spot WordPress on a site they admire).

1.2

Your Local Development Environment

80 min
Objectives (from the lesson page)
  • Install Docker and start the course's Docker Compose project: WordPress, MySQL, WP-CLI and Mailpit
  • Install WordPress from the command line with WP-CLI and use the wp shortcut for everyday tasks
  • Fix the Linux and WSL file-ownership problem so your editor can save into wp-content/
  • Find and read PHP errors on the page and in wp-content/debug.log, and catch WordPress email in Mailpit
  • Start, stop and reset the site safely, and know when wp-env or WordPress Playground is the better tool
Timing in the room
10mFrame: the food truck; four services; the bind mount; the wp shortcut
25mInstall clinic: the machines that were NOT READY, by platform
15mLive demo: versions, options, cron, debugging, a warning in the page and the log, Mailpit
15mGuided lab: site_report_starter.sh
15mStart the lesson project: the Dev Site Health Check, Steps 1 to 3
Mental model to say

Back to the board: "Installing a server stack on your laptop is building a restaurant kitchen into your home. Docker is a food truck parked next to the house: everything the kitchen needs comes with the truck, you can drive it away with docker compose down and park an identical one tomorrow. The one thing that stays in the house is your work: the wordpress/ folder, which the truck reaches through a window, the bind mount."

Then the four services in a row: wordpress (Apache and PHP 8.5, the site on port 8080), db (MySQL 9.7, its data in a volume), wpcli (WP-CLI, started only when you call it, removed afterwards), mailpit (a fake mail server with an inbox on port 8025). "Everyone in this room runs the same images, so your site behaves like the one every lesson was tested on."

Then the two habits that save the most time: "Every command runs in the project folder, and wp is a shortcut for docker compose run --rm wpcli wp. When something breaks, the answer is in wordpress/wp-content/debug.log." Triage line on the board: docker not found = install · daemon = start Docker · no configuration file = wrong folder · Permission denied = the Linux fix · critical error = debug.log.

Install clinic

Learners from the opening's NOT READY pile sit together by platform; ready learners pair with them as helpers. You move from table to table; each fix ends with check_environment.sh run again. Twenty-five minutes is enough to start Docker, fix an owner or a missing plugin, and to start a download, not to download a gigabyte on slow Wi-Fi: use the USB stick.

PlatformMost likely stateClinic fix (in this order)
Windows (WSL 2)Docker Desktop installed, Ubuntu cannot see it; or the project under /mnt/cWSL integration on for Ubuntu, a new Ubuntu terminal; the project in ~ inside WSL; then the Linux file-owner steps (WSL counts as Linux).
Windows (no WSL yet)wsl --install not run, or not restartedwsl --install in an administrator PowerShell, restart, create the Ubuntu user; finish Docker at home if the restart takes too long.
macOSDocker Desktop installed but not started; or the Intel build on Apple siliconStart it from Applications and wait for "running"; the right build for the chip. No file-owner steps on macOS.
Linuxdocker group not active; the distribution's old docker-composesudo usermod -aG docker "$USER" and log in again; Docker's own repository for Engine and the Compose plugin (docs.docker.com/engine/install).
Linux and WSL, started without the fixFiles owned by uid 33; VS Code cannot saveLesson 1.2's repair box: chown through a root wpcli container, the .env, compose.override.yaml, docker compose up -d.
Site up, not installedThe two install commands were skippedwp core install ... and wp rewrite structure '/%postname%/' exactly as in the lesson; then the Mailpit plugin copy.
Nothing installedSetup guide not doneStart the Docker install now (and docker load from the USB stick); pair for the rest of today; finish at home with the setup guide.

Done for each machine = check_environment.sh prints READY (or READY WITH NOTES). Anyone not done by 2:05 leaves with a numbered plan written in their workbook's Start Here box, and you check it at the start of Session 2.

Live demo (you type, they follow)

From the project folder on the projector, with the wp shortcut. The outputs below come from a fresh course site; on yours the time stamps differ and everything else matches.

  1. Which versions? (2m). "First question on any site: which WordPress, which PHP?" From the project folder, with the wp shortcut: 
    wp core version --extra
wp eval 'echo "PHP ", PHP_VERSION, "\n";'
    WordPress version: 7.1.3
Database revision: 61833
TinyMCE version:   4.9110 (49110-20250317)
Package language:  en_US
PHP 8.5.12
    WordPress 7.1.3 on PHP 8.5.12: the versions every output in the course was made with. On PHP 8.4 the last line says 8.4 and the lessons say where that matters.
  2. Options, and an escaped title (2m). "Settings live in the options table. Read three." 
    wp option get siteurl
wp option get blogname
wp option get permalink_structure
    http://localhost:8080
Pages &amp; Co.
/%postname%/
    Stop on Pages &amp; Co.: WordPress stored the title HTML-escaped. Ask: "where would that bite you?" (comparing strings, the subject line of an email).
  3. WordPress can call itself (1m). "The reason for the port-8080 setup, tested in one command." 
    wp cron test
    Success: WP-Cron spawning is working as expected.
  4. Debugging is on (2m). "Where do these come from?" The WORDPRESS_* lines of compose.yaml, read by wp-config.php. 
    wp eval 'var_dump( WP_DEBUG, WP_DEBUG_LOG, WP_DEBUG_DISPLAY, SCRIPT_DEBUG, wp_get_environment_type() );'
    bool(true)
bool(true)
bool(true)
bool(true)
string(5) "local"
    Open wordpress/wp-config.php in VS Code for ten seconds and point at the getenv_docker() lines (the workbook's worked example shows them).
  5. A warning in the page and in the log (5m). "A real mistake, caught twice." Create the must-use plugins folder in the container shell, save the lesson's buggy demo in VS Code as wordpress/wp-content/mu-plugins/pagesco-debug-demo.php, reload the home page. Have learners tail the log in a second terminal: tail -f wordpress/wp-content/debug.log. 
    <?php
/**
 * Plugin Name: Pages & Co. Debug Demo
 * Description: Lesson 1.2 demo: a deliberate bug in the page footer.
 */

function pagesco_debug_demo_footer() {
	echo '<p class="pagesco-demo">Hello, ' . $pagesco_name . '!</p>';
}
add_action( 'wp_footer', 'pagesco_debug_demo_footer' );
    The new line in debug.log (the time stamp is the time of your reload): 
    [26-Oct-2026 11:58:58 UTC] PHP Warning:  Undefined variable $pagesco_name in /var/www/html/wp-content/mu-plugins/pagesco-debug-demo.php on line 8
    And in the page itself, just above the footer greeting (here with curl from the container): 
    curl -s http://localhost:8080/ | grep -o 'Warning: [^<]*\|<p class="pagesco-demo">[^<]*</p>'
    Warning: Undefined variable $pagesco_name in /var/www/html/wp-content/mu-plugins/pagesco-debug-demo.php on line 8
<p class="pagesco-demo">Hello, !</p>
    Read it from the left: level, message, file inside the container (/var/www/html/... is your wordpress/...), line. Fix it with the lesson's second version (a value, and esc_html()), reload: 
    <p class="pagesco-demo">Hello, reader!</p>
    Delete the demo file (rm wp-content/mu-plugins/pagesco-debug-demo.php): real must-use plugins start in Lesson 2.3.
  6. Email that never leaves the laptop (3m). "WordPress sends email all the time; on a development site, Mailpit catches it." Show the must-use plugin, send one message, open http://localhost:8025. 
    wp plugin list --status=must-use
wp eval 'var_dump( wp_mail( "admin@example.com", "Hello from Pages & Co.", "If you can read this in Mailpit, email works." ) );'
    +--------------+----------+--------+---------+----------------+-------------+
| name         | status   | update | version | update_version | auto_update |
+--------------+----------+--------+---------+----------------+-------------+
| mailpit-smtp | must-use |        |         |                | off         |
+--------------+----------+--------+---------+----------------+-------------+
bool(true)
    Then open the message in Mailpit's inbox. What Mailpit caught: 
    From: WordPress <wordpress@example.com>
To: admin@example.com
Subject: Hello from Pages & Co.

If you can read this in Mailpit, email works.
Three mistakes to expect, and how to coach each
  • Typing commands in the wrong folder. no configuration file provided, or a wp eval-file that cannot find a file. Coach: "Where is compose.yaml? And wp eval-file x.php means wordpress/x.php: where did you save it?" (Self-check Q10.)
  • Reaching for sudo or chmod 777 on Linux and WSL when the editor cannot save. Coach: "Who owns the files? ls -ln wordpress. The fix is to run the containers as you, once." (Lesson quiz Q2.)
  • Ignoring the log. "The page is blank" or "There has been a critical error" with debug.log never opened. Coach: "What does the last line of debug.log say? Read it from the left." Make tail -f wordpress/wp-content/debug.log in a second terminal a habit from today.
Guided lab

File: labs/module-01/l1_2-local-environment/site_report_starter.sh; your reference is labs/module-01/l1_2-local-environment/site_report_solution.sh. It practices WP-CLI on the learner's own site: each TODO is one wp command (read an option, list a theme or plugin with --status and --field, list pages as a table), with wp help as the reference. A script in the container needs no shortcut: wp is installed there.

  • Run it as shipped (3m). cp labs/module-01/l1_2-local-environment/site_report_starter.sh wordpress/ then docker compose run --rm wpcli sh site_report_starter.sh: the WordPress line works, the rest say TODO.
  • TODOs 1 to 5 in pairs (9m). Encourage trying each command alone first (wp option get admin_email), then putting it in the script. Circulate for --status=active spelled --active (WP-CLI says which options exist), and for TODO 5 without --orderby=ID --order=asc (the two install pages share a date, so the order is not guaranteed).
  • Expected when done (a fresh course site):
== Pages & Co. site report ==
WordPress: 7.1.3
Title: Pages &amp; Co.
Admin email: wordpress@example.com
Active theme: twentytwentyfive
Inactive plugins:
akismet
hello
Pages:
+----+----------------+-------------+
| ID | post_title     | post_status |
+----+----------------+-------------+
| 2  | Sample Page    | publish     |
| 3  | Privacy Policy | draft       |
+----+----------------+-------------+
  • Debrief (3m): "Why does the title say &amp;?" (stored escaped, the demo). "Which of these could you have done in the admin, and which not?" (All could, but none in one second, and none from a script you can rerun on any site.)
  • Fast finishers: the folder lab labs/module-01/l1_2-local-environment/store_hours_starter/ (a must-use plugin like the debug demo: Saturday's hours in the footer and one line in debug.log; copy pagesco-hours.php into wordpress/wp-content/mu-plugins/, test with labs/module-01/l1_2-local-environment/test_store_hours.sh), then labs/module-01/l1_2-local-environment/debug_health_check.php (two loud bugs and a silent one).
Start the lesson project

The lesson project is the Dev Site Health Check: a PHP script that WP-CLI runs with WordPress loaded and that checks every piece the lesson set up. In the room: Steps 1 to 3 (15 minutes); the environment check already did most of Step 1.

  • Step 1: docker compose ps, the site, the admin login, Mailpit, wp core version in a new terminal (two minutes after the check).
  • Step 2: type wordpress/pagesco-check.php from the lesson (ten minutes). Type, do not paste: every line is PHP they know plus one WordPress function explained in its comment.
  • Step 3: wp eval-file pagesco-check.php until all nine lines say OK, then find the health-check email in Mailpit.
  • Done in the room = "All checks passed." on the screen. Goes home: Step 4 (stop Mailpit, watch one check fail, start it again, delete the script) and the checklist.
Checks for understanding

Ask these out loud during the clinic, the demo and the lab:

  • Where does wp option get blogname actually run? Answer: in a new wpcli container that is removed when the command ends (Lesson quiz Q1).
  • Your posts after docker compose down and up -d? And after down -v? Answer: still there; gone (the volume holds the database).
  • A page shows "There has been a critical error on this website." First move? Answer: read the end of wordpress/wp-content/debug.log.
  • Why is there a Mailpit at all? Answer: so test email from a development site never reaches real people; the mu-plugin sends it there, and fixes the sender address WordPress would build from localhost.

Workbook self-check, items Q7 to Q12 (learners do them at the end of the block or at home).

Answers: Q7 C) docker compose down -v; Q8 Pages &amp; Co.; Q9 B) wordpress/wp-content/mu-plugins/pagesco-debug-demo.php in your project folder; Q10 A) You are not in the project folder: Docker Compose found no compose.yaml here or above; Q11 D) WordPress calls its own address, http://localhost:8080, from inside the container (WP-Cron, Site Health), and that must reach Apache; Q12 local: for example, Mailpit's mu-plugin only reroutes email when the environment is local; application passwords work over plain HTTP; WordPress 7.1 turns pings off. Full set with explanations in the Answer Key.

Differentiation

Support: learners who spent the clinic installing do the lab at home with the README's expected output; for anyone overwhelmed by containers, one card with three lines: cd ~/pagesco-dev, wp ... for WordPress commands, docker compose run --rm wpcli sh for a shell with ls, grep and curl.

Stretch: the store-hours folder lab and debug_health_check.php; the lesson's Exercise 3 (the wplog and wpclean shortcuts) and Exercise 4 (wp-env alongside, with the right package name); the Bonus Challenge (Site Health against what they configured).

Closing

Exit ticket (3 questions, no notes, 4 minutes)

Put the three questions on the slide. Learners answer in the workbook's Exit Ticket box or on a sticky note and leave it on the way out. Sort the notes into "got it" and "not yet" before Session 2: question 1's pile tells you how much of Session 2's warm-up goes back to "core is not yours".

  1. Where does your own code go in WordPress, and why never in core? Answer: in wp-content/: your theme, your plugin, a must-use plugin; core files are replaced by every update (and an edited core file looks like a hack).
  2. Name the four services of the course project and the job of each. Answer: wordpress (Apache + PHP, the site on 8080), db (MySQL, data in a volume), wpcli (WP-CLI on demand), mailpit (catches email, inbox on 8025).
  3. A page says "There has been a critical error on this website." Where do you look first, and with which command? Answer: wordpress/wp-content/debug.log, for example tail -n 20 wordpress/wp-content/debug.log (or tail -f while you reload).
Homework (about 2 to 3 hours)
  • Finish both lesson projects. The Pages & Co. plan (Playground Steps 1 and 2, the rest of the feature list) and the health check Step 4 (break it, read it, clean up: mu-plugins/ holds only mailpit-smtp.php afterwards).
  • Lesson exercises. 1.1: Exercises 1 to 3 (theme, plugin or content; follow /books/dune/; choose the hosting); Exercise 4 is a stretch. 1.2: Exercises 1 to 3 (a restart, your MySQL skills with wp db query, the wplog shortcut); Exercise 4 (wp-env) is a stretch.
  • Both Quick Quizzes on the lesson pages (five questions each; answers are in the Answer Key).
  • Journal: both entries. The 1.2 prompt asks for a cheat card of the development site; it is the page learners will open most in the next weeks.
  • Before the Next Lesson (from 1.2): the health check passes and wp works in a brand-new terminal; mailpit-smtp.php stays in mu-plugins/; docker compose stop at the end of a session, up -d at the start.
  • If the environment check was not READY: follow the numbered plan from the clinic, run the check again and email you its last line.
  • Optional: labs/module-01/l1_0-orientation/diagnostic_starter.php for anyone who missed two or more diagnostic questions; wp_paths_starter.php, the store-hours lab and debug_health_check.php for anyone who did not reach them.
Bring list for Session 2
  • A laptop on which check_environment.sh ends with READY (or READY WITH NOTES), and VS Code with a PHP extension.
  • The project folder with the labs/ folder in it. Session 2 (Lessons 1.3 and 2.1) installs a translation and runs Composer from the composer:2 image: run docker pull composer:2 at home, on a good connection.
  • pagesco-plan.txt, the journal, and the workbook.

If You Run Long or Short

Running long: what to protect and what to cut first
  • Protect: the check result for every learner; the install clinic; the 1.1 demo through Mistake 1; the 1.2 debug demo.
  • Cut first (saves 4m): the 1.1 demo's Link header and the 1.2 Mailpit step (the health check shows Mailpit at home).
  • Cut second (saves 10m): the 1.1 project start. Show the lesson's site map, send Steps 1 to 4 home.
  • Cut third (saves 15m): the 1.2 project start: learners type the health check at home; the demo already showed every piece it checks.
Running short: what to add
  • Run debug_old_tutorial.php for everyone and fix it together, one call per volunteer, reading the replacement from each message.
  • Lesson 1.2's Exercise 2 live: wp db query "SHOW TABLES" and a SELECT on wp_posts. Ask who can predict the table prefix and which page is a draft.
  • Start the 1.1 Bonus Challenge together on a real site: View Source, /wp-content/ paths, the generator tag, /wp-json/.
Instructor Kit · Facilitator Guide

Session 2: PHP the WordPress Way and the Content Model

How to teach the session where learners start writing WordPress code and stock the site with content: the house rules of WordPress PHP (coding standards checked by PHPCS, prefixes, sanitize early and escape late, translatable strings, callbacks, arrays of arguments, WP_Error), then the content model seen from WP-CLI and PHP, ending with the Pages & Co. staff, pages and News posts that every later lesson starts from.

2 lessons 3 hrs session Lessons 1.3–2.1 Session 2 of 18 · Part 1

How to Use This Guide

  • Same rhythm for both lessons: frame (the goal and one mental model) → live demo (you type, they type along) → guided lab (a kit lab, new practice on the lesson's ideas) → start the lesson's own project. The lesson exercises, quiz and journal are homework.
  • Type, do not paste (the block-markup files of the 2.1 project are the one exception: learners copy them from the lesson page). Every command below was run to produce the output printed under it, on WordPress 7.1.3, PHP 8.5, MySQL 9.7 and WP-CLI 2.12: a fresh course site, exactly what a learner has at the end of Session 1. Ask for a prediction before every run.
  • The lessons are the reference. Keep lesson_03.html and lesson_04.html open in browser tabs for the bridge table, the WPCS rules table, the escaping table and the Settings-to-options table. Labs live in labs/module-02/ (learners keep the folder in their project folder): _starter files are handouts, _solution files are yours.
  • Session 2 is where the course site starts to hold real content. Lesson 1.3 leaves the site as it found it; Lesson 2.1's project creates the staff accounts, pages and News posts that every later lesson starts from, with fixed IDs (users 2 and 3, pages 12 to 14, posts 15 to 17). Protect that project's start above everything else in the session.
  • Part 1, "Themes" (Sessions 1 to 8), can run on its own; nothing here depends on Part 2. Teal blocks are hands-on, amber blocks are watch-outs.
The #1 risk of Session 2: the IDs drift

Lesson 2.1's project prints IDs 12 to 17 because every earlier block of the lesson used one up: attachment 5, the revision demo's post 6 and its revisions 7 and 8, the Gift Cards draft 9, the duplicate Sample Page 10 and its trash revision 11. A learner who watched the demo instead of typing it along gets pages 5 to 7 and posts 8 to 10, and every later lesson that names an ID (2.2 adds meta to post 15, Session 3's site check lists 12 to 17) stops matching. So: in the 2.1 demo everybody types along, and before the project every machine runs the next-ID check below. It must print 12. If it prints less, the catch-up line uses up the missing IDs on drafts it deletes again. Run the check AFTER the guided lab: the lab only reads.

Before the Session

  • ☐ Read Session 1's exit tickets and the list of NOT READY machines: anyone who is still not ready pairs with a neighbor today and gets the install clinic's plan checked in the warm-up.
  • ☐ Network: Lesson 1.3 downloads the WordPress coding standards with Composer (the composer:2 image, about 70 MB once, which Session 1's bring list asked learners to pull at home, and about 3 MB of packages) and a Spanish translation (about 1 MB). Test the venue Wi-Fi with both the day before. Without it: show the lesson's output cards for the PHPCS and es_ES steps, and PHPCS moves to homework.
  • ☐ Files to hand out: the labs/ folder without the *_solution.* files (learners who copied the whole folder in Session 1 already have it); the workbook.
  • ☐ Run the kit check once: python3 labs/check_labs.py module-02 from this kit's folder (every line PASS; 10 results in about a minute). With your own course project at the end of Session 1: WP_LABS_COMPOSE=~/pagesco-dev python3 labs/check_labs.py module-02.
  • ☐ Projector machine: the course site exactly as Session 1 left it (only mailpit-smtp.php in mu-plugins, no content beyond the install: run the warm-up's site check), the composer:2 image pulled, VS Code on pagesco-dev at a large font, two terminals in the project folder (one for commands, one for tail -f wordpress/wp-content/debug.log), lesson_03.html and lesson_04.html in tabs, http://localhost:8080/wp-admin/ logged in as admin.
  • ☐ Board, before learners arrive: the escaping table (text → esc_html(), attribute → esc_attr(), href/src → esc_url(), post HTML → wp_kses_post()); "sanitize early, escape late"; the next-ID check command; a box labeled one filing cabinet: wp_posts.
Known traps today
SymptomCauseFix
Composer shell: Permission denied writing composer.json (Linux, WSL)The practice folder was created by a container (root) or --user was left outmkdir wordpress/pagesco-practice as yourself first, then the lesson's docker run --rm -it --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" ... line exactly.
PowerShell: docker run ... $PWD/wordpress mounts nothingPowerShell writes the variable differentlyLesson 1.3's note: leave --user out and write ${PWD}; better, use the Ubuntu terminal like every other command.
Cannot create cache directory /composer-cache/...Composer's cache is not writable for your user in the containerHarmless: Composer proceeds without a cache.
vendor/bin/phpcs: not foundPHPCS runs outside the Composer shell, or in the wrong folderIn the Composer shell, in /var/www/html/pagesco-practice (the prompt shows it).
wp eval-file pagesco-practice/escape.php: Error: 'pagesco-practice/escape.php' does not exist.The file was saved in the project folder, not in wordpress/pagesco-practice/Save it in VS Code under wordpress/pagesco-practice/; wp runs in the WordPress root.
The es_ES install hangs or failsNo internet or translate.wordpress.org blockedShow the lesson's output card; nothing later depends on it (the language is uninstalled again).
Project 2.1: Error: Invalid category 'news' or the posts land in UncategorizedStep 3's wp term create category News --slug=news skippedCreate the term, then wp post term set <ID> category news for each post (or delete and recreate the posts).
Project 2.1: About Us is page 5 (or 8), not 12The learner did not type along the 2.1 demoDelete the new content (wp post delete <IDs> --force, wp user delete maria devon --yes... and recreate after the catch-up line). Better: run the next-ID check before Step 2.
wp post create pagesco-content/about.html: Error: Unable to read content from 'pagesco-content/about.html'The folder is in the project folder, not in wordpress/mkdir wordpress/pagesco-content; the files go there.

In the room. The lesson pages estimate 130 + 120 = 250 minutes for a learner working alone; after the warm-up, the break and the wrap-up the room has 150 (70 for 1.3, 80 for 2.1). Lesson 1.3 keeps model, demo and lab; its project starts with Step 1 (typing the helper is where the habits meet). Lesson 2.1's demo runs the lesson's blocks in order, typed along, and its project gets the longest segment of the day because Session 3 starts from it. Not in the room: 1.3's i18n.php, args.php, price.php and globals.php examples and its Common Mistakes 1, 2 and 4 (the escape.php demo covers 1; 2 and 4 take the whole site down and are best read with the lesson's output cards); the strict-types box and the FAQ; 2.1's image sizes and srcset (wp_get_attachment_metadata, wp_get_attachment_image), the roles table, the user meta behind roles, Mistakes 3 and 4 (a role checked instead of a capability: self-check Q9 and the debug handout; HTML without block comments) and the version note.

Goes home (about 2 to 3 hours). 1.3: project Steps 2 to 4 (render three books, the break test, PHPCS until it is silent, then delete the practice folder); 2.1: project Step 4 (Maria's edit and its revision, Devon refused, rm -r pagesco-content, the final list); each lesson's Hands-on Exercises; both Quick Quizzes; both journal entries; both "Before the Next Lesson" lists.

Protect, in this order: the 2.1 project Steps 1 to 3 on every machine, with the right IDs; the 2.1 demo's ID-using steps (the attachment, the revisions, the two mistakes); the 1.3 PHPCS and escaping steps; the 1.3 guided lab. Retrieval questions and answers
  1. Which folder of the WordPress root is yours, and why is nothing else? Answer: wp-content/ (themes, plugins, mu-plugins, uploads), plus your settings in wp-config.php. Everything else is core and every update replaces it.
  2. Put them in order: the main query, init, the template. Answer: init (the end of loading: core, mu-plugins, plugins, the theme), then wp() runs the main query, then the template loader draws the page: load, query, template.
  3. docker compose down and docker compose down -v: what survives each? Answer: down keeps the files and the database (the volume); -v deletes the database volume too.
  4. A page says "There has been a critical error on this website." Where do you look first? Answer: The end of wordpress/wp-content/debug.log (tail -n 20 wordpress/wp-content/debug.log, or tail -f while reloading).
  5. What does wp option get blogname print on the course site, and why? Answer: Pages &amp; Co.: WordPress stored the title HTML-escaped when it was saved. Today's first lesson explains when to escape yourself.

Lesson Plans

1.3

PHP the WordPress Way

70 min
Objectives (from the lesson page)
  • Write PHP that follows the WordPress coding standards, and check it with PHPCS and the WordPress ruleset
  • Choose the right escaping function for each output context (esc_html, esc_attr, esc_url, wp_kses_post) and the right sanitizing function for each input
  • Make strings translatable with __(), esc_html__(), _n() and sprintf(), with a text domain and translator comments
  • Pass callbacks in every form WordPress accepts, and write functions that take an array of arguments merged with wp_parse_args()
  • Handle WP_Error results, and use core's globals ($wpdb, $post, $wp_query) and classes without fighting them
Timing in the room
10mFrame: the shared house; the bridge table; core on PHP 7.4, your code above its own minimum
25mLive demo: PHPCS before and after, escaping per context, slashes, core in Spanish, callbacks, WP_Error, the silent _e()
20mGuided lab: signup_form_starter.php in pairs
15mStart the lesson project: the Book Card Helper, Step 1
Mental model to say

"In PHP Foundations your code was the whole application. In WordPress it is a guest. Moving from your own apartment into a shared house: you label your food (prefixes), you use the shared kitchen tools the way everyone does (core's functions instead of your own helpers), you leave notes others can read (coding standards and DocBlocks), and you do not rearrange the living room (globals). None of the rules is hard. Ignoring them is what causes the fights."

Then the lesson's bridge table, four rows on the board: htmlspecialchars() → esc_html() and friends · filter_input() → wp_unslash() + sanitize_*() · exceptions → WP_Error · PDO → $wpdb. And one sentence on versions: "WordPress 7.1 still runs on PHP 7.4, so core looks old-fashioned. Your plugin declares its own minimum (Lesson 5.1) and may use modern PHP above it. You are learning conventions, not going back in time."

Live demo (you type, they follow)

From the project folder on the projector, with the wp shortcut; the Composer shell is a second terminal. Files are saved in VS Code under wordpress/pagesco-practice/, exactly as the lesson names them (the lesson page has each one).

    Read three lines from the left: line, ERROR or WARNING, [x] when phpcbf can fix it. 20 errors and 1 warning, 16 of them mechanical. Stop on line 8: "All output should be run through an escaping function". PHPCS just found a cross-site scripting hole. That is the real reason professionals run it. Then the WordPress version: 
    vendor/bin/phpcs --standard=WordPress style-after.php && echo "No problems found."
    No problems found.
    Show style-after.php side by side for one minute: tabs, spaces inside parentheses, the Yoda condition, single quotes, the DocBlocks, esc_html() at the echo, and the one // phpcs:ignore with a reason. Learners type exit to leave the Composer shell; keep it in the terminal history for the project's Step 4.
  2. One value, four contexts (4m). "Escape late, for the exact place the value goes." Save the lesson's escape.php in the practice folder and run it from the project folder: 
    wp eval-file pagesco-practice/escape.php
    esc_html:    Dune &lt;script&gt;alert(&quot;hi&quot;)&lt;/script&gt; &amp; &quot;Friends&quot;
esc_attr:    Pages &amp; Co. &quot;staff pick&quot;
esc_url:     https://example.com/search?q=dune&#038;page=2
esc_url:     (empty)
wp_kses_post: <p>A <strong>classic</strong>alert(1) <a href="https://example.com">link</a></p>
twice:       Pages &amp; Co.
    Line by line: text between tags (esc_html()), an attribute (esc_attr()), a URL whose & becomes &#038; and whose javascript: disappears (esc_url()), user HTML kept but defanged (wp_kses_post()), and the kindness on the last line: no double-encoding.
  3. WordPress adds slashes to your input (3m). "One surprise for PHP developers." Save the lesson's pagesco-slashes.php in wordpress/wp-content/mu-plugins/, open the address in the browser (View Source, search for pagesco-q), or with curl in the container: 
    curl -s 'http://localhost:8080/?pagesco_q=O%27Reilly%20%3Cb%3Ebooks%3C%2Fb%3E' | grep -o '<p class="pagesco-q">.*</p>'
    <p class="pagesco-q">raw: O\&#039;Reilly &lt;b&gt;books&lt;/b&gt; | clean: O&#039;Reilly books</p>
    Raw: O\'Reilly (the backslash from wp_magic_quotes(), the quote escaped for printing). Clean: unslashed, then sanitized: quote kept, tags gone. "Save a raw value and every apostrophe in your database grows a backslash." Delete the demo: rm wp-content/mu-plugins/pagesco-slashes.php in the container.
  4. Core speaks Spanish (3m). "Every visible string goes through a translation function." Install Spanish, ask core for two of its strings, uninstall again (it needs the internet; if the venue blocks it, show the lesson's output card): 
    wp language core install es_ES
wp eval 'switch_to_locale( "es_ES" ); echo __( "Posts" ), " / ", _n( "%s comment", "%s comments", 3 ), "\n"; restore_previous_locale(); echo __( "Posts" ), "\n";'
wp language core uninstall es_ES

    __( 'Posts' ) found "Entradas" in Spanish and returns the English string otherwise. Your theme adds a text domain, its folder slug: pagesco. On the board: __() returns, _e() echoes, esc_html__() is the everyday choice, _n() for plurals, sprintf() with a translators comment for variables.
  5. Seven shapes of a callback (3m). "WordPress asks for callbacks everywhere: every hook, shortcode, REST route." Save callbacks.php from the lesson and run it: 
    wp eval-file pagesco-practice/callbacks.php
    function name   DUNE!
closure         Dune
arrow function  enud
object method   dune (staff pick)
static method   "dune"
static, string  "dune"
first-class     DUNE!
    Point at the column of names. Ask: "which of these can another plugin unhook later?" (The named function and the methods; never the closure or the arrow function: Lesson 2.3.)
  6. Errors come back as values (3m). "Core predates exceptions." Save errors.php and run it: 
    wp eval-file pagesco-practice/errors.php
    Code:    existing_user_login
Message: Sorry, that username already exists!
int(0)
Content, title, and excerpt are empty.
    wp_insert_user() returns a WP_Error; wp_insert_post() returns 0 unless you pass true. "Read the Return line of the Code Reference before you trust a result." Nothing was created: both calls failed before the database.
  7. Mistake 3: _e() in an expression (silent) (2m). "One last trap, and it makes no noise." Save mistake-e.php and run it: 
    wp eval-file pagesco-practice/mistake-e.php
    New arrivals
<h2></h2>
New arrivalsNULL
    The text printed before the heading was even built, and the heading is empty. _e echoes, the others return. Leave the practice folder in place: the project uses it (and its PHPCS) next; Mistakes 2 and 4 (a name already taken, strict types) take the whole site down and go home, with the lesson's output cards.
Three mistakes to expect, and how to coach each
  • The wrong escaper, or one for everything. esc_html() around an href, or esc_attr() everywhere. Coach with the board's table and one question: "Where does this value land: between tags, in an attribute, in a URL?" (Self-check Q1, lesson quiz Q1, the guided lab's TODOs 6 and 7.)
  • Sanitizing on output, escaping on input. $nick = esc_html( $_POST['nickname'] ). Coach: "Sanitize is for the way in, escape for the way out; the database should hold the clean value, not HTML entities." (Lesson quiz Q5.)
  • Forgetting wp_unslash(). The apostrophe in O'Neil grows a backslash. Coach: "WordPress added it on the way in; take it off before you clean." (The slashes demo, the guided lab's TODO 1.)
Guided lab

File: learners copy labs/module-02/l1_3-php-the-wordpress-way/signup_form_starter.php into wordpress/ and run it with wp eval-file --use-include signup_form_starter.php; your reference is labs/module-02/l1_3-php-the-wordpress-way/signup_form_solution.php. It practices both halves of the rule on data nobody has seen: a book club sign-up with the backslashes WordPress adds, a name with tags, a shouting email address, a negative seat count, a shelf that is not on the list, and a javascript: website.

  • Run it as shipped (2m). Every value prints TODO, and the two HTML lines show where escaping is missing.
  • TODOs 1 to 4 in pairs (10m): sanitize early. Circulate for wp_unslash() missing (the name keeps O\'Neil), and for TODO 4 written as a sanitize call: the shelf must be VALIDATED against the three allowed values with in_array( ..., true ).
  • TODOs 5 to 7 (5m): escape late. esc_attr() in the value attribute, esc_url() around the unslashed website (it comes back empty), esc_html() for the link text.
  • Expected when done:
name:  string(18) "Siobhan O'Neil VIP"
email: Siobhan.ONeil@Example.COM (valid: yes)
seats: 3
shelf: fiction
field: <input name="name" value="Siobhan O&#039;Neil VIP">
link:  <a href="">Siobhan O&#039;Neil VIP</a>
  • Debrief (3m): "Why did the name keep VIP?" (sanitize_text_field() strips the tags, not the text between them.) "Seats: -3 became 3. Is that right?" (No: absint() flips the sign; a real form should REJECT a negative, the lesson's point about validating.) "Why is the href empty?" (esc_url() drops a javascript: URL.)
  • Fast finishers: labs/module-02/l1_3-php-the-wordpress-way/event_line_starter.php (an events list with an array of arguments, _n() and sprintf() with translator comments, a sort callback and a WP_Error), then labs/module-02/l1_3-php-the-wordpress-way/debug_book_badge.php (two loud bugs and a silent one in a badge helper).
Start the lesson project

The lesson project is The Book Card Helper: pagesco_book_card( $book, $args ) in wordpress/pagesco-practice/book-card.php, using every habit of the lesson, with a clean PHPCS report at the end. In the room: Step 1 (15 minutes).

  • Step 1: type book-card.php from the lesson, reading each comment aloud with a neighbor: it names the rule the line follows (the DocBlock with @type keys, wp_parse_args(), the heading level validated, esc_attr() / esc_url() / esc_html(), __() and _n() with translators comments).
  • If there is time: Step 2's render-cards.php and wp eval-file pagesco-practice/render-cards.php. Three cards, "1,178 pages".
  • Done in the room = book-card.php saved and loading without a message (Step 2 prints three cards when it runs). Goes home: Steps 2 to 4: the break test (a javascript: link, quotes in the class, a heading level of 99), PHPCS until "no coding standards problems", then rm -r pagesco-practice and ls wp-content/mu-plugins (only mailpit-smtp.php). Keep a copy of book-card.php in the course notes: Lesson 6.2 compares it with a block, and Session 3's warm-up asks whether it passed PHPCS.
Checks for understanding

Ask these out loud during the demo and the lab (cold-call gently, or think-pair-share):

  • Which escaper for a link's href, for its title attribute, and for its text? Answer: esc_url(), esc_attr(), esc_html().
  • Why does every function in the course theme start with pagesco_? Answer: one global namespace per request, shared by core and every plugin; two functions with one name are a fatal error.
  • What do __() and _e() do differently? Answer: __() returns the translation, _e() echoes it (and returns null).
  • A WordPress function failed. Exception, false, or something else? Answer: usually a WP_Error (check with is_wp_error()); some return 0 or false unless you ask for the error: read the Return line.

Workbook self-check, items Q1 to Q6 (learners do them at the end of the block or at home).

Answers: Q1 B) esc_attr(); Q2 Tom &amp; Jerry; Q3 C) "Staff picks" first, then an empty <h2></h2>; Q4 A) A class inside the namespace PagesCo\Books, such as PagesCo\Books\Plugin; Q5 

int(7)
string(10) "staffpicks"
; Q6 D) 0: pass true as the second argument to get a WP_Error with the message. Full set with explanations in the Answer Key.

Differentiation

Support: learners who are slow in the Composer shell watch the PHPCS step on the projector and set it up at home (the project's Step 4 needs it). For the lab, a card with the four sanitizers and the four escapers, each with one example input and output, from the demo.

Stretch: event_line_starter.php and debug_book_badge.php; the lesson's Exercise 1 (make PHPCS happy with phpcbf), Exercise 4 (wp_list_filter() and friends) and the Bonus Challenge (PHPCS on Hello Dolly and Twenty Twenty-Five, with the three rule sets).

2.1

The Content Model

80 min
Objectives (from the lesson page)
  • Explain why posts, pages, media, revisions, templates and navigation menus are all posts with a different post_type, and read a WP_Post object
  • Choose between posts and pages, use post statuses, and organize content with categories, tags and terms
  • Describe how roles, capabilities and users fit together, and check capabilities rather than roles in code
  • Find the option behind a Settings screen, and read the block markup the editor stores in post_content with parse_blocks()
  • Create users, pages and posts from the command line, with authors, categories, dates and revisions
Timing in the room
10mFrame: one filing cabinet; posts and pages; terms; roles and capabilities; options; block markup
20mLive demo: the lesson's blocks in order, typed along, then the next-ID check
15mGuided lab: content_census_starter.sh
35mStart the lesson project: Stock the Pages & Co. site, Steps 1 to 3
Mental model to say

Draw a filing cabinet with one drawer labeled wp_posts: "Every document goes into the same kind of folder with the same fields: title, content, author, date, status. A colored label says what it is: blog post, page, image, old version, template, menu. Code that works on 'a folder' (saving, revisions, permissions, the REST API) works on every label at once. That is why a custom post type, Lesson 5.2's book, gets all of it for free."

Then the rest of the picture around the cabinet: terms (colored tabs: categories, tags, later genre), users (who may open which drawer: roles are bundles of capabilities, and code checks the capability), options (the settings on the wall: every Settings field is one), and block markup (what is written on the paper: HTML wrapped in comments). "Every feature you meet later, in core or in a plugin, is one of these in disguise."

Live demo (you type, they follow)

The lesson's own commands, in the lesson's order, from the project folder with the wp shortcut. Everyone types along: the attachment, the revision demo and the two mistakes each use up post IDs that the project's IDs (12 to 17) count on. Keep the commands on the projector for the slow typists; skip nothing that creates a post.

  1. Sixteen types, one table (2m). "Everything in the admin is a post with a label." Everyone types along from here on, in the project folder: the lesson's IDs depend on it (the box below). 
    wp post-type list --fields=name,label,hierarchical,public
    +---------------------+-----------------------+--------------+--------+
| name                | label                 | hierarchical | public |
+---------------------+-----------------------+--------------+--------+
| post                | Posts                 |              | 1      |
| page                | Pages                 | 1            | 1      |
| attachment          | Media                 |              | 1      |
| revision            | Revisions             |              |        |
| nav_menu_item       | Navigation Menu Items |              |        |
| custom_css          | Custom CSS            |              |        |
| customize_changeset | Changesets            |              |        |
| oembed_cache        | oEmbed Responses      |              |        |
| user_request        | User Requests         |              |        |
| wp_block            | Patterns              |              |        |
| wp_template         | Templates             |              |        |
| wp_template_part    | Template Parts        |              |        |
| wp_global_styles    | Global Styles         |              |        |
| wp_navigation       | Navigation Menus      |              |        |
| wp_font_family      | Font Families         |              |        |
| wp_font_face        | Font Faces            |              |        |
+---------------------+-----------------------+--------------+--------+
    16 types; five of them are what an editor calls content. Point at wp_template, wp_navigation and wp_global_styles: "block themes keep their templates, menus and styles in this same table. Module 3 lives here."
  2. A post as PHP sees it (2m). "One row, one WP_Post object." 
    wp post get 1 --fields=ID,post_type,post_status,post_name,post_title,post_author,post_parent,comment_status
    +----------------+--------------+
| Field          | Value        |
+----------------+--------------+
| ID             | 1            |
| post_author    | 1            |
| post_title     | Hello world! |
| post_status    | publish      |
| comment_status | open         |
| post_name      | hello-world  |
| post_parent    | 0            |
| post_type      | post         |
+----------------+--------------+
    post_name is the slug, post_author a user ID, post_parent a post ID. A book's price will NOT be a column: it goes to post meta (Lessons 2.2 and 5.2).
  3. Posts, pages and statuses (2m). "Two tools, two defaults." 
    wp post list --post_type=page --orderby=ID --order=ASC --fields=ID,post_title,post_name,post_status
wp eval 'foreach ( get_posts( array( "post_type" => "page" ) ) as $page ) { echo $page->ID, " ", $page->post_title, " ", $page->post_status, "\n"; }'
    +----+----------------+----------------+-------------+
| ID | post_title     | post_name      | post_status |
+----+----------------+----------------+-------------+
| 2  | Sample Page    | sample-page    | publish     |
| 3  | Privacy Policy | privacy-policy | draft       |
+----+----------------+----------------+-------------+
2 Sample Page publish
    WP-CLI lists every status; get_posts() and WP_Query default to publish, like the front end. That one line explains half of all "my page does not show" questions.
  4. Terms (1m). "Categories and tags are two taxonomies of seven." 
    wp taxonomy list --fields=name,label,hierarchical,public
wp term list category --fields=term_id,name,slug,count
    +-----------------------+---------------------+--------------+--------+
| name                  | label               | hierarchical | public |
+-----------------------+---------------------+--------------+--------+
| category              | Categories          | 1            | 1      |
| post_tag              | Tags                |              | 1      |
| nav_menu              | Navigation Menus    |              |        |
| post_format           | Formats             |              | 1      |
| wp_theme              | Themes              |              |        |
| wp_template_part_area | Template Part Areas |              |        |
| wp_pattern_category   | Pattern Categories  |              |        |
+-----------------------+---------------------+--------------+--------+
+---------+---------------+---------------+-------+
| term_id | name          | slug          | count |
+---------+---------------+---------------+-------+
| 1       | Uncategorized | uncategorized | 1     |
+---------+---------------+---------------+-------+
    Every post must have a category: the default_category option names Uncategorized. The News category arrives in the project.
  5. An attachment is a post too (3m). "An upload is a file AND a post." The lesson switches the year/month folders off so the paths match: 
    wp option update uploads_use_yearmonth_folders 0

  7. Roles bundle capabilities (2m). "Code asks: may this user do X? Never: is this user an editor?" 
    wp eval 'var_dump( user_can( 1, "manage_options" ), user_can( 1, "edit_post", 1 ), current_user_can( "edit_posts" ) );'
wp eval 'var_dump( current_user_can( "edit_posts" ) );' --user=admin
    bool(true)
bool(true)
bool(false)
bool(true)
    The last two lines differ only by --user=admin: WP-CLI runs as nobody unless you name a user, and so does code that runs too early or from cron.
  8. Settings are options, all strings (1m). "Every Settings field is a row in wp_options." 
    wp eval 'foreach ( array( "show_on_front", "posts_per_page", "date_format", "timezone_string", "gmt_offset", "default_role", "default_category", "wp_page_for_privacy_policy" ) as $name ) { printf( "%-27s %s\n", $name, var_export( get_option( $name ), true ) ); }'

Before the project: the next-ID check (everyone)

One read-only query: the ID the next post will get. It must print 12.

wp db query "SET SESSION information_schema_stats_expiry = 0; SELECT AUTO_INCREMENT AS next_id FROM information_schema.TABLES WHERE TABLE_SCHEMA = DATABASE() AND TABLE_NAME = 'wp_posts'"
next_id

  • Less than 12 (a learner skipped demo steps: a site that ran none of them says 5): run the catch-up line in the WP-CLI container shell (docker compose run --rm wpcli sh), with as many numbers in the list as IDs are missing (seven from 5), then the check again. It creates drafts and deletes each at once, so only the IDs are used up:
for i in 1 2 3 4 5 6 7; do wp post delete $(wp post create --post_title=filler --porcelain) --force; done
