More than 12: the learner experimented (fine): their IDs are higher throughout, and later lessons that name an ID need their own number. Note it on a sticky note on their laptop lid.

Three mistakes to expect, and how to coach each
  • "My page is not there." A draft (the default of wp post create and wp_insert_post()) or a PHP list that only shows published content. Coach: "Which status? Which default does this tool have?" (Mistake 1, self-check Q8.)
  • Checking a role. in_array( 'editor', $user->roles ) for "may edit others' posts" locks out the administrator. Coach: "Which capability does the feature need?" (Lesson Mistake 3, self-check Q9, the debug handout.)
  • Copying block markup by hand and changing it. A missing wp-block-heading class: fine on the front end, "invalid block" in the editor. Coach: "Copy it from the Code editor or the lesson, never retype the HTML." (The lesson's warning box; in the project, learners copy the files from the page.)
Guided lab

File: labs/module-02/l2_1-content-model/content_census_starter.sh; your reference is labs/module-02/l2_1-content-model/content_census_solution.sh. Each TODO is one WP-CLI command inside $( ) that counts or names part of the content model (posts by status, pages, terms, an option, a role's capabilities, the blocks of a post). It only reads, so it is safe right before the project, and its counts are those of the site Session 1 left (the demo deleted everything it created).

  • Run it as shipped (2m). cp labs/module-02/l2_1-content-model/content_census_starter.sh wordpress/ then docker compose run --rm wpcli sh content_census_starter.sh: the post-type count works, the rest say TODO.
  • TODOs 1 to 7 in pairs (10m). Try each command alone first. Circulate for --format=count (WP-CLI counts for you), TODO 2 with a --post_status (any status means leaving it out), and TODO 7's pipe (--field=post_content, then grep).
  • Expected when done (the course site before the project):
== Pages & Co. content census ==
Post types: 16
Published posts: 1
Pages, any status: 2
Draft pages: 1
Categories: Uncategorized
Home page shows: posts
Editor capabilities: 34
Blocks in post 1:
      1 <!-- wp:paragraph
  • Debrief (3m): "Two pages, one of them a draft: which?" (the Privacy Policy WordPress made for you to finish). "34 capabilities for an editor: why do roles exist at all?" (So nobody hands out 34 permissions one by one; code still checks one capability at a time.)
  • Fast finishers: labs/module-02/l2_1-content-model/post_report_starter.php (one row of wp_posts seen through the whole model: the type object, the author's capability, terms, revisions, blocks, the address, for five IDs including the navigation menu), then labs/module-02/l2_1-content-model/debug_page_report.php (two loud bugs and a silent one about what posts and pages have). Both only read; run them before the project too, or accept different counts after it.
Start the lesson project

The lesson project is **Stock the Pages & Co. Site**: two staff accounts, three pages and a News category with three posts, created with WP-CLI from files of block markup. It is the content every later lesson starts from: names, slugs, dates and IDs exactly as the lesson prints them. In the room: Steps 1 to 3 (35 minutes).

  • Step 1 (8m): wp user create maria ... and wp user create devon ... exactly as in the lesson (the course passwords maria-pass, devon-pass matter: later lessons log in as them). Maria is user 2, Devon user 3.
  • Step 2 (12m): mkdir wordpress/pagesco-content, the three page files COPIED from the lesson page into it (typing block markup invites invalid blocks), then the three wp post create ... --user=maria lines. They must print 12, 13 and 14; open http://localhost:8080/about/ and watch the header menu list the new pages.
  • Step 3 (12m): wp term create category News --slug=news ... (prints 2), the three post files, the three wp post create ... --post_date=... lines (15, 16, 17), and http://localhost:8080/category/news/ lists them newest first.
  • Done in the room = pages 12 to 14 and posts 15 to 17 exist, by the right authors. Check two machines with the last command of the lesson's Step 4 (wp post list --post_type=page,post --orderby=ID --order=ASC ...).
  • Goes home: Step 4: Maria's edit of About Us (revision 18), Devon refused on the Pages screen, rm -r pagesco-content, the final list. Session 3 starts from exactly that site.
Checks for understanding

Ask these out loud during the demo, the lab and the project:

  • Where are a page, an uploaded image and an old version of a post stored? Answer: all three in wp_posts, with post_type page, attachment and revision.
  • wp post list shows the Privacy Policy; get_posts() does not. Why? Answer: different defaults: WP-CLI lists every status, get_posts() only published content.
  • Code must let "people who can edit everyone's posts" see a tool. What does it check? Answer: current_user_can( 'edit_others_posts' ), never the role.
  • Where is "Blog pages show at most" stored? Answer: the option posts_per_page (a string, '10').

Workbook self-check, items Q7 to Q12 (learners do them at the end of the block or at home).

Answers: Q7 D) wp_navigation; Q8 1 1: one published page for get_posts() (it defaults to publish), and one draft page counted by wp_count_posts() (the Privacy Policy); Q9 A) false: edit_post is a meta capability that maps to edit_others_posts here, which authors lack; Q10 core/separator; Q11 B) Two: the newest is identical to the current post; Q12 C) home. Full set with explanations in the Answer Key.

Differentiation

Support: in the project, pair a fast typist with a learner who struggles; the second reads each command aloud before the first runs it, and both check the printed ID against the lesson. A learner who falls behind in the demo copies its commands from the lesson page: the IDs only need the commands to RUN, in order.

Stretch: post_report_starter.php and debug_page_report.php (before the project); after it, the lesson's Exercise 1 (who may do what) and Exercise 2 (the block outline of Staff picks); the Bonus Challenge (a child page of Events, the revisions screen, the wp_navigation post) at home.

Closing

Exit ticket (3 questions, no notes, 4 minutes)

Put the three questions on the slide. Learners answer in the workbook's Exit Ticket box or on a sticky note and leave it on the way out. Sort the notes before Session 3: question 1's pile tells you how much of Session 3's warm-up goes back to escaping.

  1. Which escaping function for text between tags, for an attribute value, and for an href? Answer: esc_html(), esc_attr(), esc_url() (and wp_kses_post() for HTML a post may contain).
  2. Why does every global name in your theme and plugin start with pagesco_? Answer: WordPress, the theme and every plugin share one PHP process (and one options table): two functions with the same name are a fatal error, and you cannot know which plugins the client installs next year.
  3. Posts, pages, uploaded images, revisions and block-theme menus: where are they stored, and what tells them apart? Answer: all are rows of wp_posts; the post_type column (post, page, attachment, revision, wp_navigation).
Homework (about 2 to 3 hours)
  • Finish both lesson projects. 1.3: Steps 2 to 4 (render three cards, the break test, PHPCS with the WordPress standard until it says "no coding standards problems", then rm -r pagesco-practice; keep a copy of book-card.php in your notes). 2.1: Step 4 (Maria's edit and revision 18, Devon refused, rm -r pagesco-content) and the final list, which must match the lesson: users 2 and 3, pages 12 to 14, posts 15 to 17.
  • Lesson exercises. 1.3: Exercises 1 to 3 (PHPCS on a sale badge, one link in three contexts, a sale option for the price); Exercise 4 (list helpers) is a stretch. 2.1: Exercises 1 to 3 (who may do what, the block outline, a static front page, put back afterwards); Exercise 4 (deleting a user safely) is a stretch. Each exercise undoes itself.
  • Both Quick Quizzes on the lesson pages (five questions each; answers in the Answer Key).
  • Journal: both entries (1.3: habits you keep and habits you change; 2.1: your pagesco-plan.txt sorted into the content model).
  • Before the Next Lesson (both lists): pagesco-practice/ deleted and mu-plugins/ holding only mailpit-smtp.php; the final list of 2.1 checked; no user sam, Settings > Reading back on "Your latest posts"; log in as Maria once.
  • Optional: labs/module-02/l1_3-php-the-wordpress-way/event_line_starter.php, labs/module-02/l1_3-php-the-wordpress-way/debug_book_badge.php, labs/module-02/l2_1-content-model/post_report_starter.php and labs/module-02/l2_1-content-model/debug_page_report.php for anyone who did not reach them (the two 2.1 files print other counts once the content exists: their README says which).
Bring list for Session 3
  • The course site at the end of Lesson 2.1 (Session 3's two lessons start from it): users maria (2) and devon (3), pages About Us, Contact and Events (12 to 14), the News posts 15 to 17, revision 18 of About Us, pagesco-content/ deleted. Check: wp post list --post_type=page,post --orderby=ID --order=asc --fields=ID,post_type,post_name,post_author.
  • Your copy of book-card.php, PHPCS-clean (Session 3's warm-up asks), and pagesco-plan.txt sorted into the content model.

If You Run Long or Short

Running long: what to protect and what to cut first
  • Protect: the 2.1 project Steps 1 to 3 with the right IDs; the ID-using steps of the 2.1 demo; the 1.3 PHPCS and escaping steps; the 1.3 guided lab.
  • Cut first (saves 6m): the 1.3 es_ES and callbacks steps (the lesson has both outputs).
  • Cut second (saves 15m): the 1.3 project start: show book-card.php on the projector, send Steps 1 to 4 home, give the time to the 2.1 project.
  • Cut third (saves 15m): the 2.1 guided lab: learners do it at home, after the project, so their counts are those of the stocked site (the README lists them). Never cut the 2.1 demo's ID-using steps: run them without discussion instead.
Running short: what to add
  • Lesson 1.3's Exercise 1 live: PHPCS on the sale badge, phpcbf for the mechanical fixes, the rest by hand. Ask which problems a tool cannot fix, and why.
  • Lesson 2.1's Exercise 1 together after Step 3 (who may do what: admin, maria, devon), predicted first on the board.
  • debug_book_badge.php for everyone, one bug per volunteer, starting from the messages and ending with the silent one.
Instructor Kit · Facilitator Guide

Session 3: Core Architecture, the Database and Hooks

How to teach the session where WordPress opens up: the files and the load order, the twelve tables and their key-value pattern read with SQL from the course site, then the hooks system that every theme and plugin is built on, ending with the first file of the course that stays, the Pages & Co. store notice as a must-use plugin with hooks of its own.

2 lessons 3 hrs session Lessons 2.2–2.3 Session 3 of 18 · Part 1

How to Use This Guide

  • Same rhythm for both lessons: frame (the goal and one mental model) → live demo (you type, they type along) → guided lab (a kit lab, new practice on the lesson's ideas) → start the lesson's own project. The lesson exercises, quiz and journal are homework.
  • Type, do not paste (the long grep of wp-settings.php is the exception). Every command below was run to produce the output printed under it, on WordPress 7.1.3, PHP 8.5 and MySQL 9.7, on the site exactly as Lesson 2.1 leaves it: the users maria and devon, the pages About Us, Contact and Events, three News posts. Ask for a prediction before every run.
  • The lessons are the reference. Keep lesson_05.html and lesson_06.html open in browser tabs (the table diagram, the action table, the full stack trace of Mistake 2). Labs live in labs/module-03/: _starter files are handouts, _solution files and the title_parts_solution/ folder are yours.
  • Session 3 is the hinge of Part 1. Lesson 2.2 is read-only: the site ends exactly as it started. Lesson 2.3's project, mu-plugins/pagesco-site.php with the store notice, is the first file of the course that STAYS: Session 4 and every lesson after it assume it. Protect its start in the room.
  • Lesson 2.2 is SQL-heavy. Learners came through MySQL Foundations, so the joins are review; the new ideas are the schema (no foreign keys, the key-value pattern, serialized arrays, autoload) and the rule that follows from them: change WordPress data through WordPress.
The #1 risk of Session 3: the database hour eats the hooks hour

Lesson 2.2 is the longest lesson so far (140 minutes for a learner alone) and full of queries learners enjoy running; every one invites "what if I also ...". Lesson 2.3 is shorter but it is the lesson the rest of the course stands on, and its project must exist on every machine before Session 4. Hold the line at the break (1:15): the 2.2 demo is 20 minutes and has a cut list (below), the inventory starts with two SQL steps and its PHP half goes home. After the break, the 2.3 project start gets 30 minutes, the longest segment of the day: learners who leave with pagesco-site.php printing the notice are ready for Session 4; Steps 3 and 4 can be finished at home in 20 minutes.

Before the Session

  • ☐ Learners' sites: Session 2's homework finished Lesson 2.1's project. Remind them two days before: wp user list shows maria and devon, wp post list --post_type=page shows About Us, Contact and Events. A learner who skipped it can build the state in 15 minutes at the start of the break with Lesson 2.1's project steps; until then the 2.2 SQL shows fewer rows (fine) and the labs find no Maria (less fine).
  • ☐ Files to hand out: labs/module-03/ without the *_solution.* files and the title_parts_solution/ folder; the workbook.
  • ☐ Run the kit check once: python3 labs/check_labs.py module-03 from this kit's folder (every line PASS; 14 results in about a minute). With your own course project at the end of Lesson 2.1: WP_LABS_COMPOSE=~/pagesco-dev python3 labs/check_labs.py module-03 (labs/README.md).
  • ☐ Projector machine: the course site at the end of Lesson 2.1 (the instructor's site follows the lessons too), VS Code open on pagesco-dev at a large font with wordpress/wp-content/mu-plugins/ expanded, two terminals in the project folder (commands; tail -f wordpress/wp-content/debug.log), a third for wp db cli, a browser with http://localhost:8080/hello-world/ and View Source, plus lesson_05.html and lesson_06.html.
  • ☐ Board, before learners arrive: the load order as a column (database · mu-plugins · plugins · pluggable · theme · user · init · wp() · template); the five table groups (content, taxonomies, users, comments, settings) with the ID arrows; and a two-column box action = a moment, does something · filter = a value, returns it.
  • ☐ A safety net for Mistake 3: the demo skips the typo'd callback (it takes the site and WP-CLI down). If a learner's own typo does it in the lab, the fix is rm of the file in wordpress/wp-content/mu-plugins/ from the host terminal, not WP-CLI (which is down too).
Known traps in this session
SymptomCauseFix
wp db cli greets "Welcome to the MariaDB monitor" and the prompt says MySQL [wordpress]>The WP-CLI image's client program is MariaDB's; the server is MySQL 9.7Nothing: every query works the same. Leave with exit.
The lesson's counts differ from a learner's (more revisions, _edit_lock rows)The learner opened posts in the editor after Lesson 2.1Expected; the queries are the answer, not the numbers (the lesson says so).
A query at the prompt prints nothing and waitsThe semicolon is missing; the prompt shows ->Type ; and Enter.
wp db query output is tab-separated, no tablewp db query never draws tables; wp db cli doesUse the prompt for reading, wp db query in scripts.
wp eval-file query-news.php: File not foundSaved in the project folder instead of wordpress/WP-CLI's current folder is the WordPress root: wordpress/query-news.php.
A must-use plugin edit takes down every page, the admin AND WP-CLIA fatal error in mu-plugins/ (Lesson 2.3, Mistake 3); WordPress cannot pause a must-use pluginFrom the host: rm wordpress/wp-content/mu-plugins/<file>, read the end of debug.log, fix, copy back.
The notice does not appear; no messageThe file is in plugins/ instead of mu-plugins/, or named .php.txt, or the hook name is misspelledwp plugin list --status=must-use; wp eval 'var_dump( has_action( "wp_body_open", "pagesco_render_store_notice" ) );'.
curl ... | grep -c exits with an error in a scriptgrep -c exits 1 when it counts zeroExpected (the lesson's Step 4 says so).

In the room. The lesson pages estimate 140 + 120 = 260 minutes for a learner working alone; after the warm-up, the break and the wrap-up the room has 150. Lesson 2.2 keeps model, demo and lab, and its project starts with the two SQL steps (the prompt is where discussion helps); the PHP half of the inventory and the settings check go home. Lesson 2.3 keeps its full shape and gives its project the longest segment, because the file stays for the rest of the course. Not in the room: Lesson 2.2's drop-ins section and constant table, the indexes and EXPLAIN (the workbook's worked example covers EXPLAIN), Mistakes 2 to 4 of 2.2 (orphans, a typed table name, the third argument: self-check Q4 and the debug handout practice two of them), and 2.3's "Finding the Hook You Need" beyond has_filter() (the second 2.3 lab, hook_finder_starter.sh).

Goes home (about 2 to 3 hours). The inventory Steps 3 and 4 (the same report from PHP with $wpdb, the settings check, the clean-up); the store notice Step 4 (and Step 3 if it did not fit); each lesson's Hands-on Exercises; both Quick Quizzes; both journal entries; both "Before the Next Lesson" lists; and the review for Checkpoint 1 in Session 4 (Modules 1 and 2: Lessons 1.1 to 2.3).

Protect, in this order: the 2.3 project start (pagesco-site.php printing the notice on every machine); the 2.3 demo through removing a hook; the 2.2 demo through "every value is a string"; the 2.2 guided lab. Cut first: the 2.2 autoload step and the 2.3 Mistake 4 step (4 minutes; both are in the lesson and the handouts), then the 2.2 project start (send both SQL steps home: 15 minutes), then the 2.2 lab's Steps 4 and 5 (5 minutes).

Retrieval questions and answers
  1. Which escaping function goes around a URL in an href attribute? Answer: esc_url() (text between tags: esc_html(), other attribute values: esc_attr()).
  2. Name the four shapes a WordPress callback can take. Which one is hard for anyone else to unhook? Answer: A function name, a closure, array( $object, 'method' ), a static method ('Class::method' or array( 'Class', 'method' )). The closure: nobody else has a handle on it (Lesson 2.3 comes back to this).
  3. A page and a post: which table holds each, and which column tells them apart? Answer: Both are rows in wp_posts; post_type is page or post (Lesson 2.1's filing cabinet).
  4. Code must decide whether the current user may publish pages. What does it check, and why not the role? Answer: current_user_can( 'publish_pages' ): a capability. Roles are bundles that sites change; capabilities are what WordPress checks.
  5. What does wp_parse_args( $args, $defaults ) return? Answer: One array: the defaults, overridden by whatever the caller passed in $args.

Lesson Plans

2.2

Core Architecture & the Database

65 min
Objectives (from the lesson page)
  • Find your way around a WordPress install: what lives in wp-admin/, wp-includes/ and wp-content/, and what a drop-in is
  • Read wp-config.php and explain its settings, including the table prefix and the security keys
  • Trace how wp-settings.php loads WordPress, and say what is available at each stage
  • Map the twelve wp_* tables, their keys and indexes, and join them with SQL the way WordPress's own queries do
  • Explain the meta (key-value) pattern, serialized values and options autoloading, with their trade-offs
  • Query the Pages & Co. site with wp db cli, wp db query and WP-CLI, and choose the API over raw SQL in your code
Timing in the room
10mFrame: opening the shop in the morning; twelve tables; no foreign keys; the key-value pattern
20mLive demo: wp-config.php, wp-settings.php, tables, a join, WP_Query's SQL, meta as text, serialized data, autoload
20mGuided lab: meta_pivot_starter.sh in pairs
15mStart the lesson project: the database inventory, Steps 1 and 2
Mental model to say

Draw on the load-order column from the board: "Think of a bookseller opening Pages & Co. in the morning. First the lights and the till: the database connection and the cache. Then the things that are always there, whatever happens: must-use plugins. Then the departments open today: active plugins. Then the window display: the theme. Only when the staff member on duty has signed in, the current user, does the shop open its doors, init, and serve the first customer, the main query. Code that tries to serve a customer while the lights are still off is the 'too early' bug of the next lesson."

Then the database in three sentences: "Twelve tables, the same on every WordPress site, linked by ID columns but with no foreign keys: integrity lives in PHP, so you change data through WordPress. Extra fields are rows, not columns: post_id, meta_key, meta_value, the key-value pattern, and every value is text. Arrays are stored serialized, with their lengths inside, so you never edit them as text." Write the rule under the drawing: read with SQL if you like; write through the API.

Live demo (you type, they follow)

    wp option add pagesco_demo_shop '{"city":"Springfield","phone":"555-0142"}' --format=json

a:2:{s:4:"city";s:11:"Portland";s:5:"phone";s:8:"555-0142";}

Error: Could not get 'pagesco_demo_shop' option. Does it exist?
    s:11:"Portland" says eleven characters; Portland has eight. unserialize() fails, WordPress returns false, WP-CLI says the option does not exist. In a theme the address just vanishes. Fix: wp option patch, update_option(), and wp search-replace for whole sites (Lesson 8.4). wp option delete pagesco_demo_shop.
  7. What autoload saves (1m). Save the lesson's options-cost.php and run it: $wpdb->num_queries counts queries. 
    <?php
global $wpdb;

foreach ( array( 'blogname', 'fresh_site', 'fresh_site', 'pagesco_no_such_option' ) as $pagesco_name ) {
	$pagesco_before = $wpdb->num_queries;
	$pagesco_value  = get_option( $pagesco_name );
	printf( "%-24s %-18s queries: %d\n", $pagesco_name, var_export( $pagesco_value, true ), $wpdb->num_queries - $pagesco_before );
}
    blogname                 'Pages &amp; Co.'  queries: 0
fresh_site               '0'                queries: 1
fresh_site               '0'                queries: 0
pagesco_no_such_option   false              queries: 1
    Autoloaded: free. Not autoloaded: one query, then cached. Missing: still one query. Then clean up: rm options-cost.php and the lesson's three wp post meta delete lines.
Three mistakes to expect, and how to coach each
  • Typing wp_posts in PHP. It works on the course site and breaks on the first client site with the prefix pc_. Coach: "Where does the prefix come from?" {$wpdb->posts} in code, wp_posts only at the prompt. (The lesson's Mistake 3; wpdb_report_starter.php.)
  • Fixing data with UPDATE or DELETE because it is quicker. Coach with the two broken demos: "Which PHP would have run if you had used wp post delete?" (wp_delete_post()'s four cleanup lines.) The prompt is for reading. (Self-check Q5.)
  • Comparing meta as numbers in SQL. ORDER BY meta_value and meta_value > 10 on text. Coach: "What type is meta_value?" (LONGTEXT.) CAST in SQL, meta_value_num in WP_Query. Forgetting true in get_post_meta() is the PHP version of the same surprise (self-check Q4, debug_meta_report.php).

Start the lesson project

The lesson project is A Database Inventory of Pages & Co.: the same report twice, at the SQL prompt as an auditor would and in PHP with $wpdb as a plugin would, plus a settings check; nothing on the site changes. In the room: Steps 1 and 2 at the prompt (15 minutes).

  • Step 1 (5m): content by type and status with GROUP BY, then the same numbers from wp_count_posts(). Ask before running: "how many published pages?" (Four: the Sample Page counts.)
  • Step 2 (10m): who wrote what and where it is filed, with LEFT JOINs to the term tables and GROUP_CONCAT(). The teaching moment is the condition tt.taxonomy = 'category' in ON rather than WHERE: ask a pair to move it to WHERE and watch the pages disappear.
  • Done in the room = both queries return the lesson's rows and are saved in pagesco-inventory.sql in the learner's notes.
  • Goes home: Step 3 (the PHP report with $wpdb->prepare() and get_the_category()) and Step 4 (the largest autoloaded options, the clean-up, the final check).
Checks for understanding

Ask these out loud during the demo and the lab:

  • Why can a plugin call get_option() at the top of its file, but not wp_get_current_user()? Answer: the database and the options are ready at line 136; pluggable.php (and the current user) come after the plugins.
  • A plugin needs a featured flag per post. Column, meta, taxonomy or table? Answer: post meta (one value per post; Lesson 2.2 quiz Q1). A taxonomy if it were a shared label to filter by.
  • Where does $wpdb->posts get its prefix? Answer: $table_prefix in wp-config.php.
  • Why does WP_Query's SQL join only one term table? Answer: it looked up the term's ID first and filters on term_taxonomy_id directly.

Workbook self-check, items Q1 to Q6 (learners do them at the end of the block or at home).

Answers: Q1 C) It is defined too late: wp-settings.php has already loaded WordPress, so the file editors stay; Q2 db: the name of the database service in compose.yaml (on a typical host it is localhost); Q3 B) Must-use plugins, active plugins, pluggable.php, the theme's functions.php; Q4 

array(1) {
  [0]=>
  string(5) "Devon"
}
; Q5 B) It works, but only because both words have 6 characters: the s:6 length still matches. Change roles through WordPress anyway; Q6 D) Nobody chose, and WordPress decided not to autoload it, usually because the value is large (over 150,000 bytes). Full set with explanations in the Answer Key.

Differentiation

Support: learners rusty on joins get the Step 2 query of the lab written on a card with blanks for the ON clause; pair them with someone who did MySQL Foundations recently. For anyone lost in the tables, the workbook's table-groups diagram is the map: point at it before every query.

Stretch: wpdb_report_starter.php and debug_meta_report.php; the lesson's Exercise 4 (SAVEQUERIES in a must-use plugin, and why the autoloaded options are missing from it) and the Bonus Challenge (SHORTINIT).

2.3

The Hooks System

85 min
Objectives (from the lesson page)
  • Explain the difference between an action and a filter, and choose the right one for a task
  • Attach callbacks with add_action() and add_filter(), using priorities and the accepted-arguments count correctly
  • Remove a hook someone else added with remove_action() / remove_filter(), and say why a removal silently fails
  • Create your own action and filter hooks with do_action() and apply_filters() so other code can extend yours
  • Find the hook you need: in the core source, with has_filter() and $wp_filter, and from the command line with WP-CLI
  • Build the Pages & Co. store notice as a must-use plugin that others can customize through its own hooks
Timing in the room
10mFrame: the radio show with call-ins; actions and filters; must-use plugins; the prefix rule
25mLive demo: a first hook, the order of a request, filters, priorities and accepted arguments, removing, has_filter(), three mistakes
20mGuided lab: filter_chain_starter.php
30mStart the lesson project: the store notice, Steps 1 to 3 (Step 4 if time)
Mental model to say

"WordPress is a radio host working through a running order. An action is the host saying 'we are now at the weather, any callers?': callers may talk, and the show goes on the same way afterwards. A filter is the host saying 'here is today's headline, any corrections?': each caller gets the headline, may rewrite it, and hands it to the next caller, and the host reads out whatever comes back from the last one. If a caller keeps the headline and hands back nothing, the host reads out nothing." (That is Mistake 1, the filter that forgets to return: promise it.)

Then the box on the board: action = a moment, your function does something · filter = a value, your function returns it. Then where hooks live until Module 5: "a must-use plugin, any PHP file in wp-content/mu-plugins/, loaded on every request without activation, before all plugins. You wrote a throwaway one in Lesson 1.2; today you write one that stays." And the prefix rule in one breath: everything you name, pagesco_.

Live demo (you type, they follow)

Files in VS Code (wordpress/wp-content/mu-plugins/ for must-use plugins, wordpress/ for wp eval-file scripts), checks in the WP-CLI container or the browser's View Source. Outputs below come from the site at the end of Lesson 2.1; your debug.log time stamps differ.

  1. Your first hook (3m). "The question for every WordPress task from today: which hook, and is it an action or a filter?" Save the lesson's file in VS Code as wordpress/wp-content/mu-plugins/pagesco-hello.php (must-use plugins: Lesson 2.2's line 506), reload http://localhost:8080/hello-world/, View Source: 
    <?php
/**
 * Plugin Name: Pages & Co. Hello Hooks
 * Description: Lesson 2.3 demo: prints a line at the bottom of every page.
 */

function pagesco_hello_footer() {
	echo '<p class="pagesco-hello">Hello from a hook!</p>';
}
add_action( 'wp_footer', 'pagesco_hello_footer' );
    <p class="pagesco-hello">Hello from a hook!</p>
    Two lines do the work: the function says what, add_action() says when. The name is a string without parentheses: you are not calling it, you are telling WordPress what to call later. Ask: "why the pagesco_ prefix?" (One shared PHP program: Lesson 1.3.)
  2. The order of one request (3m). "The load order from before the break, logged by a request." Save the lesson's pagesco-hook-order.php, reload the post once, and read the new lines of debug.log (a second terminal: tail -f wordpress/wp-content/debug.log): 
    <?php
/**
 * Plugin Name: Pages & Co. Hook Order
 * Description: Lesson 2.3 demo: logs the order of the main actions of a front-end request.
 */

$pagesco_hooks = array( 'plugins_loaded', 'after_setup_theme', 'init', 'wp_loaded', 'template_redirect', 'wp_head', 'wp_footer', 'shutdown' );

foreach ( $pagesco_hooks as $pagesco_hook ) {
	add_action(
		$pagesco_hook,
		function () {
			if ( ! is_admin() && ! wp_doing_cron() && ! defined( 'WP_CLI' ) ) {
				error_log( 'hook order: ' . current_action() );
			}
		}
	);
}
    [26-Oct-2026 14:08:26 UTC] hook order: plugins_loaded
[26-Oct-2026 14:08:26 UTC] hook order: after_setup_theme
[26-Oct-2026 14:08:26 UTC] hook order: init
[26-Oct-2026 14:08:26 UTC] hook order: wp_loaded
[26-Oct-2026 14:08:26 UTC] hook order: template_redirect
[26-Oct-2026 14:08:26 UTC] hook order: wp_head
[26-Oct-2026 14:08:26 UTC] hook order: wp_footer
[26-Oct-2026 14:08:26 UTC] hook order: shutdown
    Same closure eight times; current_action() names the hook. Point at template_redirect: the query is done, nothing printed yet, the place for redirects (self-check Q8). Delete the file (rm wp-content/mu-plugins/pagesco-hook-order.php): a log line per request gets noisy fast.
  3. A filter, from both sides (4m). "A filter in core: the last line of get_the_title()." 
    grep -n "apply_filters( 'the_title'" wp-includes/post-template.php
    174:	return apply_filters( 'the_title', $post_title, $post_id );
    Then append the lesson's separator filter to pagesco-hello.php and reload: the <title> in View Source. 
    function pagesco_title_separator( $separator ) {
	return '|';
}
add_filter( 'document_title_separator', 'pagesco_title_separator' );
    <title>Hello world! | Pages &amp; Co.</title>
    Then the signature on the_content (append it too); the post's content area, as text: 
    function pagesco_content_signature( $content ) {
	return $content . '<p class="pagesco-signature">Thanks for reading, from the Pages &amp; Co. team.</p>';
}
add_filter( 'the_content', 'pagesco_content_signature' );
    Welcome to WordPress. This is your first post. Edit or delete it, then start writing!
Thanks for reading, from the Pages & Co. team.
    "A filter takes the value and returns the value." Under the hood add_action() is one line: return add_filter( ... );.
  4. Priorities and accepted arguments (4m). "Who goes first?" Save the lesson's wordpress/priorities.php, ask for a prediction, wp eval-file priorities.php: 
    <?php
add_filter( 'pagesco_demo', fn( $text ) => $text . ' [priority 20]', 20 );
add_filter( 'pagesco_demo', fn( $text ) => $text . ' [priority 5]', 5 );
add_filter( 'pagesco_demo', fn( $text ) => $text . ' [default 10, added first]' );
add_filter( 'pagesco_demo', fn( $text ) => $text . ' [default 10, added second]' );

echo apply_filters( 'pagesco_demo', 'Start:' ), "\n";
    Start: [priority 5] [default 10, added first] [default 10, added second] [priority 20]
    Lower first; ties in the order added. Then title-ids.php: the_title passes two values, and 10, 2 asks for both. 
    <?php
function pagesco_title_with_id( $title, $post_id ) {
	return "{$title} (#{$post_id})";
}
add_filter( 'the_title', 'pagesco_title_with_id', 10, 2 );

echo get_the_title( 1 ), "\n";
echo get_the_title( 2 ), "\n";
    Hello world! (#1)
Sample Page (#2)
    rm priorities.php title-ids.php.
  5. Removing a hook, and asking the site (4m). "Every page tells the world your exact version." Append the lesson's one line to pagesco-hello.php and count the generator tags from the container: 
    remove_action( 'wp_head', 'wp_generator' );

curl -s http://localhost:8080/ | grep -c 'name="generator"'
    0
    (grep -c exits with 1 when it counts zero: expected.) The three rules on the board: same priority, after it was added, a handle on the callback. Then ask the running site what is attached: 
    wp eval 'var_dump( has_action( "wp_head", "_wp_render_title_tag" ), has_filter( "the_content", "pagesco_content_signature" ), has_filter( "the_content", "no_such_function" ) );'
    int(1)
int(10)
bool(false)
    A number is a priority, false is nothing attached; 0 is a valid priority, so compare with false !==.
  6. Mistake 1: a filter that forgets to return (3m). Save the lesson's mistake-no-return.php in mu-plugins/ and reload /hello-world/: the title is gone. From the container: 
    <?php
add_filter( 'the_title', function ( $title ) {
	$title = strtoupper( $title );
} );

curl -s http://localhost:8080/hello-world/ | head -n 3
curl -s http://localhost:8080/hello-world/ | grep -c 'wp-block-post-title'
    Deprecated: str_replace(): Passing null to parameter #3 ($subject) of type array|string is deprecated in /var/www/html/wp-includes/formatting.php on line 5777
<!DOCTYPE html>
0
    The only message blames core (formatting.php, line 5777): your closure handed null to the next callback on the_title, core's capital_P_dangit() at 11. It sits above <!DOCTYPE html> because a block theme renders the template before the head. "When a notice blames core, look at what your code handed to it." rm the file.
  7. Mistake 2: two arguments asked, one registered (2m). Save mistake-args.php and reload /hello-world/. The page is replaced by the fatal error; read the first line from the left: 
    <?php
add_filter( 'the_title', function ( $title, $post_id ) {
	return "{$title} (#{$post_id})";
} );
    Fatal error: Uncaught ArgumentCountError: Too few arguments to function {closure:/var/www/html/wp-content/mu-plugins/mistake-args.php:2}(), 1 passed in /var/www/html/wp-includes/class-wp-hook.php on line 355 and exactly 2 expected in /var/www/html/wp-content/mu-plugins/mistake-args.php:2
    Closure named after its file and line (PHP 8.4 and later; PHP 8.3 says only {closure}), 1 passed, exactly 2 expected. The stack trace below it (in the lesson) is the way back: WP_Hook, apply_filters( 'the_title' ), get_the_title(), the Post Title block. Fix: 10, 2. rm the file.
  8. Mistake 4: removing with the wrong priority (2m). "The silent one." Save mistake-remove.php in the WordPress root and run it: 
    <?php
var_dump( remove_action( 'wp_head', '_wp_render_title_tag' ) );
var_dump( remove_action( 'wp_head', '_wp_render_title_tag', 1 ) );
    bool(false)
bool(true)
    False, then true: _wp_render_title_tag was added at 1. If nobody looks at the return value, the first line "just does not work". rm mistake-remove.php and the demo plugin pagesco-hello.php: the project starts clean. (Mistake 3, the typo in a callback name, is in the deck and the lesson: it takes the site and WP-CLI down, which is too much drama in front of the room right before the project.)
Three mistakes to expect, and how to coach each
  • Echoing in a filter or returning nothing. Coach with the radio host: "What does the host read out if you hand back nothing?" Every path of a filter ends in return. (Self-check Q11, debug_price_tag.php.)
  • Calling instead of naming: add_action( 'wp_footer', pagesco_hello_footer() ). The function runs immediately, while plugins load, and WordPress gets its return value (null) as the callback. Coach: "Are you calling it now, or telling WordPress what to call later?" Strings, no parentheses.
  • "My removal does nothing." Wrong priority, too early, or a closure. Coach: var_dump( remove_action( ... ) ) first, then the three rules on the board. (Self-check Q9, the lab's TODO 3.)
Guided lab

File: labs/module-03/l2_3-hooks/filter_chain_starter.php; your reference is labs/module-03/l2_3-hooks/filter_chain_solution.php. It practices the three rules of a hook with several callbacks on a filter of the bookstore's own: the order (priorities), the values a callback receives (accepted arguments), and taking someone else's callback off (removal with the right priority), checked with has_filter().

  • Run it as shipped (2m). cp labs/module-03/l2_3-hooks/filter_chain_starter.php wordpress/ then wp eval-file --use-include filter_chain_starter.php:
Removed the sale badge: TODO
pagesco_lab_capitalize: TODO
Line: fahrenheit 451 [SALE]
  • TODOs 1 and 2 (8m). Capitalize at 5, the author at the default priority with 10, 2. Circulate for the fatal ArgumentCountError (the demo's Mistake 2, now in their own file: read it from the left together) and for ucwords at a later priority than the author ("Fahrenheit 451 By Ray Bradbury": ask why By is capitalized).
  • TODOs 3 and 4 (6m). remove_filter() without the 30 returns false and the badge stays: let them find it with var_export(). has_filter() after the removal returns false for the badge.
  • Expected when done:
Removed the sale badge: true
pagesco_lab_capitalize: 5
pagesco_lab_add_author: 10
pagesco_lab_sale_badge: false
Line: Fahrenheit 451 by Ray Bradbury
  • Debrief (4m): "Which line would you change if the theme had to add [SALE] after the author?" (Nothing in the theme: its priority 30 already runs after 10.) "What changes if TODO 1 is hooked at 20 instead of 5?" (ucwords then runs after the author was added and capitalizes it too: Fahrenheit 451 By Ray Bradbury.)
  • Fast finishers: labs/module-03/l2_3-hooks/hook_finder_starter.sh (find hooks in core with exact grep patterns, then ask the site), the folder lab labs/module-03/l2_3-hooks/title_parts_starter/ (a must-use plugin on document_title_parts; test with labs/module-03/l2_3-hooks/test_title_parts.sh), then labs/module-03/l2_3-hooks/debug_price_tag.php.
Start the lesson project

The lesson project is The Pages & Co. Store Notice: wordpress/wp-content/mu-plugins/pagesco-site.php, a notice bar printed from wp_body_open that offers its own hooks (a filter for the text, two actions) and is extended from the outside. This file stays for the rest of the course: Session 4 and every later lesson start from a site that has it. In the room: Steps 1 to 3 (30 minutes).

  • Step 1 (8m): the plugin header and the notice on wp_body_open, escaped with esc_html(). Check: View Source, the <div class="pagesco-notice"> is the first thing inside <body>.
  • Step 2 (10m): replace the function with the version that offers pagesco_store_notice, pagesco_before_store_notice and pagesco_store_notice_end, each with its DocBlock. Nothing visible changes: "you are building the doors other code will use." Insist on typing the DocBlocks: hooks are a public API.
  • Step 3 (10m): be "another developer": the Thursday hours at priority 20, the events link inside the bar, and the generator removal moved in from the demo file.
  • Done in the room = every page starts with Free shipping on orders over $35. Open until 9 p.m. on Thursdays. See events. Check two or three screens yourself; the rest check with curl -s http://localhost:8080/ | grep -o '<div class="pagesco-notice">.*</div>' in the container.
  • Goes home: Step 4 (delete pagesco-hello.php, the has_action and grep checks) and the checklist, including "returning '' hides the bar" (try it, then remove the test). Anyone who did not reach Step 3 finishes it first: Session 4 checks for the full notice.
Checks for understanding

Ask these out loud during the demo and the lab:

  • Banner at the top of every page, or excerpts shortened to 20 words: action or filter? Answer: an action (wp_body_open) for the banner, a filter (excerpt_length) for the number.
  • What does add_action() do with a function name that does not exist? Answer: nothing, until the hook fires; then a fatal TypeError. It stores a string.
  • Two callbacks at priority 10 on one hook: which runs first? Answer: the one added first.
  • Why does the project's filter for the Thursday hours use priority 20? Answer: to add to whatever earlier callbacks produced; a later one (99) could still change it, which is how a "quiet day" filter switches the bar off (the lesson's Exercise 1).

Workbook self-check, items Q7 to Q12 (learners do them at the end of the block or at home).

Answers: Q7 XAb; Q8 C) template_redirect; Q9 A) The plugin ran before the theme added the hook, so there was nothing to remove: remove it on init; Q10 int(9): do_blocks is attached to the_content at priority 9, before wpautop at 10; Q11 A) Your callback does not return the title, so the next callback (core's, at priority 11) received null; Q12 D) do_action( 'pagesco_before_gift_form' ); with a DocBlock above it. Full set with explanations in the Answer Key.

Differentiation

Support: learners who freeze at an empty file get a card with the two-line pattern (function pagesco_x() { ... } / add_action( 'hook', 'pagesco_x' );) and the box from the board. In the project, pair a learner who struggles with the guided lab with one who finished it; the typing stays with the first.

Stretch: hook_finder_starter.sh, the title-parts folder lab and debug_price_tag.php; the lesson's Exercise 3 (every callback on the_content, in order) and Exercise 4 (the all hook counter); the Bonus Challenge (the body_class filter).

Closing

Exit ticket (3 questions, no notes, 4 minutes)

Put the three questions on the slide. Learners answer in the workbook's Exit Ticket box or on a sticky note. Sort the notes before Session 4: question 3's pile tells you how much of the Checkpoint review to give to removing hooks.

  1. Why should code change WordPress data through WordPress (functions or WP-CLI) and not with UPDATE or DELETE? Answer: there are no foreign keys, so WordPress's PHP does the cascading (meta, terms, revisions, comments); serialized values carry their lengths; and the API keeps caches and hooks in step.
  2. Action or filter, and which hook: a banner at the very top of every page; the length of every excerpt. Answer: an action on wp_body_open; a filter on excerpt_length (return the number).
  3. remove_action() returns false and the hook keeps running. Name two possible reasons. Answer: a different priority than the one it was added with; called before the hook was added (too early); a different callback (a closure or another object).

The store notice: Step 3 if it did not fit, Step 4 and the checklist. Afterwards mu-plugins/ holds exactly mailpit-smtp.php and pagesco-site.php, and every page starts with the full notice.
  • Lesson exercises. 2.2: Exercises 1 to 3 (the only comment, roles from the database, content without meta); Exercise 4 (SAVEQUERIES) is a stretch. 2.3: Exercises 1 to 3 (the quiet day, the login branding, who is on the_content); Exercise 4 (the all counter) is a stretch. Each exercise file is deleted afterwards.
  • Both Quick Quizzes on the lesson pages (five questions each; answers in the Answer Key).
  • Journal: both entries (2.2: your MySQL Foundations bookstore schema next to WordPress's tables; 2.3: a website you use, described as hooks).
  • Before the Next Lesson (both lists): no demo or exercise files left in the WordPress root or mu-plugins/; the orphan query returns no rows; skim wp-includes/default-filters.php; read mailpit-smtp.php again and explain its two hooks.
  • Prepare for Checkpoint 1 (Session 4, 30 minutes, Modules 1 and 2: Lessons 1.1 to 2.3): reread the Key Takeaways of the six lessons and redo the self-checks of Sessions 1 to 3.
  • Optional: labs/module-03/l2_2-core-database/wpdb_report_starter.php, labs/module-03/l2_2-core-database/debug_meta_report.php, labs/module-03/l2_3-hooks/hook_finder_starter.sh, the title-parts lab and labs/module-03/l2_3-hooks/debug_price_tag.php for anyone who did not reach them.
Bring list for Session 4

Check: curl -s http://localhost:8080/ | grep -o '<div class="pagesco-notice">.*</div>' in the WP-CLI container.

If You Run Long or Short

Running long: what to protect and what to cut first
  • Protect: the 2.3 project start; the 2.3 demo through removing a hook; the 2.2 demo through "every value is a string"; the 2.2 guided lab.
  • Cut first (saves 4m): the 2.2 autoload step and the 2.3 Mistake 4 step.
  • Cut second (saves 15m): the 2.2 project start: show the Step 1 query, send Steps 1 to 4 home; give the time to the 2.3 project.
  • Cut third (saves 5m): the 2.2 lab's Steps 4 and 5 (the README's expected output shows them).
Running short: what to add
  • Lesson 2.2's Mistake 2 live (orphans): the DELETE, the LEFT JOIN that finds them, the multi-table DELETE that cleans up. It makes "write through the API" stick.
  • Lesson 2.3's Exercise 1 together (the quiet day at priority 99): it uses the hooks the project just built, from the outside.
  • debug_price_tag.php for everyone, one bug per volunteer.
Instructor Kit · Facilitator Guide

Session 4: Theme Anatomy and Building a Block Theme

How to teach Session 4: a ten-minute warm-up and Checkpoint 1 on Modules 1 and 2 (a 30-minute individual must-use plugin task with a five-row rubric), then Twenty Twenty-Five taken apart and the template hierarchy logged on a running site, and the birth of pagesco: the smallest block theme, a theme.json design system and the CSS it generates, a header part, two quiet mistakes, a book-fair theme lab and the start of the pagesco project.

2 lessons 3 hrs session Lessons 3.1–3.2 Checkpoint 1 Session 4 of 18 · Part 1

How to Use This Guide

  • Same rhythm for both lessons: frame (one mental model) → live demo (you type, they type along) → guided lab (a kit lab, new practice) → start the lesson's own project. Exercises, quizzes, journals and the rest of each project are homework.
  • Session 4 is a checkpoint session: the first 40 minutes are a short warm-up and Checkpoint 1 on Modules 1 and 2, so both lessons get less room time than usual. The cuts are planned below; do not let the checkpoint run over.
  • Every command below was run to produce the output printed under it, on WordPress 7.1.3, PHP 8.5, MySQL 9.7 and WP-CLI 2.12, on the site exactly as the lessons leave it: the checkpoint and Lesson 3.1 on the site of Lesson 2.3, Lesson 3.2 on the site of Lesson 3.1. Time stamps in debug.log lines differ on every run.
  • Keep lesson_07.html and lesson_08.html open: the hierarchy table, the full theme.json and the five templates are long, and learners paste them from the page in the room. Labs live in labs/module-04/: _starter files and folders are handouts, _solution ones and checkpoint_solution/ are yours.
  • Session 4 is where pagesco is born: learners leave with the theme active (finished at home). Sessions 5 to 7 and Part 1's project build on it.
The #1 risk of Session 4: two long lessons after a checkpoint

The lesson pages estimate 120 + 140 = 260 minutes; after the warm-up, the checkpoint, the break and the wrap-up the room has 120. Before: in Session 3's wrap-up, tell learners the checkpoint opens Session 4 (30 minutes, open site and closed notes, Modules 1 and 2, not a grade that follows them; Session 3's homework says so too) and that pagesco-site.php must be in mu-plugins/. In the room: start the checkpoint at 0:10 sharp, call time at 0:33 and collect at 0:40 whatever state it is in; in 3.2, learners PASTE theme.json and the templates from the lesson page and you spend the time on reading them. After: mark with the rubric; anyone under 5 gets a short conversation before Session 5.

Before the Session

  • ☐ In Session 3's wrap-up: announce Checkpoint 1 and its rules; ask learners to finish Lesson 2.3's project (pagesco-site.php in mu-plugins/), because the checkpoint builds on its hooks.
  • ☐ Run the kit check once: python3 labs/check_labs.py module-04 from this kit's folder (15 results, about a minute and a half). With your own project: WP_LABS_COMPOSE=~/pagesco-dev python3 labs/check_labs.py module-04 (labs/README.md; your site must be at the state each file names).
  • ☐ Projector machine: the course site at the end of Lesson 2.3 (Twenty Twenty-Five active, pagesco-site.php in mu-plugins/), two terminals in the project folder at 18 pt or larger (one for tail -f wordpress/wp-content/debug.log), VS Code open on wordpress/wp-content/themes/, the browser with http://localhost:8080 and lesson_07.html / lesson_08.html in tabs. Delete any pagesco folder from a rehearsal first: learners watch you create it.
  • ☐ Files to hand out: the checkpoint starter folder labs/module-04/checkpoint-1/checkpoint_starter/ with test_checkpoint.sh (on every laptop before 0:10), the labs/module-04/ starters, the workbook (its Checkpoint 1 page holds the task and the rubric). Keep checkpoint_solution/ and the *_solution* files back.
  • ☐ Board, before learners arrive: the three answers of wp_is_block_theme() / wp_theme_has_theme_json() (block true/true, hybrid false/true, classic false/false); a request arrow → "candidate list, most specific first" → "first one the theme has" → index; and a box theme.json = style guide · templates = floor plans · parts = signs.
  • ☐ Print: five copies of the rubric for your own marking, sticky notes for the exit ticket.

Opening Segment

0:00

Warm-up

10 min
Sequence
  • Retrieval (6m). Put W1 to W3 on the slide; learners write answers in the workbook, then run each command on their own site. Take answers from three different people; the answer key has the reasons.
  • State check (4m). "Twenty Twenty-Five active, two must-use plugins: hands up when W2 matches." Anyone whose pagesco-site.php is missing saves it now from Lesson 2.3's project on the lesson page (the checkpoint builds on its hooks), and anyone whose theme is not Twenty Twenty-Five runs wp theme activate twentytwentyfive.
Answers
  • W1 20: The priority: has_filter() returns the priority of that callback on that hook, or false. pagesco-site.php adds the late-opening text at 20, so it runs after a callback at the default 10.
  • W2 mailpit-smtp and pagesco-site: mailpit-smtp (Lesson 1.2) and pagesco-site (Lesson 2.3). Every PHP file in wp-content/mu-plugins/ runs on every request, before the normal plugins (the load order of Lesson 2.2).
  • W3 0: pagesco-site.php calls remove_action( 'wp_head', 'wp_generator' ), so the generator meta tag is never printed (and grep -c with no match exits 1).
0:10

Checkpoint 1 (Modules 1–2)

30 min
Timing
2mBrief: the workbook's Checkpoint 1 page; the starter is already in wordpress/wp-content/mu-plugins/ and the test in wordpress/
23mWork alone; open site, closed notes (their own course site, wp help, the starter's comments; no lesson pages, notes, neighbors or AI assistants)
5mSelf-check: run the test, compare with the workbook's "done" line, write one line "what I would fix with ten more minutes", hand in (file on a USB stick or the shared folder, or a photo of the test output)
What it checks

One small must-use plugin that uses every Module 1 and 2 skill at once: callbacks hooked by name with priorities, a filter that returns (2.3), Lesson 2.3's own custom hooks, WordPress functions that take an arguments array (1.3), the content model (posts in a category, a user and her author archive, 2.1), a prepared $wpdb query on the posts table (2.2), escaping at output and the pagesco_ prefix (1.3). Nothing from Module 3 is tested.

Say: "A readiness check for you and for me, not a grade that follows you. Work alone for 23 minutes. Partial work is fine. If (a) fights you, do (b) and (c) and come back."

The task as learners see it:

  • Start: cp labs/module-04/checkpoint-1/checkpoint_starter/pagesco-checkpoint.php wordpress/wp-content/mu-plugins/ and cp labs/module-04/checkpoint-1/test_checkpoint.sh wordpress/, then docker compose run --rm wpcli sh test_checkpoint.sh after each part.
  • (a) Latest news. pagesco_checkpoint_latest_news() on the filter pagesco_store_notice (your hook from Lesson 2.3), priority 30: add " Latest news: <title>." with the title of the newest post in the category News (slug news), found with get_posts() and an arguments array. Return the text.
  • (b) Ask Maria. pagesco_checkpoint_ask_link() on the action pagesco_store_notice_end, priority 20: print " · " and a link to the author archive of the user with the login maria, with the text "Ask " and her display name. Escape the URL and the text.
  • (c) Page count. pagesco_checkpoint_page_count() on wp_footer: <p class="pagesco-pages">Published pages: N</p>, N counted with ONE prepared $wpdb query on the posts table.
  • Rules: 23 minutes, alone, open site, closed notes (your own course site, WP-CLI with wp help, the starter's comments; no lesson pages, notes, neighbors or AI assistants). Partial work is fine. Done = the test shows the newest post, the link and the count, with no message in the page or in debug.log.
Rubric (2 / 1 / 0 per row, 10 points)
Criterion2 · Meets1 · Partly0 · Not yet

Reading the scores. 8 to 10: ready for Module 3's pace. 5 to 7: name the row that cost the points and the lesson to reread (row 1 → 2.3, row 2 → 1.3 and 2.1, row 3 → 1.3, row 4 → 2.2). 0 to 4: a five-minute conversation before Session 5, and the checkpoint redone at home, this time with the lesson pages open.

Watch-outs during the checkpoint
  • Do not help with the code. Answer only questions about the task wording. A learner whose site is broken (a fatal error in the mu-plugin takes WP-CLI down too, Lesson 2.3) may mv the file out of mu-plugins/ to read the error: that is debugging, and allowed.
  • The filter that echoes. The notice text vanishes. Do not point it out: rubric row 1 measures it.
  • Priority 20 forgotten in (b). "Ask Maria" lands before "See events": mu-plugins load alphabetically, so pagesco-checkpoint.php adds its callback before pagesco-site.php does. A good debrief question for Session 5's warm-up.
  • Collect at 0:40 sharp, whatever the state. Model answer and its test output are in the answer key.

Lesson Plans

3.1

Theme Anatomy & the Template Hierarchy

50 min
Objectives (from the lesson page)
  • Explain what belongs in a theme and what belongs in a plugin, and where WordPress records which theme is active
  • Tell block, classic and hybrid themes apart by their files, and confirm it with wp_is_block_theme() and wp_theme_has_theme_json()
  • Find your way around a block theme: style.css, theme.json, templates/, parts/, patterns/, styles/ and functions.php in Twenty Twenty-Five
  • Predict which template WordPress uses for a URL, for block themes and classic themes, from the template hierarchy
  • Watch WordPress make that choice on a running site with the *_template_hierarchy filters and template_include
Timing in the room
10mFrame: the shop fit-out; block, classic and hybrid; the information desk
15mLive demo: Twenty Twenty-Five taken apart, the hierarchy logged, the home.html mistake
15mGuided lab: which_template_starter.php
10mStart the lesson project (after the break): Step 1, the template map
Mental model to say

"Pages & Co. moves into a newly decorated shop. The books (content) and the till system (plugins) move across unchanged; the shelving, the signs, the paint (the theme) are new. A good fit-out can be replaced next year without losing a single book. That is the test for where code belongs: would we keep this after a redesign? Then it is a plugin."

Then the three kinds, on the board: block = templates/*.html + theme.json (true, true); classic = PHP templates (false, false); hybrid = classic plus a theme.json (false, true; not an official name). "You will meet all three on client sites for years."

Then the information desk: "A customer asks for Dune. The bookseller checks the most specific place first: a display for this book? a shelf for Frank Herbert? the science fiction section? Every shop has general shelves: in WordPress that is index, and every theme must have it." Write most specific first, the first one the theme has wins, index last.

Three mistakes to expect, and how to coach each
  • "home means the home page." Coach with the log from the demo and one question: "What does the front page show today, posts or a page?" home is the list of latest posts, wherever it lives. (Self-check Q5, lesson quiz Q3.)
  • Titles instead of slugs, or the type missing. page-About Us, single-hello-world. Coach: "Where would WordPress get that name from?" The slug, and posts include their post type. (Self-check Q1.)
  • Editing Twenty Twenty-Five to try something. Coach: "Who updates that folder?" Read it, never edit it; experiments go in a throwaway theme of their own, as in the project's Steps 2 to 5.

Start the lesson project

The lesson project is Map the Templates of Pages & Co.: the template map (Step 1), then a throwaway theme that goes classic, hybrid, block (Steps 2 to 5). After the break, Step 1 only (10 minutes); the logger from the demo is still in mu-plugins/.

  • Learners write the TEMPLATE MAP into pagesco-plan.txt, with the third column "pagesco will need". Ask: "How many templates does pagesco need?" (Six: index, single, page, archive, search, 404; index doubles as home.)
  • Done in the room = the map with eight rows and the six-template conclusion. Goes home: Steps 2 to 5, which end by deleting the sketch theme AND the logger (rm wp-content/mu-plugins/pagesco-template-map.php). Anyone who will not do the steps at home deletes the logger now: Lesson 3.2 expects only the two must-use plugins.
Checks for understanding

Ask these out loud during the demo and the lab:

  • What makes a theme a block theme? Answer: a templates/index.html (wp_is_block_theme() is true); theme.json alone makes it hybrid.
  • Which file does WordPress include for a block theme's page? Answer: core's wp-includes/template-canvas.php, which renders the block template and calls wp_head, wp_body_open and wp_footer.
  • The News category gets its own design. Which file? Answer: templates/category-news.html (slug before ID); every other category still falls through to archive.
  • A Site Editor save on a template: where does it go? Answer: a wp_template post with source custom, which wins over the file.

Workbook self-check, items Q1 to Q6 (learners do them at home).

Answers: Q1 B) page-about, page-12, page, singular, index; Q2 author-devon, author, archive, index; Q3 D) It disappears, with no message anywhere; Q4 A) So a child theme can define a function of the same name first and replace it; Q5 C) front-page.html; Q6 category_template_hierarchy. Full set with explanations in the Answer Key.

Differentiation

Support: pair learners who struggled in the checkpoint; for the lab, give them TODO 2's loop shape on the board (foreach ( ... as $c ) { if ( in_array( $c, $have, true ) ) { $used = $c; break; } }).

Stretch: the theme inspector and the debug handout; then the lesson's Exercise 4 (a custom page template assigned with _wp_page_template) and the Bonus Challenge (register_block_template(): who wins, theme or plugin?).

3.2

Building a Block Theme

70 min
Objectives (from the lesson page)
  • Write a theme header in style.css that WordPress reads and checks on activation
  • Define a design system in theme.json: settings (palette, fonts, sizes, spacing, layout) and styles (global, elements, blocks), and read the CSS WordPress generates from it
  • Write templates and template parts in block markup, combining static blocks with dynamic ones such as the Query Loop, Post Title and Post Content
  • Activate and verify a block theme with WP-CLI and the Site Editor, with site features such as the store notice still working
  • Diagnose an invalid theme.json, a missing template part and a Site Editor copy that overrides your file
Timing in the room
10mFrame: style guide, floor plans, signs; the file list from the template map
20mLive demo, typed along: the smallest theme, theme.json and its CSS, the header and index, two quiet mistakes
20mGuided lab: the book-fair theme (book_fair_starter/)
20mStart the lesson project: Step 1 (the full theme.json) and Step 2 (the footer part)
Mental model to say

"Designing a shop interior, you write a style guide first (the colors, the typefaces, the spacing), then floor plans for each room, then the signs you hang at every entrance. A block theme has the same three layers: theme.json is the style guide, templates are the floor plans, template parts are the signs. Change the style guide and every room follows."

Then the two halves of theme.json, side by side on the board: settings = what is available (the palette, font sizes, spacing steps, widths, which controls editors see); styles = what is applied (the page, elements such as links and headings, single block types), usually by pointing at a preset. And the file list from the template map: style.css, theme.json, two parts, six templates, no functions.php.

Three mistakes to expect, and how to coach each
  • Hex values in templates. "style":{"color":{"background":"#e3eadf"}} copied from somewhere. Coach: "What happens when the shop rebrands?" Presets: "backgroundColor":"sage". (Self-check Q8, the journal prompt.)
  • Hand-edited static markup that the editor calls invalid. Coach: "Build it in the Site Editor, open the Code editor, copy the markup" (the lesson's tip), and never save there for real in this course: a save makes a copy.
  • "My change does nothing." Three quiet causes, in this order: a JSON syntax error (debug.log), a slug that matches no file (look logged in), a Site Editor copy (wp post list --post_type=wp_template,wp_template_part). (Self-checks Q10 and Q11, lesson quiz Q5.)

Start the lesson project

The lesson project is Finish the pagesco Theme: the full design system, the footer, the five other templates and a check of every URL. In the room: Steps 1 and 2 (20 minutes); pagesco must be active again first.

  • Step 1: paste the full theme.json over the first one; read what it adds (appearanceTools, root padding, elements, blocks, the css string for the store notice, templateParts), then the lesson's grep for the link rule and the notice CSS. Stop on a:where(:not(.wp-element-button)): :where() adds no specificity, so content can override the theme.
  • Step 2: parts/footer.html; reload the home page and read the footer text.
  • Done in the room = a paper-colored site with the ink notice bar, sans headings and the dark footer. Goes home: Step 3 (single, page, archive, search, 404) and Step 4 (the per-URL loop: every page 200 with one notice, header, footer and h1; 404 for /nothing-here/).
Checks for understanding

Ask these out loud during the demo, the lab and the project start:

  • settings or styles: the five shop colors? The page background? Answer: settings (available); styles (applied, pointing at paper).
  • What does "inherit":true on the Query Loop mean? Answer: show what the main query found, so one block serves the blog home, every archive and the search page.
  • Why does the store notice appear in a theme that never mentions it? Answer: template-canvas.php fires wp_body_open for block themes, and pagesco-site.php hooks it.
  • A teammate's theme.json change has no effect and no message. First move? Answer: debug.log (a JSON syntax error is a Notice there), then the saved copies.

Workbook self-check, items Q7 to Q12 (learners do them at home).

Answers: Q7 1180px; Q8 C) font-size: var(--wp--preset--font-size--large); Q9 D) Post Title; Q10 A) The site in core's default design: the theme's colors, fonts and sizes are gone, with no message; Q11 parts/footer.html; it wraps the part in a <footer> element (the contentinfo landmark); Q12 B) Hides WordPress's own palette from the editors, so they choose from the theme's colors. Full set with explanations in the Answer Key.

Differentiation

Support: learners who fell behind in the demo copy the lesson's files in order (style.css, index.html, theme.json, header.html, index.html) and run the activate command: the build is the same, the reading happens at home with the lesson. Skip the book-fair lab for them and go straight to the project start.

Stretch: the theme.json reader and the café handout; the lesson's Exercise 4 (style every Quote block from theme.json) and the Bonus Challenge (the Navigation overlay colors, with contrast checked).

Closing

Exit ticket (3 questions, no notes, 4 minutes)

Put the questions on the slide; learners answer in the workbook's Exit Ticket box or on a sticky note. Question 2's pile tells you whether Session 5's warm-up goes back to settings and styles.

  1. A block theme has index.html, page.html and archive.html. Which draws /author/maria/, and why? Answer: archive.html: author-maria, author-2 and author do not exist, archive is the next candidate.
  2. In theme.json, where does the shop's palette go, and where the page's background color? Answer: settings.color.palette (what is available); styles.color.background as var:preset|color|paper (what is applied).
  3. Your header vanished and there is no message. Name two quiet causes. Answer: a template-part slug that matches no file; a Site Editor copy of the template or part; (a theme.json syntax error loses the styles, not the header).
Homework (about 2 to 3 hours)
  • Finish both lesson projects. 3.1: Steps 2 to 5 (the sketch theme classic → hybrid → block, then Twenty Twenty-Five back and the sketch theme and the logger deleted; read Common Mistakes 1 and 3 first). 3.2: Step 3 (the five other templates) and Step 4 (the per-URL verification loop), then the completion checklist: pagesco active, six templates with source theme.
  • Lesson exercises. 3.1: Exercises 1 to 3 (predict then ask core, the palette, style variations); Exercise 4 is a stretch. 3.2: Exercises 1 to 3 (a sixth color, a News template, the requirements check), each undone afterwards; Exercise 4 is a stretch.
  • Reading: 3.2 Common Mistake 3 (the Site Editor copy) and the FAQ; 3.1's anatomy table.
  • Both Quick Quizzes and both journal entries (the 3.2 prompt: which files would a rebrand touch?).
  • Checkpoint 1: anyone who did not finish redoes it at home with the lesson pages open and runs the test; under 5 points: bring questions to Session 5.
  • Optional: the labs not reached: labs/module-04/l3_1-theme-anatomy/theme_inspector_starter.sh, labs/module-04/l3_1-theme-anatomy/debug_theme_report.php, labs/module-04/l3_2-block-theme/theme_json_reader_starter.php, the café handout.
Bring list for Session 5
  • The site at the end of Lesson 3.2: pagesco active, the six templates and two parts, wp post list --post_type=wp_template,wp_template_part empty, mu-plugins/ = mailpit-smtp.php + pagesco-site.php.
  • pagesco-plan.txt with the template map checked off, the journal, the workbook.
  • One thing you would like the site to look different on a phone (Lesson 3.2, Before the Next Lesson): Session 5 adds patterns, a style variation and a child theme.

If You Run Long or Short

Running long: what to protect and what to cut first
  • Protect: the checkpoint's 30 minutes; an active pagesco with theme.json and the header part; the hierarchy log; the template map.
  • Cut first (saves 5m): the 3.1 functions.php step and the 3.2 part-slug mistake.
  • Cut second (saves 15m): the 3.1 guided lab: show the solution's output, send which_template home.
  • Cut third (saves 20m): the book-fair lab: go straight to the project start; the lab goes home.
Running short: what to add
  • 3.1 Mistake 3 live: the bare classic theme without wp_body_open(), the notice gone (then delete the theme).
  • 3.2 Exercise 2 together: templates/category-news.html with a welcome line, proved on the News archive and not on Maria's.
  • Open the Site Editor on the projector (Appearance > Editor > Templates), show the six templates with live data, and close without saving: "a save makes a copy".
Instructor Kit · Facilitator Guide

Session 5: Patterns, Style Variations and Child Themes

How to teach the second half of Module 3. Give the Pages & Co. theme ready-made sections: pattern files that stay translatable, a front page built from them, a synced pattern shared by two pages, a section style, and the Site Editor round trip that keeps files and database copies apart. Then customize a theme you did not write: a child of Twenty Twenty-Five, the merge rules of theme.json, a stylesheet that must be enqueued, and functions.php's load order, with a Twenty Twenty-Four child as the lab.

2 lessons 3 hrs session Lessons 3.3–3.4 Session 5 of 18 · Part 1

How to Use This Guide

  • Same rhythm for both lessons: frame (one mental model) → live demo (you type, they type along) → guided lab (a kit lab, new practice on the lesson's ideas) → start the lesson's own project. Exercises, the Quick Quiz and the journal are homework.
  • Type, do not paste. Every command below was run to produce the output printed under it, on WordPress 7.1.3 and PHP 8.5: for 3.3 a course site exactly as Lesson 3.2 leaves it (pagesco active, no patterns yet), for 3.4 the site at the end of Lesson 3.3. Ask for a prediction before every run. IDs (the synced pattern's 20, the template copy's 24) can differ on learners' sites; say so when they appear.
  • The lessons are the reference. Keep lesson_09.html and lesson_10.html open for the long file listings (hero.php, the about/contact markup, theme.json): paste-free typing of those is not the goal, reading them is. Labs live in labs/module-05/ (learners keep the folder in their project folder): _starter files and folders are handouts, _solution ones are yours.
  • Session 5 is Module 3's second half: the theme becomes something editors use (patterns, styles) and you learn to customize themes you did not write (child themes). It ends with pagesco active again, as Session 6 expects.
The #1 risk of Session 5: three copies of "the design"

After today the design of Pages & Co. lives in theme files, in synced patterns, in user global styles and in Site Editor template copies. Learners who click around in the Site Editor at home end the week with database copies that make every later output differ, and they do not know it. Before: the warm-up's second command counts the copies; anyone above 0 resets them. In the room: spend the full six minutes on the Site Editor round trip and write the loop on the board. After: "Before the Next Lesson" in 3.3 asks for the list of template, template-part and global-styles posts to be empty; make it the first line of the homework.

Before the Session

  • ☐ Learner sites: at the end of Lesson 3.2 (pagesco active with the ten files of the handoff, no Site Editor copies). Anyone who did not finish Session 4's project copies the lesson's files from lesson_08.html before class; the warm-up check shows who.
  • ☐ Run the kit check once: python3 labs/check_labs.py module-05 from this kit's folder (17 results in about two minutes; every line PASS). On your own course project: WP_LABS_COMPOSE=~/pagesco-dev python3 labs/check_labs.py module-05 (labs/README.md; your site must be at the states the module README lists).
  • ☐ Projector machine: a course site at the end of Lesson 3.2 for the 3.3 demo (and ready to continue into 3.4: the demo's commands build on each other), VS Code on the theme folder at a large font, two terminals in the project folder (one with docker compose run --rm wpcli sh open), the browser on http://localhost:8080/ and on Appearance > Editor, lesson_09.html and lesson_10.html in tabs.
  • ☐ Files to hand out: labs/module-05/ without the *_solution* files and folders; the workbook. The pagesco-content/ files of the synced-pattern demo are on the lesson page (learners copy them from there).
  • ☐ Board, before learners arrive: the three-tools table (theme pattern: a file, copied when inserted; synced pattern: a wp_block post, one original; template part: parts/, included by slug); the Site Editor loop (list copies → find the change → right file → delete the copy); and an empty inheritance table for 3.4 (style.css, theme.json, templates, patterns, styles/, functions.php) to fill during the demo.
  • ☐ Print or share: the workbook; sticky notes for the exit ticket.
Known traps today
SymptomCauseFix
A new pattern file is ignored, no messageThe 30-minute cache of pattern files (no development mode yet)wp config set WP_DEVELOPMENT_MODE theme (local only), or raise the theme's Version.
Notice: Function get_block_patterns was called incorrectly ... ("Slug" field missing)A pattern header without Slug:Add Slug: pagesco/<name> (letters, digits, /, _, -).
The hours vanished from About and ContactThe synced pattern was deleted (Patterns screen Delete is permanent)Recreate it from a copy with wp post create ... --import_id=<old ID> (Lesson 3.3, Common Mistakes 3).
The page shows the Evening colors after a demo clickSomeone saved a variation in the Site Editor: a wp_global_styles postStyles > ⋮ > Reset styles, or delete the post (wp post list --post_type=wp_global_styles).
The font never loads, no messageA wrong path after file:./ (or the folder name)Network tab, filter Font: the 404 names the path.
Error: The parent theme is missing. Please install the "twenty-twenty-five" parent theme.Template: has the display name instead of the folderTemplate: twentytwentyfive (the folder name from wp theme list).
The child's style.css has no effectA block child's style.css is not loaded until functions.php enqueues itThe lesson's pagesco_tt5_child_enqueue_styles() with the parent's handle as dependency.
Cannot redeclare twentytwentyfive_...() (in another parent)A non-pluggable parent function defined again in the childOnly functions wrapped in function_exists() can be replaced; otherwise remove the parent's hook on after_setup_theme.

In the room. The lesson pages estimate 145 + 125 = 270 minutes for a learner working alone; after the warm-up, the break and the wrap-up the room has 150. Lesson 3.3 keeps its core (patterns, the cache, front-page, synced patterns, a section style, the Site Editor loop) and sends its second half home: the Evening style variation and what the Site Editor saves when someone chooses it, the web font with fontFace and its license, the Export zip, Common Mistakes, the project's Steps 2 to 4. Protect, in this order: the Site Editor round trip in 3.3 (the hardest idea of the module); the theme.json merge rule with the partial palette; the stylesheet-nobody-loads moment and the load order; the synced pattern's one-edit-two-pages test. Cut first: the transient listing in the 3.3 demo (just say "a cache"), then the "Which tool" sorting (it becomes Exercise 3 at home), then the 3.4 project start (learners write the footer pattern at home; the lab practiced the same override).
