The readiness check (W5): the two commands

Learners run them in the project folder; the projector's site prints:

wp eval 'var_dump( wp_is_block_theme(), wp_theme_has_theme_json() );'
wp post list --post_type=wp_template,wp_template_part,wp_global_styles --format=count
bool(true)
bool(true)
0

Anything but 0 on the second line: the learner opened the Site Editor and saved. List the posts (wp post list --post_type=wp_template,wp_template_part,wp_global_styles --fields=ID,post_type,post_name) and delete them with wp post delete <ID> --force before the demo, or the front page they see will not be the one the lesson draws.

Warm-up answers
  1. W1 In theme.json, what is the difference between settings and styles? Answer: settings say what editors may choose (the palette, font sizes, layout widths); styles say what is applied (the page's colors, fonts, element and block styles). Presets in settings become custom properties and classes (Lesson 3.2).
  2. W2 The front page shows the latest posts. In a block theme, which templates does WordPress look for, in order? Answer: front-page, then home, then index (Lesson 3.1). pagesco has only index.html so far; Lesson 3.3 adds front-page.html today.
  3. W3 The manager changed the Single Posts template in the Site Editor. Where is that change, and which version does a visitor see? Answer: In the database, a wp_template post whose source is custom; it wins over templates/single.html until someone resets it (Lesson 3.2, Common Mistakes 3).
  4. W4 A template part is included as {"slug":"heder"}. What do visitors see? And a logged-in administrator? Answer: Visitors: nothing, the header is just missing. Logged in: "Template part has been deleted or is unavailable: heder" (Lesson 3.2).
  5. W5 Run the two commands on the slide. What should a site ready for today print? Answer: bool(true) twice (pagesco is a block theme with a theme.json), then 0: no Site Editor copies. A learner with copies resets them first (wp post delete ID --force), or today's outputs will not match.

Lesson Plans

3.3

Patterns, Style Variations & the Site Editor

70 min
Objectives (from the lesson page)
  • Write PHP pattern files with the right header fields, translatable text and escaped theme URLs, and place them in templates with the Pattern block
  • Explain the difference between theme patterns, synced patterns and template parts, and create a synced pattern that updates every page it is used on
  • Define section styles and a style variation as JSON files in styles/ and read what the Site Editor saves when someone chooses one
  • Bundle a web font with fontFace in theme.json, checking that its license allows redistribution
  • Bring Site Editor changes back into the theme's files with Export and WP-CLI, then reset the database copies
Timing in the room
10mFrame: the rubber stamp and the hanging sign; three tools in one table
25mLive demo: hero.php, the cache and development mode, front-page.html, a synced pattern, a section style, the Site Editor loop
20mGuided lab: hours_band_starter/ in pairs
15mStart the lesson project: Step 1 (featured books) and the start of Step 2
Mental model to say

"A theme pattern is a rubber stamp. You press it onto the page and get a perfect print; after that the print is just ink on paper, and changing the stamp does not change prints you already made. A synced pattern is a sign hung in several rooms: there is only one sign, so repainting it changes what every room shows. Template parts are the signs fixed to the building itself, at every entrance."

Then the table on the board, one row at a time, with the question that decides: must every copy change when the original changes? No: a theme pattern (a starting point). Yes, and it is content the owner runs: a synced pattern. Yes, and it is site structure: a template part.

Then the PHP argument in one breath: "Pattern files are PHP so they can be translated, build URLs that work on any site, and escape their output. Keep those three in mind; the Site Editor will take all three away from you at the end of the demo."

Live demo (you type, they follow)

Run everything in the WP-CLI container shell (docker compose run --rm wpcli sh), where wp, curl and grep all work. Files are saved in VS Code from the lesson page. Ready learners type along on their own Lesson 3.2 site.

  1. Nothing registered yet (2m). "The shop's staff face an empty canvas. Patterns are how you hand them finished sections." In the WP-CLI container shell, copy Twenty Twenty-Five's public-domain book image into the theme, then count the patterns whose name starts with pagesco/.

cp wp-content/themes/twentytwentyfive/assets/images/book-image.webp wp-content/themes/pagesco/assets/images/
ls wp-content/themes/pagesco/assets/images
wp eval 'echo count( array_filter( WP_Block_Patterns_Registry::get_instance()->get_all_registered(), fn( $p ) => str_starts_with( $p["name"], "pagesco/" ) ) ), "\n";'
    book-image.webp
0

    One edit, two pages. Then the rule, out loud: a synced pattern is a wp_block post referenced by ID, <!-- wp:block {"ref":20} /-->; IDs differ per site, so a theme never ships one. Leave pagesco-content/ for now (the lesson deletes it after Common Mistakes).
  7. A section style (3m). "A JSON file in styles/ with blockTypes is a section style: a color band editors apply to one Group." Save the lesson's styles/sections/section-sage.json. The hero already carries the class; look at what WordPress generated:

Three mistakes to expect, and how to coach each
  • "My pattern doesn't show up." Either the cache (no development mode: is_registered() is false and nothing says why) or a header without Slug: (a notice at the top of every page). Coach: "Ask the registry first, then read the top of the page." (Self-check Q1; the handout debug_pattern_files.sh.)
  • Copying the Site Editor's markup back over the file. It looks like the newest version. Coach: "Where is your wp:pattern line? What happened to esc_html_e()?" (Self-check Q4, the lesson quiz Q4.)
  • A synced pattern's reference in a theme file. <!-- wp:block {"ref":20} /--> in front-page.html "because it worked". Coach: "On the live site, what is post 20?" (Self-check Q3.)
Guided lab

Folder: labs/module-05/l3_3-patterns-style-variations/hours_band_starter/ with labs/module-05/l3_3-patterns-style-variations/test_hours_band.php; your reference is labs/module-05/l3_3-patterns-style-variations/hours_band_solution/. The folder is a one-file child theme of pagesco, so pagesco itself stays untouched ("Lesson 3.4 explains how this works, in an hour").

Start the lesson project

The lesson project is The Pages & Co. Front Page: featured books, an ink call to action with its own section style, the final front-page.html, a screenshot and a check of the whole site (about 45 minutes alone). In the room: Step 1 and the start of Step 2 (15 minutes).

  • Step 1: patterns/featured-books.php from the lesson: the books are a PHP array (the Book post type arrives in 5.2) looped into columns; prefixed variables, number_format_i18n(), a translators comment. Check it with the lesson's two wp eval lines.
  • Step 2, start: styles/sections/section-ink.json. Ask: "why do headings need their own color in a section style?" (theme.json's styles.elements.heading would not reach them.)
  • Done in the room = featured-books registered and printing three books. Goes home: the call-to-action pattern, Step 3 (the final front-page.html), Step 4 (screenshot, the per-URL loop), and before all of it the lesson's Evening and web-font sections, which Step 4's check expects (fonts:1).
Checks for understanding

Ask these out loud during the demo and the lab:

  • Theme pattern, synced pattern or template part: the shop's returns policy on six pages? Answer: a synced pattern (the lesson quiz Q2).
  • Why are pattern files PHP and not .html? Answer: translatable strings, URLs built for the site they run on, escaping.
  • What does WP_DEVELOPMENT_MODE theme switch off, and where must it never be set? Answer: the theme caches such as the pattern-file list; on production.
  • Where does the Site Editor store a saved template, and what happens to the patterns in it? Answer: a wp_template post (source custom); the patterns are expanded into plain blocks.

Workbook self-check, items Q1 to Q6 (learners do them at the end of the block or at home).

Answers: Q1 A) Raise the theme's Version in style.css; Q2 1 2: one site variation (Evening) and two section styles (Sage band, Ink band); Q3 C) <!-- wp:block {"ref":20} /-->; Q4 D) The pattern was expanded before saving: its PHP already ran, so the URL is hard-coded and the strings are frozen in English; Q5 B) Nothing: it is still a section style, because it has blockTypes; Q6 The browser's developer tools, Network tab filtered by Font: the font request answers 404, so the src path after file:./ (or the folder name) is wrong. Full set with explanations in the Answer Key.

Differentiation

Support: pair learners who are still unsure about block markup with someone who finished Session 4's project; they own the test runs, the partner edits. Point at the lesson's header-fields table while they do TODOs 1 and 2.

Stretch: the debug handout, then the lesson's Exercise 4 (pattern overrides) and the Bonus Challenge (a "Meet the staff" pattern offered on pages but not in templates: which header?).

3.4

Child Themes & Customizing Existing Themes

80 min
Objectives (from the lesson page)
  • Create and activate a child theme with the Template header, and explain the template and stylesheet options it sets
  • Predict how a child's theme.json, templates, template parts, patterns and style variations combine with the parent's
  • Use a child functions.php to enqueue the child's stylesheet, replace a pluggable parent function and remove a parent hook at the right time
  • Build a classic child theme and explain how get_stylesheet_directory(), get_template_directory() and locate_template() choose files
  • Choose between the Site Editor, a child theme, your own theme and a plugin for a requested change
Timing in the room
10mFrame: tracing paper over a floor plan; the inheritance table
25mLive demo: the one-file child, template and stylesheet, theme.json merged and broken, the stylesheet nobody loads, the load order, a hook removed too early
20mGuided lab: tt4_child_starter/
15mStart the lesson project: Steps 1 and 2
10mWhich tool for which change? (the lesson's decision table, as a sorting exercise)
Mental model to say

"Picture the parent theme as an architect's printed floor plan. You lay tracing paper on top and draw only what you want different. Anyone looking at the stack sees the combined plan. When the architect sends a revised plan, you slide your tracing paper onto the new print, and your changes are still there."

Then fill the table on the board during the demo, one row per step: style.css the child's header replaces it, its CSS loads only if enqueued · theme.json merged, but preset lists replaced · templates, parts same name replaces · patterns same slug wins · styles/ same file name replaces · functions.php both run, the child's first.

And the warning that frames the end of the lesson: "A child theme is still a theme. Switch themes in three years and everything in it is gone. That is why the store notice is a plugin and the Book post type will be one too."

  3. The stylesheet nobody loads (4m). Append the lesson's notice rule to the child's style.css, then ask whether the page loads the file: 
    curl -s http://localhost:8080/ | grep -c 'pagesco-tt5-child/style.css'
    0
    Zero. A block theme's style.css is a header file first; CSS is loaded only when functions.php enqueues it, and Twenty Twenty-Five enqueues its own with get_parent_theme_file_uri(). Save the lesson's first functions.php: 
    <?php
/**
 * Pages & Co. TT5 Child functions and definitions.
 *
 * @package pagesco-tt5-child
 */

/**
 * Loads the child theme's style.css after the parent's styles.
 */
function pagesco_tt5_child_enqueue_styles() {
	wp_enqueue_style(
		'pagesco-tt5-child-style',
		get_stylesheet_uri(),
		array( 'twentytwentyfive-style' ),
		wp_get_theme()->get( 'Version' )
	);
}
add_action( 'wp_enqueue_scripts', 'pagesco_tt5_child_enqueue_styles' );
    curl -s http://localhost:8080/ | grep -o "<link rel='stylesheet' id='pagesco-tt5-child-style-css'[^>]*>\|<style id=\"twentytwentyfive-style-inline-css\">"
    <style id="twentytwentyfive-style-inline-css">
<link rel='stylesheet' id='pagesco-tt5-child-style-css' href='http://localhost:8080/wp-content/themes/pagesco-tt5-child/style.css?ver=1.0.0' media='all' />
    The parent's CSS inlined, the child's <link> after it, with the child's Version. The dependency on twentytwentyfive-style is what puts it second.
  4. Who loads first? (3m). "Both functions.php files run. In which order?" 
    wp eval 'foreach ( get_included_files() as $f ) { if ( str_contains( $f, "/themes/" ) ) { echo $f, "\n"; } }'
    /var/www/html/wp-content/themes/pagesco-tt5-child/functions.php
/var/www/html/wp-content/themes/twentytwentyfive/functions.php
    Child first, then parent. Two consequences, both used in the project: pluggable parent functions (wrapped in function_exists()) can be replaced by defining them in the child; parent hooks cannot be removed yet when the child's file runs.
  5. Mistake 3: removing a parent hook too early (5m). Append the lesson's logging line to the end of the child's functions.php (it removes Twenty Twenty-Five's block styles at the top level and logs what remove_action() returns), then check: 
    error_log( 'remove_action returned ' . var_export( remove_action( 'init', 'twentytwentyfive_block_styles' ), true ) );

wp eval 'var_dump( WP_Block_Styles_Registry::get_instance()->is_registered( "core/list", "checkmark-list" ) );'
grep 'remove_action returned' wp-content/debug.log | tail -n 1
    bool(true)
[26-Oct-2026 13:24:18 UTC] remove_action returned false
    Still registered, and the only clue is the return value you logged: false, nothing to remove yet. The fix is a callback on after_setup_theme, which the project's Step 2 writes. Then switch back so the site stays as the lesson expects: 
    wp theme activate pagesco

Three mistakes to expect, and how to coach each
  • The display name in Template:. Twenty Twenty-Five or twenty-twenty-five. Coach: "Which column of wp theme list is the folder?" (Self-check Q7.)
  • Half a palette. Only the colors they wanted to change. Coach with the demo's count: "How many accent variables does the page define now?" (Self-check Q9.)
  • Removing or replacing at the wrong moment. A top-level remove_action() that returns false, or redefining a parent function that is not pluggable (Cannot redeclare). Coach: "Which file runs first? Is the parent's function wrapped in function_exists()?" (Self-check Q10; debug_child_theme.sh.)

Start the lesson project

The lesson project is Finish pagesco-tt5-child (about 40 minutes alone). In the room: Steps 1 and 2 (15 minutes).

  • Step 1: patterns/footer.php with the parent's slug twentytwentyfive/footer, the parent's presets and the child's text domain. Check the footer text on the home page.

Which tool for which change? (10m)

The lesson's decision table as a quick sort: read five requests aloud, learners hold up S (Site Editor), C (child theme), T (own theme) or P (plugin), then one volunteer says who owns the change and whether it must survive a theme switch.

  1. "Make the buttons a different red; we may change it again at Christmas." S: owner-changeable, database.
  2. "Remove the comments from all posts on our Twenty Twenty-Five site, for good." C: copy single.html, delete one line, in Git.
  3. "A booking form for author readings." P: a feature with data and security (Module 5).
  4. "Our design has outgrown Twenty Twenty-Five: new templates everywhere." T: your own theme (Lessons 3.2 and 3.3).
  5. "The store notice must survive any redesign." P: it already is a must-use plugin (Lesson 2.3).

Self-check Q12 and the lesson's Exercise 3 are the same skill; the journal prompt asks for the real-life version.

Checks for understanding

Ask these out loud during the demo and the lab:

  • With a child active, which option holds the parent? Answer: template (the lesson quiz Q1).
  • The child has no templates/index.html. Which file draws the blog home? Answer: the parent's index.html; single comes from the child.
  • Why does the child's stylesheet need array( 'twentytwentyfive-style' )? Answer: so it prints after the parent's and wins ties; the dependency must be a handle the parent really registers.
  • Why can't a top-level remove_action() remove a parent hook? Answer: the child's functions.php runs first; the parent has not added the hook yet.

Workbook self-check, items Q7 to Q12.

Answers: Q7 B) It refuses: the parent theme is missing, and the theme is listed under Broken Themes; Q8 pagesco-tt5-child, then twentytwentyfive; Q9 A) They disappear: the child's palette replaces the parent's whole palette, and styles that use accent variables silently lose their colors; Q10 D) The child's functions.php loads first, and the parent defines that function only if ( ! function_exists( ... ) ); Q11 C) array(); Q12 The Site Editor's Styles: a visual choice the owner wants to change again; it is saved in the database (the user global styles) and needs no developer. Full set with explanations in the Answer Key.

Differentiation

Support: learners who find the TT24 lab too open do TODOs 1 and 2 only, with the lesson's child files open side by side; TODOs 3 and 4 go home. The workbook's worked example lists the lesson child's files and where each template comes from.

Stretch: merge_layers_starter.php and the debug handout; the lesson's Exercise 4 (a child file that replaces TWO parent variations: why the count drops to 22) and the Bonus Challenge (override only the hidden-written-by pattern).

Closing

Exit ticket (3 questions, no notes, 4 minutes)

Put the three questions on the slide. Learners answer in the workbook's Exit Ticket box or on a sticky note. Question 2's pile tells you whether Session 6's warm-up needs the three-copies picture again.

  1. Theme pattern or synced pattern: the shop's opening hours on four pages? And a hero section for new landing pages? Answer: synced (one original, edit once); theme pattern (a starting point, copied and then edited).
  2. Name two places where the Site Editor stores changes, and the command that lists them. Answer: wp_template / wp_template_part posts and the wp_global_styles post; wp post list --post_type=wp_template,wp_template_part,wp_global_styles.
  3. In a child theme, which runs first, the child's functions.php or the parent's, and what does that mean for removing a parent hook? Answer: the child's; remove the hook in a callback on after_setup_theme.

If You Run Long or Short

Running long: what to protect and what to cut first
  • Protect: the Site Editor round trip; the merge rule with the partial palette; the stylesheet nobody loads and the load order.
  • Cut first (saves 3m): the transient listing in the 3.3 demo; say "a cache keyed on the theme's version" and move on to development mode.
  • Cut second (saves 10m): the "Which tool" sort; it is the lesson's Exercise 3 and self-check Q12 at home.
  • Cut third (saves 15m): the 3.4 project start; the TT4 lab practiced the same pattern override and pluggable function.
Running short: what to add
  • Do the Evening variation live: create styles/evening.json, choose it in Appearance > Editor > Styles, show the wp_global_styles post, reset it. Then the three-copies picture is complete.
  • Run debug_child_theme.sh for everyone and fix it together, one bug per volunteer, reading debug.log after each run.
  • The 3.3 Common Mistake 3 live: delete the synced pattern, watch the hours vanish from two pages, recreate it with --import_id.
Instructor Kit · Facilitator Guide

Session 6: The Loop and Custom Queries

How to teach Module 4's first two lessons. Build pagesco-classic and show what a classic template really does: walk the posts the main query already found, with template tags printed or returned, parts and conditional tags. Then ask for lists of your own: secondary queries and their three numbers, the reset that keeps template tags honest, pre_get_posts with guards, and pagination that never ends in a 404.

2 lessons 3 hrs session Lessons 4.1–4.2 Session 6 of 18 · Part 1

How to Use This Guide

  • Same rhythm for both lessons: frame (one mental model) → live demo (you type, they type along) → guided lab (new practice on the lesson's ideas) → start the lesson's own project. Exercises, the Quick Quiz and the journal are homework.
  • Type, do not paste. Every command below was run to produce the output printed under it, on WordPress 7.1.3 and PHP 8.5: for 4.1 a course site exactly as Lesson 3.4 leaves it (pagesco active), for 4.2 the site at the end of Lesson 4.1 (pagesco-classic active). Ask for a prediction before every run.
  • The lessons are the reference. Keep lesson_11.html and lesson_12.html open for the template listings: reading them aloud matters more than typing them fast. Labs live in labs/module-06/: _starter files and folders are handouts, _solution ones are yours.
  • Session 6 turns to the classic theme world most existing sites live in: pagesco-classic is built today and stays active until Lesson 4.3 switches back. The Loop and WP_Query are also how plugins and dynamic blocks print posts later (Modules 5 and 6).
The #1 risk of Session 6: the bugs are quiet

Every mistake in these two lessons produces no message: a title before an empty heading, a template part that is not found, a page-2 link that 404s, navigation computed for the wrong post, a callback that changes every query on the site. Learners who only watch for errors will miss all of them. In the room: for every demo step ask "which query is this, and has it run yet?" and make learners compare what they see with what they expected. After: the self-check and the two debug handouts are built from exactly these quiet bugs.

Before the Session

  • ☐ Learner sites: at the end of Lesson 3.4: pagesco active, pagesco-tt5-child installed, no Site Editor copies (the warm-up's two commands show it).
  • ☐ Run the kit check once: python3 labs/check_labs.py module-06 from this kit's folder (15 results in about a minute and a half; every line PASS). On your own project: WP_LABS_COMPOSE=~/pagesco-dev python3 labs/check_labs.py module-06.
  • ☐ Projector machine: a course site at the end of Lesson 3.4 for the 4.1 demo (it continues into 4.2), VS Code on wp-content/themes/pagesco-classic/, two terminals (one with docker compose run --rm wpcli sh, one with tail -f wordpress/wp-content/debug.log), the browser on http://localhost:8080/ with View Source handy, lesson_11.html and lesson_12.html in tabs.
  • ☐ Files to hand out: labs/module-06/ without the *_solution* files and folders; the workbook.
  • ☐ Board, before learners arrive: the Loop as a loop (have_posts()? → the_post() → template tags → back), the request order (URL → query vars → main query → template → the Loop), and the decision table of 4.2 (change the main list: pre_get_posts · an extra list: new WP_Query + wp_reset_postdata · just data: get_posts).
  • ☐ Print or share: the workbook; sticky notes for the exit ticket.
Known traps today
SymptomCauseFix
The page hangs, then a fatal "Maximum execution time of 30 seconds exceeded"A Loop without the_post()Every while ( have_posts() ) needs the_post() inside.
Each title appears BEFORE an empty headingA the_ tag concatenated into a stringget_the_title() in strings, or the_title( $before, $after ).
Block comments in the page source, synced pattern or shortcode emptyget_the_content() printed directlythe_content(), or apply_filters( 'the_content', get_the_content() ).
A template part prints nothing, no message.php in the slug, or a typoNo extension; var_dump() the return value (false = not found).
Notice: Function is_home was called incorrectlyA conditional tag at the top level of a pluginAsk inside a callback on template_redirect (or later).
Page 2 of a list answers 404A custom WP_Query paged in the templatepre_get_posts on the main query; the_posts_pagination().
Previous/next links point at the wrong postsA secondary Loop without wp_reset_postdata()wp_reset_postdata() right after the while.
WP-CLI or the admin shows one postA pre_get_posts callback without guardsis_admin(), $query->is_main_query(), the query's own conditionals.
'cat' => 'news' returns everythingcat takes IDs'category_name' => 'news'.

Warm-up answers
  1. W1 Theme pattern or synced pattern: which one is a post in the database, and why does a theme never ship one? Answer: The synced pattern: a wp_block post referenced by ID, and IDs differ on every site (Lesson 3.3).
  2. W2 Two JSON files in styles/: what makes one a section style and the other a style variation? Answer: The blockTypes key: with it, a section style for the listed blocks; without it, a look for the whole site.
  3. W3 A child theme is active. What do the template and stylesheet options hold? Answer: template = the parent's folder, stylesheet = the child's (Lesson 3.4).
  4. W4 Why did the child's style.css not load until functions.php enqueued it, and why must a parent hook be removed on after_setup_theme? Answer: A block theme's style.css is a header file; CSS loads only when enqueued. The child's functions.php runs first, so the parent's hooks do not exist yet when it runs.
  5. W5 Run the two commands on the slide. What should a site ready for today print? Answer: pagesco active, pagesco-tt5-child inactive (Twenty Twenty-One deleted), and 0 Site Editor copies. Today's demo starts by building pagesco-classic and switching to it.

Lesson Plans

4.1

The Loop & Template Tags

70 min
Objectives (from the lesson page)
  • Explain what the Loop does with the main query, step by step, and write it correctly with have_posts() and the_post()
  • Use template tags and their the_ / get_ pairs, and choose between printing and returning (and escaping) a value
  • Split a classic theme into header.php, footer.php and template parts with get_template_part(), including passing arguments
  • Use conditional tags such as is_home(), is_singular() and is_search(), and say when they work and when they are called too early
  • Build pagesco-classic with index.php, singular.php and 404.php, and turn it into a hybrid theme with theme.json
Timing in the room
10mFrame: the reading list at the till
25mLive demo: two files, every list, the Loop in core, template tags, parts, conditional tags, Mistake 1
20mGuided lab: shelf_theme_starter/
15mStart the lesson project: Step 1, singular.php
Mental model to say

"A customer hands the bookseller a list of books they ordered. The bookseller does not search the shop again; the list is done. They go down it one line at a time: is there another book on the list? (have_posts()) Take the next one off the pile and put it on the counter (the_post()). Read out its title, author and price (template tags). Start again. If they forget to take the next book off the pile, they read out the same title forever."

Then the request on the board: URL → query vars → the main query → the template → the Loop. "The template never asks which posts. It only walks the list." And the two-halves rule for template tags: the_ prints HTML-ready text, get_ returns a value you escape for its spot.

    grep -n "^function have_posts\|^function the_post\|^function rewind_posts\|^function in_the_loop" wp-includes/query.php

1018:function the_post() {
    have_posts() asks $wp_query; the_post() moves on and calls setup_postdata(), which sets the global $post every template tag reads. Say the warning out loud: a Loop without the_post() never ends (30 seconds, then a fatal timeout).
  3. Template tags (4m). Save the lesson's second index.php (an article per post). Predict: which tags print, which return? 
    <?php
/**
 * The main template file. For now it does everything itself.
 *
 * @package pagesco-classic
 */

?>
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html <?php language_attributes(); ?>>
<head>
	<meta charset="<?php bloginfo( 'charset' ); ?>">
	<title><?php echo esc_html( wp_get_document_title() ); ?></title>
	<?php wp_head(); ?>
</head>
<body <?php body_class(); ?>>
<?php wp_body_open(); ?>
<main>
	<?php
	if ( have_posts() ) {
		while ( have_posts() ) {
			the_post();
			?>

				<h2><a href="<?php the_permalink(); ?>"><?php the_title(); ?></a></h2>
				<p><?php echo esc_html( get_the_date() ); ?> by <?php the_author(); ?></p>
				<?php the_excerpt(); ?>
			</article>
			<?php
		}
	} else {
		echo '<p>Nothing here yet.</p>';
	}
	?>
</main>
<?php wp_footer(); ?>
</body>
</html>

    Each title BEFORE an empty heading: PHP evaluates the string first, the_title() prints on the spot and returns null. Fix: get_the_title() inside strings, or the_title( $before, $after ). Delete the scratch file (rm wp-content/themes/pagesco-classic/category-news.php).
Three mistakes to expect, and how to coach each
  • Concatenating a tag that prints. Coach: "Does this function print or return? Then what does the string contain?" (Self-check Q3; debug_loop_report.php.)
  • Forgetting the_post(). The page hangs for 30 seconds. Coach: "Who moves the list on?" (Self-check Q6.)
  • Conditional tags too early. In a must-use plugin's top level, or in functions.php outside a callback. Coach: "Has the main query run yet? Which hook comes after it?" (Self-check Q5.)

Checks for understanding

Ask these out loud during the demo and the lab:

  • Who decides which posts a classic template shows? Answer: the main query, before the template runs.
  • the_title() or get_the_title() inside echo '<h2>' . ... . '</h2>'? Answer: get_the_title(), escaped.
  • Which file loads get_template_part( 'template-parts/content', 'none' ) first? Answer: content-none.php (the lesson quiz Q5).
  • Why can conditional tags not be used at the top of a must-use plugin? Answer: the main query has not run; they return false and WordPress says so.

Workbook self-check, items Q1 to Q6.

Answers: Q1 B) index.php, with a Loop over Maria's posts; Q2 bool(false) and string(0) "": WP-CLI loads WordPress but runs no main query, so is_home() has nothing to answer from and there is no current post for get_the_title(); Q3 D) title="<?php the_title_attribute(); ?>" and the_title( '<h2>', '</h2>' );; Q4 A) It looked for template-parts/content.php.php, found nothing and returned false; Q5 C) template_redirect; Q6 The main query holds exactly one post, and the_post() is what sets the global $post that every template tag reads (and fires loop_start / loop_end for plugins). Full set with explanations in the Answer Key.

Differentiation

Support: learners who are new to PHP templates work TODOs 1 and 2 of the Shelf lab only, with the lesson's second index.php open as a model; the heading can stay "TODO". The workbook's worked example shows the body classes per URL.

Stretch: the debug handout; the lesson's Exercise 3 (category.php with found_posts and _n()) and Exercise 4 (two passes with rewind_posts()); the Bonus Challenge (the get_template_part_{$slug} action).

4.2

Custom Queries

80 min
Objectives (from the lesson page)
  • Tell the main query from secondary queries, and pick WP_Query, get_posts() or pre_get_posts for a task
  • Write WP_Query arguments for post types, categories, authors, dates, searches, ordering and limits, and read found_posts and max_num_pages
  • Run a secondary Loop on the same page as the main one and restore the current post with wp_reset_postdata()
  • Change the main query with a pre_get_posts callback guarded by is_main_query() and is_admin()
  • Paginate lists with the_posts_pagination(), and explain why paging a custom query in a template leads to a 404
Timing in the room
10mFrame: the customer's order and the shop's displays
25mLive demo: a secondary query, the reset, pre_get_posts, pagination, two mistakes
20mGuided lab: query_shelf_starter.php
15mStart the lesson project: Step 1, front-page.php
10mWhich query? (the decision table as a sort)
Mental model to say

"The main query is the customer's order at the counter: they asked for News, so they get News, and the whole page is organized around it. Secondary queries are the displays next to the counter, staff picks, you might also like; they never change the order. And when you want the order itself to be different, news in bundles of three, you do not grab the receipt after it is printed; you tell the person taking orders before they write it down. That is pre_get_posts."

Then the decision table on the board, with one question per row: does it change the page's own list? pre_get_posts. Is it an extra list with template tags? new WP_Query, then wp_reset_postdata(). Do you only need the data? get_posts(). query_posts() gets a line through it.

  2. pre_get_posts: tell the order-taker, before the order is written (6m). "The shop wants three posts per page on the home page. A WP_Query in the template looks right on page 1 and breaks on page 2." Where can you change the main query? Line 1916 of class-wp-query.php:

    <?php
/**
 * Pages & Co. Classic functions and definitions.
 *
 * @package pagesco-classic
 */

/**
 * Shows three posts per page on the blog home.
 *
 * @param WP_Query $query The query WordPress is about to run.
 */
function pagesco_classic_adjust_main_query( $query ) {
	if ( is_admin() || ! $query->is_main_query() ) {
		return;
	}

	if ( $query->is_home() ) {
		$query->set( 'posts_per_page', 3 );
	}
}
add_action( 'pre_get_posts', 'pagesco_classic_adjust_main_query' );

Three mistakes to expect, and how to coach each
  • A custom query where the main query should change. "Pages of three" done in the template; page 2 404s. Coach: "Which query does WordPress use to decide that page 2 exists?" (Self-check Q8 and Q12; the lesson quiz Q1.)
  • No wp_reset_postdata(). The related box and the wrong navigation. Coach: "Which post is the global $post right now?" (Self-check Q10; debug_related_box.php.)
  • Argument names of the wrong kind. cat with a slug, author with a login, p with a slug: no warning, too much data. Coach: "Slug or ID? Check the argument table." (The lesson's Common Mistakes 4; the guided lab's TODO 1.)

The helper prints post_count, found_posts and max_num_pages for each.

Which query? (10m)

Read each request; learners answer P (pre_get_posts), Q (new WP_Query + reset) or G (get_posts()), then one says why.

  1. "News in pages of three on the blog home." P: the page's own list; pagination agrees.
  2. "Three links to our pages above the news." Q: an extra list with template tags (the project).
  3. "An array of page URLs for a sitemap I build in PHP." G: data, no template tags.
  4. "Search results: posts only." P: the lesson's Exercise 1.
  5. "Other posts from this category under each post." Q: the related box, with its reset.
  6. "Count the News posts for a dashboard number." Q or G with fields ids; found_posts, or count() of the array.
Checks for understanding

Ask these out loud during the demo and the lab:

  • What do post_count, found_posts and max_num_pages mean? Answer: on this page; in total; pages of this size.
  • Why the guard $query->is_main_query()? Answer: the callback runs for every query on the site.
  • /page/3/ answers 404 before your template runs. Who decided? Answer: WordPress, from the main query's result.
  • After get_posts(), do you reset? Answer: no, as long as you pass each post along.

Workbook self-check, items Q7 to Q12.

Answers: Q7 2 0: two pages loaded; found_posts is 0 because no_found_rows skips the counting query; Q8 B) Every other WP_Query that runs on the blog home (a box, a widget, a block) is also cut to three posts; Q9 A) 1, 7, 3; Q10 D) After get_posts(), when each WP_Post is passed to the functions you call (get_the_title( $post )); Q11 C) If it changes the page's main list: pre_get_posts on the main query (category_name, posts_per_page); if it adds a list: new WP_Query plus wp_reset_postdata(); Q12 (a) a secondary WP_Query (or get_posts()) with posts_per_page 3, plus wp_reset_postdata() after a Loop; (b) pre_get_posts on the main query (is_post_type_archive( 'book' ), posts_per_page 12). Full set with explanations in the Answer Key.

Stretch: the archive-rules folder lab and the debug handout; the lesson's Exercise 4 (sticky posts and pagination) and the Bonus Challenge (two News posts per page the right way, then decide whether the shop wants it).

Closing

Exit ticket (3 questions, no notes, 4 minutes)

Put the three questions on the slide. Question 3's pile tells you whether Session 7's warm-up needs the order-taker picture again.

  1. In one sentence: what does the Loop do, and what does the_post() do inside it? Answer: it walks the posts the main query already found; the_post() moves to the next one and sets the global $post the template tags read.
  2. Name a template tag pair and say when you use each half. Answer: for example the_title() / get_the_title(): the_ prints HTML-ready text; get_ returns a value you escape yourself, for attributes, strings or further processing.
  3. The blog home should show three posts per page. Where does that change go, and which two guards must it have? Answer: a pre_get_posts callback (functions.php or a plugin) with is_admin() / $query->is_main_query(), then $query->is_home().

If You Run Long or Short

Running long: what to protect and what to cut first
  • Protect: index.php drawing every list; printed vs returned; pre_get_posts with guards; the paged custom query's 404.
  • Cut first (saves 5m): the parts step of the 4.1 demo; show the finished index.php and move on.
  • Cut second (saves 10m): the "Which query" sort; self-check Q12 and the 4.2 journal cover it.
  • Cut third (saves 15m): the 4.2 project start; the guided lab already practiced the arguments.
Running short: what to add
  • Run debug_related_box.php for everyone and fix it together; the reset bug only appears after the loud one is fixed.
  • The 4.2 Common Mistake 2 live (the related box without the reset and the wrong navigation), then the fix.
  • The 4.1 Exercise 3 live: category.php with found_posts and _n(), for News and Uncategorized.

Objectives (from the lesson page)
  • Explain when functions.php runs and choose the right hook for theme setup, widgets and assets
  • Declare theme supports such as title-tag and html5 with add_theme_support(), and say which ones block themes get automatically
  • Enqueue a stylesheet and a deferred script with wp_enqueue_style() and wp_enqueue_script(), with dependencies and a version that busts browser caches
  • Register a menu location and a widget area, print them with wp_nav_menu() and dynamic_sidebar(), and fill them from WP-CLI
  • Add the accessibility and translation basics every theme needs: a skip link, screen-reader text, labeled navigation and strings WordPress can translate
Timing in the room
10mFrame: the fit-out instructions; the hook timeline
25mLive demo: supports, two titles, block-theme defaults, the stylesheet and script, the menu, the widget area
20mGuided lab: corner_theme_starter/
15mStart the lesson project: Step 1 and Step 3
15mAfter the break: accessibility, translation, Common Mistake 1
Mental model to say

"If the templates are the floor plans of the shop, functions.php is the sheet of instructions the theme hands the building manager when it moves in: we need the shop sign handled by you (theme supports), please deliver these crates of paint and these tools (stylesheets and scripts), there will be a directory board here and a notice board there (a menu location and a widget area). The manager, WordPress, does the actual work at the right moment of each day."

Then the timeline on the board, and the convention: one small, prefixed function per job, each hooked to its moment. "That is the real reason a classic template must call wp_head() and wp_footer(): without them, nobody can add a single stylesheet or script."

Live demo (you type, they follow)

Starts from the end of Lesson 4.2 (pagesco-classic active). Run commands in the WP-CLI container shell; save files in VS Code from the lesson page.

  1. functions.php runs everywhere (2m). "It is not a template: WordPress includes it on every request while the theme is active, WP-CLI included." 
    wp eval 'var_dump( function_exists( "pagesco_classic_adjust_main_query" ), did_action( "after_setup_theme" ) );'
    bool(true)
int(1)
    Your 4.2 function exists in a WP-CLI command, and after_setup_theme has fired once. So: almost everything in functions.php belongs in a callback on the right hook.
  2. Theme supports (5m). Look at the search form a classic theme gets by default: 
    wp eval 'echo get_search_form( array( "echo" => false ) );'

    The xhtml form of the early 2000s. Replace functions.php with the lesson's version (pagesco_classic_setup() on after_setup_theme: title-tag, automatic-feed-links, post-thumbnails, responsive-embeds, html5), then count the titles: 
    <?php
/**
 * Pages & Co. Classic functions and definitions.
 *
 * @package pagesco-classic
 */

/**
 * Sets up translations and the theme features WordPress should provide.
 */
function pagesco_classic_setup() {
	load_theme_textdomain( 'pagesco-classic', get_template_directory() . '/languages' );

	add_theme_support( 'title-tag' );
	add_theme_support( 'automatic-feed-links' );
	add_theme_support( 'post-thumbnails' );
	add_theme_support( 'responsive-embeds' );
	add_theme_support(
		'html5',
		array( 'search-form', 'comment-form', 'comment-list', 'gallery', 'caption', 'navigation-widgets' )
	);
}
add_action( 'after_setup_theme', 'pagesco_classic_setup' );

/**
 * Shows three posts per page on the blog home.
 *
 * @param WP_Query $query The query WordPress is about to run.
 */
function pagesco_classic_adjust_main_query( $query ) {
	if ( is_admin() || ! $query->is_main_query() ) {
		return;
	}

	if ( $query->is_home() ) {
		$query->set( 'posts_per_page', 3 );
	}
}
add_action( 'pre_get_posts', 'pagesco_classic_adjust_main_query' );
    curl -s http://localhost:8080/about/ | grep '<title>'
    	<title>About Us &#8211; Pages &amp; Co.</title>
	<title>About Us &#8211; Pages &amp; Co.</title>

  4. A versioned stylesheet and a deferred script (5m). Save the lesson's assets/js/navigation.js (it adds the class that hides the menu only once it runs), then append the enqueue callback to functions.php: 
    /**
 * Loads the theme's stylesheet and its menu script.
 */
function pagesco_classic_enqueue_assets() {
	$version = wp_get_theme( get_template() )->get( 'Version' );

	wp_enqueue_style(
		'pagesco-classic-style',
		get_parent_theme_file_uri( 'style.css' ),
		array(),
		$version
	);

	wp_enqueue_script(
		'pagesco-classic-navigation',
		get_parent_theme_file_uri( 'assets/js/navigation.js' ),
		array(),
		$version,
		array(
			'strategy'  => 'defer',
			'in_footer' => true,
		)
	);
}
add_action( 'wp_enqueue_scripts', 'pagesco_classic_enqueue_assets' );
    curl -s http://localhost:8080/ | grep 'pagesco-classic-'
    <link rel='stylesheet' id='pagesco-classic-style-css' href='http://localhost:8080/wp-content/themes/pagesco-classic/style.css?ver=1.0.0' media='all' />
<script data-wp-strategy="defer" defer id="pagesco-classic-navigation-js" src="http://localhost:8080/wp-content/themes/pagesco-classic/assets/js/navigation.js?ver=1.0.0"></script>
    Point at three choices: get_parent_theme_file_uri() (a child theme would otherwise swap the file), the version from wp_get_theme( get_template() ), and defer + in_footer. ?ver=1.0.0 changes when Step 1 raises the Version.

Three mistakes to expect, and how to coach each
  • Code at the top level of functions.php. add_theme_support() or wp_enqueue_style() outside a callback. Coach: "Which moment is this for? Put it in a function on that hook." (Self-check Q1 and Q6.)
  • Typed versions and the wrong URL function. '1.0' copied from a tutorial, get_stylesheet_uri() in a parent. Coach: "What happens on your next release? What happens with a child theme?" (Self-check Q3; the lab's TODO 2.)
  • Locations and areas without fixed ids. A location typo, register_sidebar() without id. Coach: "Which string does the template use? Copy it." (Self-check Q4; debug_theme_setup.php.)

Three notices from one misplaced line; read the first one, which names the handle. The style still loads, which is the real damage: on every request, admin and login included. (The command deletes the file again.)

Checks for understanding

Ask these out loud during the demo and the lab:

  • Where does add_theme_support( 'title-tag' ) go? Answer: a functions.php callback on after_setup_theme (the lesson quiz Q1).
  • Why the theme's Version as the version argument? Answer: it changes exactly when you release; browsers then fetch the new file.
  • Who builds the menu, and who decides where it may appear? Answer: the owner builds it; the theme registers locations.
  • Which hook for register_sidebar()? Answer: widgets_init (the lesson quiz Q4).

Workbook self-check, items Q1 to Q6.

Answers: Q1 C) after_setup_theme; Q2 pagesco-classic | inactive | 1.1.0: pagesco is active again; 1.1.0 is the Version the stylesheet is enqueued with (style.css?ver=1.1.0), so raising it on a release makes every browser fetch the new CSS; Q3 A) The page loads the CHILD's style.css under the parent's handle, and the parent's CSS is gone; Q4 B) So a location without an assigned menu prints nothing instead of wp_page_menu()'s list of every page; Q5 D) Not on WordPress 6.8 and later, which load the active theme's languages/ folder itself; it stays for 6.6 and 6.7; Q6 A "called incorrectly" notice naming the handle (scripts and styles should not be enqueued until wp_enqueue_scripts...), plus two follow-on notices; the real damage: top-level code runs on every request, so the CSS also loads on admin screens and the login page. Full set with explanations in the Answer Key.

Differentiation

Support: learners new to hooks do TODOs 1 and 2 of the lab with the lesson's functions.php open side by side; 3 and 4 go home.

Stretch: debug_theme_setup.php, then the lesson's Exercise 1 (the login logo) and the Bonus Challenge (add_editor_style).

Read the brief together (10m)

Hand out labs/module-08/p1-project/BRIEF.md. Read Odette Marsh's email aloud:

“Our website runs on a free theme from 2019 that nobody dares to touch. We would like our own theme, made for us: green and calm, our news on the front page three at a time, a big welcome at the top, a call for Saturday volunteers, and an autumn look we can switch on in October. Our volunteers write news and edit pages in the editor; none of us writes code. And please: nothing that breaks when WordPress updates itself.”

Then the requirement list on the slide. Ask, row by row: "Which module does this come from?" (R1 to R4 Module 3, R5 and R6 Module 4, R8 every module.)

Answers for items Q7 to Q12 of the workbook self-check (project skills):

Answers: Q7 A) It names the theme: the header fields WordPress reads (Theme Name, Text Domain, Version, Requires at least ...); Q8 C) theme.json: styles.elements.link and styles.elements.button with var:preset|color|primary; Q9 B) A pre_get_posts callback in functions.php with the three guards: not the admin, the main query only, the blog home only; Q10 D) A wp_template_part copy in the database wins over the file: move the change into header.html, then delete the copy; Q11 styles/autumn.json, titled Autumn, without blockTypes: the same five color slugs with autumn values, nothing else; Q12 wp theme activate pagesco: the labs, Session 8's assessment and Part 2 (Lesson 5.1) expect pagesco active, the state at the end of Lesson 4.3. Full set with explanations in the Answer Key.

Closing

Exit ticket (3 questions, no notes, 4 minutes)
  1. Name the hook for each: a theme support, a stylesheet, a widget area. Answer: after_setup_theme; wp_enqueue_scripts; widgets_init.
  2. Why does the enqueue use the theme's Version? Answer: the URL changes with each release, so browsers fetch the new file.
  3. Which Fernhill requirement will take you longest, and which lesson will you reread for it? Answer: (personal; most say R2/R3: Lessons 3.1 to 3.3).
Homework (about 2 to 3 hours)
  • Finish Lesson 4.3: Common Mistakes 2 to 4, the project's Step 2 (the per-URL check), Exercises 1 to 3 (Exercise 4 is a stretch), the Quick Quiz, the journal.
  • Part 1 project, Milestones 2 and 3 (about 1 hour 45 minutes): the design system (fonts and element styles too), then the templates, the two parts and the 404 page, with the per-URL check. Run the self-check often.
  • Switch back after each work session: wp theme activate pagesco. Edit FILES; if you try something in the Site Editor, move it into the file and delete the database copy.
  • Labs not reached: labs/module-07/l4_3-functions-php/menus_widgets_starter.sh, labs/module-07/l4_3-functions-php/debug_theme_setup.php.
Bring list for Session 8
  • The course site at the end of Lesson 4.3: pagesco active, pagesco-classic finished and inactive; fernhill in wp-content/themes/ with Milestones 2 and 3 done.
  • The last self-check output (the "Checks passed" line), your template map, questions for the studio.
  • The project folder with labs/, the journal, the workbook. Session 8 also has the timed Part 1 assessment (classic themes, open book): reread Lessons 4.1 to 4.3.

If You Run Long or Short

Running long: what to protect and what to cut first
  • Protect: Step 3 (back to pagesco); Milestone 1 on every machine; the enqueue with its version.
  • Cut first (saves 7m): the block-theme defaults and the widget steps of the demo.
  • Cut second (saves 15m): the M3 planning segment: the template map goes home with the workbook box.
  • Cut third (saves 10m): the translation demo after the break; keep the skip link and Mistake 1.
Running short: what to add
  • Run menus_widgets_starter.sh for everyone (it switches to pagesco-classic and back by itself).
  • Start Milestone 3 in the room: the header part's tagName and the main group in index.html.
  • The lesson's Exercise 4 live: WP_Classic_To_Block_Menu_Converter on the Main menu.
Instructor Kit · Facilitator Guide

Session 8: Part 1 Project and Assessment

How to run the last session of Part 1: a studio for the Part 1 project (the Fernhill Community Garden block theme), the timed Part 1 assessment (finishing the Brightwater Swim School classic theme, 60 minutes, alone), and a review that turns both into a map of Modules 1 to 4. Rubrics, scoring sheets and answer notes are in final-assessment.html. When Part 1 runs on its own, this is the course close.

0 new lessons 3 hrs session Modules 1–4 Session 8 of 18 · Part 1

How to Use This Guide

  • Session 8 teaches no new lesson. It closes Part 1 with three things: a studio for the Part 1 project (the Fernhill Community Garden block theme, briefed in Session 7, due one week from today), a timed assessment (finishing the Brightwater Swim School classic theme, 60 minutes, alone), and a review that turns both into a map of Part 1.
  • The project and the assessment are deliberately different: the project is the block-theme side (Module 3, with functions.php and the main query from Module 4) over a week, with help; the assessment is the classic-theme side (Module 4, with escaping and hooks from Modules 1 and 2) in one hour, without help. Together they cover Modules 1 to 4.
  • Rubrics, scoring guidance, scoring sheets and the answer notes (the model solutions' real output, and what each common mistake prints) are in final-assessment.html at the kit root (sections "Part 1 Project" and "Part 1 Assessment"). Print the scoring sheets before the session.
  • Every output in this guide was produced on WordPress 7.1.3, PHP 8.5, at the state Lesson 4.3 leaves (pagesco active): what every learner's site is at the start of today. Labs live in labs/module-08/: p1-project/ (Session 7 handed it out), p1-assessment/ (hold it back until 1:25 if you can) and p1-review/.
  • When Part 1 runs on its own, this is the last session: the wrap-up becomes the course close (certificates of completion, what next) and the project hand-in is the last contact. The guide marks where.
The #1 risk of Session 8: the studio eats the assessment

Learners who are behind on the project will ask to keep building through the break. Do not let them: the assessment starts at 1:25 for everyone, and the project has a week left. Say at 0:10: "The studio ends at the break, whatever happens. Your project is due in a week; the assessment is today." Second risk: a learner whose site is broken (the assessment needs a working course site at after:lesson_13). Check every machine during the status round, and keep one spare laptop with a working site, or let the learner pair-run the self-check on yours and hand in code only.

Before the Session

  • ☐ Print the scoring sheets for the project and the assessment (final-assessment.html), one per learner, and the assessment's BRIEF.md (labs/module-08/p1-assessment/BRIEF.md) on paper if you prefer paper.
  • ☐ Assessment files. If you handed out the whole labs/ folder in Session 1, learners already have p1-assessment/ (without the solution); that is acceptable (open book, and the score comes from the code and the explanation), but the cleaner way is to hold the folder back: put labs/module-08/p1-assessment/brightwater_starter/, test_brightwater.php and BRIEF.md on a USB stick or a shared folder and release them at 1:25. Never hand out brightwater_solution/ or fernhill_solution/.
  • ☐ Run the kit check: python3 labs/check_labs.py module-08 (every line PASS: the review pair and handout, and both self-checks once with the starter and once with the solution, on fresh after:lesson_13 sites). With your own project: WP_LABS_COMPOSE=~/pagesco-dev python3 labs/check_labs.py module-08 (labs/README.md); your site must be at the end of Lesson 4.3.
  • ☐ Projector machine: the course project running at the end of Lesson 4.3 (pagesco active), two terminals in the project folder, VS Code, browser tabs: http://localhost:8080, the Site Editor, final-assessment.html (for you, not the projector).
  • ☐ Board, before learners arrive: the Part 1 map (Module → skills → where in the project and the assessment; the table below), today's clock (studio until 1:15, assessment 1:35 to 2:35), and the self-check commands for both themes.
  • ☐ A timer visible to the room for the assessment, and sticky notes for the status round.

In the room. No lesson: 50 minutes of project studio, 70 minutes of assessment (setup and work), 25 minutes of review before and after, the warm-up, the break and the wrap-up. The project takes about 3 hours 45 minutes in all: about 35 minutes in Session 7, 50 today, the rest at home (Milestones 2 to 4 between the sessions, the finish in the week after today). The assessment is sized for 50 minutes of tasks plus 10 for setup checks and the hand-in.

Goes home (about 2 to 3 hours). Finish the Fernhill theme (Milestones 5 and 6 and anything left; due one week from today, with NOTES.md); the Part 1 retrospective journal; the self-check items not done in the room; Part 2 preparation (below) or, when Part 1 runs alone, nothing else.

Protect, in this order: the full 60 minutes of the assessment (start it on time, at 1:35 at the latest); the studio's triage (every learner leaves knowing their next milestone); the review of the three bug reports (it is where the assessment teaches). Cut first: the predict items in the review, then the showcase (keep the bug walkthrough), then the warm-up questions (keep the status round).

Warm-up questions and answers
  1. Name the five extension points of WordPress and the module that covers each. Hooks (Lesson 2.3), themes (Modules 3 and 4), plugins (Module 5), blocks (Module 6), APIs (Module 7). Part 1 covered the first two.
  2. Block theme or classic theme: where does each keep its templates, and in which language? Block: templates/*.html and parts/*.html, block markup. Classic: *.php in the theme root (index.php, singular.php...), PHP with template tags.
  3. Which three guards does a pre_get_posts callback for the blog home need? Not is_admin(); $query->is_main_query(); $query->is_home() (the query's method, not the global function).
  4. Name four escaping functions and where each goes. esc_html() text, esc_attr() attributes, esc_url() href/src, wp_kses_post() HTML with safe tags (and the _e / __ variants for translated text).
  5. Your project's last self-check line? Each learner's own number: the status round (see the studio triage).
Reading the status round
  • 10 to 12 of 12: on track. They work on R8 (the per-URL check, NOTES.md) and a stretch item in the studio, and help a neighbor.
  • 5 to 9: the usual. Templates and theme.json done, patterns or functions.php missing: Milestones 4 and 5 in the studio.
  • 1 to 4: behind (often theme.json or the parts). First conference in the studio goes to them; the goal today is Milestone 4 started.
  • No number (the theme is not on the machine, or the site is broken): fix the site NOW, before the review: the assessment needs it. wp theme activate pagesco and the self-check of Lesson 4.3's end (wp theme list) first.

The per-URL check of Lesson 3.2, adapted to Fernhill's landmarks (it is in the workbook):

for url in / /page/2/ /hello-world/ /about/ /category/news/ "/?s=garden" /no-such-path/; do
	page=$(curl -s -w '\n%{http_code}' "http://localhost:8080$url")
	echo "$url  $(echo "$page" | tail -n 1)  header:$(echo "$page" | grep -c '<header class="wp-block-template-part"')  main:$(echo "$page" | grep -c '<main ')  footer:$(echo "$page" | grep -c '<footer class="wp-block-template-part"')  h1: $(echo "$page" | grep -o '<h1[^>]*>.*</h1>' | head -n 1 | sed 's/<[^>]*>//g')"
done

The bugs behind the three reports: the header asks for a menu location named main while the theme registers primary (T1); search.php prints get_search_query( false ) raw (T4); related-news.php never calls wp_reset_postdata(), so the_post_navigation() works from the last related post instead of the post on the screen (T5). The bug walkthrough
  • "Our menu never shows" (T1). register_nav_menus() names the location, wp_nav_menu( theme_location ) and has_nav_menu() ask for it: the names must match, and a typo is silent (Lesson 4.3, Mistake 3).
  • "Something strange when my nephew typed HTML" (T4). The heading printed the search words as HTML. Show the fixed output: <h1 class="search-title">Results for: &lt;b&gt;water&lt;/b&gt;</h1>. esc_html() at the echo, or get_search_query() with its default escaping. Every value from a visitor is untrusted (Lessons 1.3 and 5.3).
  • "Previous and next point to the wrong posts" (T5). The related loop moved the global post. After wp_reset_postdata() Dune's navigation is its own: Staff picks for the season Hello world! (Lesson 4.2, Mistake 2).
Retrospective prompt

"Part 1 took you from a local site to three kinds of theme. Which skill would you now trust yourself with on a client's site, and which would you look up first?" Two or three answers out loud; the rest go in the journal.

Closing

Exit ticket (3 questions, 4 minutes)
  1. A client wants "news three at a time" on a block theme's front page. Where does the code go, and why not a second query in the template? Answer: a pre_get_posts callback in functions.php (guards: not admin, main query, is_home) sets posts_per_page; the Query Loop inherits the main query, so pagination and /page/2/ keep working. A second query would not page, and the main query would still run.
  2. Why does every string in a pattern go through esc_html_e() even though you wrote it? Answer: it makes the text translatable (the text domain) and escapes it at output; a translation is data you did not write.
  3. One skill from Part 1 you will use first, and one you want to review. Answer: the learner's own; read the review answers before Session 9 and pick the refresher topics from them.
Homework (about 2 to 3 hours)
  • Finish the Fernhill theme (Milestones 5 and 6, anything left, NOTES.md). Due one week from today: the zip fernhill-<yourname>.zip with NOTES.md and the last self-check output (labs/module-08/p1-project/BRIEF.md, Hand-in).
  • Journal: the Part 1 retrospective (workbook prompt).
  • Self-check Q1 to Q12 in the workbook, if not done in the room; the answer key is yours to share after the project deadline.
  • Part 2 preparation (when Part 2 follows): wp theme activate pagesco (Lesson 5.1 starts from it), Node 24 on the computer or docker pull node:24, docker pull composer:2; Session 9 opens with check_environment.sh --part2. A site that is not at the end of Lesson 4.3 (unfinished, or broken by experiments) can start Part 2 from the course download pagesco-part2-start.zip (its README.txt: about a minute; it saves the old database first).
  • Optional: labs/module-08/p1-review/debug_query_review.php and the request-map lab if you did not reach them.
Bring list for Session 9
  • A laptop with the course site at the end of Lesson 4.3, pagesco active (your Fernhill theme can stay installed, inactive).
  • Node 24 or the node:24 image, the composer:2 image, a good connection for the first npm install of Module 6 later.
  • The journal and the workbook; pagesco-plan.txt (Lesson 5.1 reads it again).
When Part 1 runs on its own: the course close
  • Replace the Part 2 items of the wrap-up with: what the learners can now do (the Part 1 map), where to go next (Part 2's plugin, blocks and REST modules; the WordPress Developer Resources; the Theme Handbook), and how the project feedback will reach them.
  • Completion: Part 1 is complete when the project and the assessment are both Met (at least 14 of 20, no row at 1; one revision each within a week). Issue the certificate of completion after the project feedback, not today.
  • Ask for course feedback in the last five minutes (paper or a form), and thank the room.

If You Run Long or Short

Running long: what to protect and what to cut first
  • Protect: the assessment's 60 minutes, starting by 1:35; the studio triage; the bug walkthrough.
  • Cut first (saves 4m): the predict items in the review.
  • Cut second (saves 6m): the showcase; keep the walkthrough and one retrospective answer.
  • Cut third (saves 5m): the warm-up questions; keep the status round (you need the numbers for the studio).
Running short: what to add
  • Run labs/module-08/p1-review/debug_query_review.php together before the break: one loud bug, three silent ones; the silent ones are what Task 5 is about.
  • In the review: switch Fernhill's style variation to Autumn in the Site Editor on the projector, then show the database copy it made (wp post list --post_type=wp_global_styles) and reset it: rule R8 in one minute.
  • After the hand-in: ask two learners to show their T3 Loop and compare the_permalink() with esc_url( get_permalink() ).
PHP and WordPress Development · Facilitator Guide

Part 2: Plugins to Launch

Sessions 9 to 18. Modules 5 to 9: the pagesco-books plugin (custom post types, security, settings, custom tables), custom blocks with the Interactivity API, the REST API and custom endpoints, external APIs and cron, debugging, testing, performance, internationalization and deployment, ending with the final project: the Pages & Co. website, launched.

Instructor Kit · Facilitator Guide

Session 9: Your First Plugin and Custom Post Types

How to teach the first session of Part 2. Open Part 2 for two groups at once (learners coming from Part 1 and learners joining here) with a refresher, a starting note and the Part 2 environment check, then build the pagesco-books plugin the way it will grow for ten sessions (a header, a namespace, Composer's autoloader, one class per feature, a life cycle) and teach WordPress about books: a post type, a genre taxonomy, typed meta and the seeded catalog.

2 lessons 3 hrs session Lessons 5.1–5.2 Session 9 of 18 · Part 2

How to Use This Guide

  • Same rhythm for both lessons: frame (the goal and one mental model) → live demo (you type, they type along) → guided lab (a kit lab, new practice on the lesson's ideas) → start the lesson's own project. The lesson exercises, quiz and journal are homework.
  • Every command below was run to produce the output printed under it, on WordPress 7.1.3 / PHP 8.5: the 5.1 demo on the Part 2 starting site (the state Lesson 4.3 leaves, after:lesson_13), the 5.2 demo on the site as Lesson 5.1 leaves it. Ask for a prediction before every run and read every message from the left.
  • Type the short files, copy the long ones. Part 2's classes are longer than anything in Part 1: learners type the main file, composer.json, the sed lines and the commands with you, and copy Plugin.php, Feature.php, Activator.php, BookPostType.php, GenreTaxonomy.php and BookMeta.php from the lesson pages, then read each one aloud with you. Typing a 60-line class in the room teaches typing.
  • The lessons are the reference: keep lesson_14.html and lesson_15.html open in browser tabs. Labs live in labs/module-09/ (learners keep the folder in their project folder): _starter files and folders are handouts, _solution ones are yours.
  • Session 9 opens Part 2, "Plugins to Launch" (Sessions 9 to 18). Some learners come straight from Part 1; some join here. The 30-minute opening serves both: a Part 1 refresher, the "starting with Part 2" note and the Part 2 environment check. Teal blocks are hands-on, amber blocks are watch-outs.
The #1 risk of Session 9: two rooms in one

Learners who finished Part 1 a week ago have the Lesson 4.3 site and the habits (debug.log, WP-CLI, hooks). Learners who join at Part 2 may have neither: their machine may not run the course project, their site may be a fresh install, and "the store notice from Lesson 2.3" means nothing to them. Before: send the setup guide (Docker, the project, the Part 2 starting site pagesco-part2-start.zip from the course's downloads) and the starting note below to every new learner a week ahead, and ask everyone to reply with the last line of check_environment.sh --part2. In the room: the check gets 12 minutes; a learner whose site is not where Part 2 starts sits with a ready partner for the demos and installs the Part 2 starting site at the break, not during Lesson 5.1. Both groups get the same refresher: R1 and R2 are exactly what Lesson 5.1 builds on.

Before the Session

  • ☐ A week before: to everyone, "run bash labs/module-01/l1_0-orientation/check_environment.sh --part2 and reply with its last line"; to learners new in Part 2, also the setup guide (the course project of Lesson 1.2 and the Part 2 starting site, downloads/pagesco-part2-start.zip) and the workbook's "Starting with Part 2" box. docker pull composer:2 and docker pull node:24 at home, on a good connection (the check pulls them if missing: about half a gigabyte to download, about 2 GB on disk).
  • ☐ Run the kit check once: python3 labs/check_labs.py module-09 from this kit's folder (16 results in about a minute and a half; every line PASS). With your own course project: WP_LABS_COMPOSE=~/pagesco-dev python3 labs/check_labs.py module-09.
  • ☐ Projector machine at the Part 2 starting site (the end of Lesson 4.3): pagesco active, wp plugin list shows no pagesco-books yet. If yours is further along, snapshot it first (wp db export before-s9.sql and a copy of wordpress/wp-content/) and reset to the starting site; after the session you can restore. VS Code on pagesco-dev at a large font, two terminals (one for commands, one for tail -f wordpress/wp-content/debug.log), lesson_14.html and lesson_15.html in browser tabs, and pagesco-seed.zip downloaded from the course site.
  • ☐ Board, before learners arrive: the plugin's layout (pagesco-books.php, composer.json, vendor/, uninstall.php, src/Plugin.php, src/Feature.php, src/Activator.php, src/StoreNotice.php); the life-cycle line activate = set up once · deactivate = pause, keep data · uninstall = remove the plugin's data; and new feature = one class in src/ + one line in feature_classes().
  • ☐ Print or share: the workbook (its Start Here page has the Part 2 check, the starting note and the refresher), sticky notes for help flags and the exit ticket.
Known Part 2 traps
SymptomCauseFix
Failed opening required '.../vendor/autoload.php' on activationComposer never ran in this copy of the plugincomposer dump-autoload in the composer:2 container, in the plugin folder (Lesson 5.1, Common Mistakes 2).
Class "PagesCo\Books\StoreNotice" not found, the whole site downA file name that does not match the class name letter for letter (Storenotice.php)Rename the file; on macOS and Windows the bug hides until a Linux server (project Step 3).
docker: invalid reference format or $(id -u) errors in PowerShellThe Linux form of the composer command on Windows PowerShellLeave out --user, write ${PWD} (Lesson 1.3); better: run it in the Ubuntu terminal where the project lives.
The plugin activates but the activation callback never ranregister_activation_hook() inside a callback (plugins_loaded, init)Top level of the main file, with __FILE__ (Common Mistakes 3).
/books/ or /books/dune/ is a 404 although the code is rightRewrite rules saved before the type existedwp rewrite flush now; the activator flushes from then on (5.2, Common Mistakes 1).
Seeded books have no genrestax_input in a script that runs as no userwp_set_object_terms(), as the seeding script does (5.2, Common Mistakes 2).
Activate the pagesco-books plugin first from the seeding scriptThe plugin is inactive, or BookPostType/GenreTaxonomy are not in feature_classes()wp plugin list, then grep -n "::class," .../src/Plugin.php.
The store notice shows the Thursday hours twice after the sessionStoreNotice listed, but Step 2 (trimming pagesco-site.php) not done yetExpected half-way through the project: Step 2 is the fix.
Error: This does not seem to be a WordPress installation from the seeding commandpagesco-seed/ unzipped somewhere other than the WordPress rootIt belongs in wordpress/pagesco-seed/, next to wp-load.php; run from the project folder with the wp shortcut.

In the room. The lesson pages estimate 135 + 130 = 265 minutes for a learner working alone; after the 30-minute opening, the break and the wrap-up the room has 130. Both lessons keep their shape (model, demo, lab, project start), with two cuts: the long classes are copied, not typed, and the demos skip what learners can read alone.

Goes home (about 2 to 3 hours). 5.1: the project Steps 3 and 4 (the case of the missing class, the final check), Common Mistakes 1 and 2 (direct access, the missing autoloader) if the demo skipped them, the version note on load_plugin_textdomain(). 5.2: "Seeing Books in the Admin" (the meta box and the columns: Session 10 hardens that meta box, so it MUST be done), Common Mistakes 2 and 3, the project Steps 3 and 4. Each lesson's Hands-on Exercises, both Quick Quizzes and both journal entries.

Protect, in this order: the Part 2 check result for every learner; the 5.1 skeleton working on every machine (activated, int(10)), because everything in Part 2 is a feature of it; the 5.1 life cycle (activate, deactivate, uninstall); the 5.2 flush (it explains the most common bug of the module). Cut first: the late-hook mistake (it is in the lesson), then the 5.2 genre step (show the class, run its block at home), then the 5.2 project start (learners seed at home; it takes eight minutes).

Refresher answers (R1 to R5)
  1. R1 wp-content/mu-plugins/pagesco-site.php; pagesco_store_notice is the filter (the text), pagesco_before_store_notice and pagesco_store_notice_end are actions. Lesson 5.1 hooks a plugin feature into the filter and the end action.
  2. R2 Load (wp-settings.php): must-use plugins, plugins, plugins_loaded, the theme, then init. pagesco-books starts its features on plugins_loaded; post types register on init.
  3. R3 A templates/index.html (Lesson 3.1); its theme.json holds the design. Part 2 never edits the theme's looks: books get their template in Module 6.
  4. R4 Because the action fires for every query, in the admin too: without the guards it would change the Books screen, widgets and REST lists (Lesson 4.2). The book archive at /books/ is a main query again.
  5. R5 A plugin (Lessons 3.4 and 4.3: the theme is the looks, the plugin is what the shop does). That rule is why Part 2 builds pagesco-books.

Watch-outs
  • Do not rebuild Part 1 in the room. A new learner without the starting site cannot catch up by typing Lessons 2.1 to 4.3 today. Pair them, and install the Part 2 starting site at the break (pagesco-part2-start.zip: copy the folder into wordpress/, then docker compose run --rm wpcli sh pagesco-part2-start/install.sh, about a minute).
  • "My site is further along" (a Part 1 learner who already started Lesson 5.1 at home): fine. They follow the 5.1 demo as a reading and help a new learner; the 5.2 demo is new for everyone.
  • Old habits. Learners who wrote plugins before often put everything in one file with global functions. Today's structure (a namespace, Composer, one class per feature) is the course's convention from here to the final project; say so once, kindly.

Lesson Plans

5.1

Your First Plugin

65 min
Objectives (from the lesson page)
  • Write a plugin header WordPress understands, including the version requirements it checks on activation
  • Organize a plugin as a short main file plus namespaced classes in src/, loaded by Composer's PSR-4 autoloader
  • Start features from one main object on plugins_loaded, and add a new feature by writing one class and listing it
  • Use activation and deactivation hooks and uninstall.php for the right jobs, and say what each must never do
  • Recognize the typical first-plugin failures: direct file access, a missing autoloader, a class the autoloader cannot find, a hook registered too late
Timing in the room
10mFrame: the shop's departments; plugin, must-use plugin, functions.php; the layout
25mLive demo: header and guard, main file, Composer, Plugin and Feature, the role's life cycle, a late hook
15mGuided lab: gift_wrap_starter/ in pairs
15mStart the lesson project: StoreNotice, Steps 1 and 2
Mental model to say

Draw the shop on the board: "pagesco-books is the shop's back office. Each feature, the notice additions, the catalog, the events calendar, the settings page, is a department with its own room. The main file is the front door with the shop's name on it: it unlocks, switches on the lights and hands a list of departments to the manager, the Plugin object, who opens each one in the morning, on plugins_loaded. A new department means a new room and one new line on the manager's list, never knocking through the walls of the existing ones."

Then the three relatives in one line each: must-use plugin = always on, no switch (Lesson 2.3); functions.php = only while that theme is active (Lesson 4.3); plugin = the owner switches it on and off, and it can clean up after itself. "Everything the shop DOES goes in a plugin, so it survives the next redesign."

Then the two tools for a plugin that will have fifteen features: a namespace (PagesCo\Books, the prefix for classes) and autoloading (Composer's PSR-4 rule: PagesCo\Books\Admin\SettingsPage lives in src/Admin/SettingsPage.php, letter for letter).

Live demo (you type, they follow)

On the Part 2 starting site. Learners type along on theirs; the long classes they copy from the lesson page as you reach them. Ask for a prediction before every run.

  1. A plugin is a header and a guard (3m). "You have met two relatives already: the must-use plugin of Lesson 2.3 and functions.php of Lesson 4.3. A normal plugin sits in between: the owner switches it on and off." In the WP-CLI container shell, show the top of Hello Dolly. Ask first: which line makes it a plugin? 
    sed -n '1,20p' wp-content/plugins/hello.php
    <?php
/**
 * @package Hello_Dolly
 * @version 1.7.2
 */
/*
Plugin Name: Hello Dolly
Plugin URI: http://wordpress.org/plugins/hello-dolly/
Description: This is not just a plugin, it symbolizes the hope and enthusiasm of an entire generation summed up in two words sung most famously by Louis Armstrong: Hello, Dolly. When activated you will randomly see a lyric from <cite>Hello, Dolly</cite> in the upper right of your admin screen on every page.
Author: Matt Mullenweg
Version: 1.7.2
Author URI: http://ma.tt/
Text Domain: hello-dolly
*/

// Don't load directly.
if ( ! defined( 'ABSPATH' ) ) {
	exit;
}
    The comment block is the header (only Plugin Name: is required; WordPress reads it WITHOUT running the file), and the first code is the ABSPATH guard. Everything after that is two functions and two hooks: Lesson 2.3's toolkit.
  2. The main file (4m). "pagesco-books starts as a folder and a main file of the same name." Learners type it with you, from the lesson page (it is short). Then ask WordPress what it sees: 
    <?php
/**
 * Plugin Name:       Pages & Co. Books
 * Plugin URI:        https://example.com/pagesco-books/
 * Description:       The bookstore features of the Pages & Co. website: books, genres, events and the shop's blocks.
 * Version:           1.0.0
 * Requires at least: 6.8
 * Requires PHP:      8.2
 * Author:            Pages & Co.
 * Author URI:        https://example.com/
 * License:           GPL-2.0-or-later
 * License URI:       https://www.gnu.org/licenses/gpl-2.0.html
 * Text Domain:       pagesco-books
 *
 * @package PagesCo\Books
 */

defined( 'ABSPATH' ) || exit;

define( 'PAGESCO_BOOKS_VERSION', '1.0.0' );
define( 'PAGESCO_BOOKS_FILE', __FILE__ );
define( 'PAGESCO_BOOKS_DIR', plugin_dir_path( __FILE__ ) );
    wp plugin list --fields=name,status,version
wp plugin get pagesco-books --fields=name,title,version,status
    +---------------+----------+---------+
| name          | status   | version |
+---------------+----------+---------+
| akismet       | inactive | 5.7.2   |
| hello         | inactive | 1.7.2   |
| pagesco-books | inactive | 1.0.0   |
| mailpit-smtp  | must-use |         |
| pagesco-site  | must-use | 1.0.0   |
+---------------+----------+---------+

| Field   | Value             |
