<div class="wp-block-pagesco-book-card has-sage-background-color has-background has-small-font-size" style="…"><a class="wp-block-pagesco-book-card__link" …
    Read the first line: the new save() starts with the badge <p>, the stored card with the link <a>. Then create the lesson's deprecated.js (the old attributes, supports and save, plus migrate() that sets showBadge: false), the new index.js, build, reload: the card opens normally and the Console logs "Block successfully updated". Nothing is saved until someone updates the post.
  6. Mistake 1: a sourced attribute in PHP (2m). "A PHP developer wants to log every card's title." Save the lesson's throwaway must-use plugin mistake-card-title.php, then in the container shell: 
    curl -s http://localhost:8080/card-test/ | head -n 2
curl -s http://localhost:8080/card-test/ | grep -o '<!-- Book Card:[^>]*>'
    Warning: Undefined array key "title" in /var/www/html/wp-content/mu-plugins/mistake-card-title.php on line 9
<!-- Book Card:  -->
    The title is not in the comment, so it is not in $block['attrs']: a Warning above the doctype and an empty comment. In PHP a static block is finished HTML; the HTML API reads it (Exercise 1, and the fast finishers' card_price lab). rm wp-content/mu-plugins/mistake-card-title.php.
Three mistakes to expect, and how to coach each
  • Reading the card's text in PHP from $block['attrs'] (the demo's Mistake 1). Coach with the board: "Is the title on the sticky note or on the print?" The fixes: the HTML API, a comment attribute, or a dynamic block. (Self-check Q2, the debug handout.)
  • Changing save() and blaming the editor. "The block broke after my change." Coach: "What does the Console's first validation line say, and does content already exist?" Test posts can be deleted while developing; client content needs a deprecation. (Self-check Q3.)
  • Translating text in save() or using a too-wide selector (Mistakes 3 and 2). Coach: "Will save() return the same HTML in Spanish? Does the selected element contain only its own value?" Insert, save, RELOAD before trusting a change. (Self-check Q6.)
Guided lab

File: learners copy labs/module-12/l6_2-static-blocks/attribute_sources_starter.php into wordpress/ and run it with wp eval-file --use-include attribute_sources_starter.php; your reference is labs/module-12/l6_2-static-blocks/attribute_sources_solution.php. It practices the lesson's central question on blocks the learner did not write: for core/heading, core/quote and core/button, which attribute lives in the HTML and which in the comment, read from the registry; then what parse_blocks() returns for a stored heading and image.

  • Run it as shipped (2m). Every line says TODO; the skip list (the attributes WordPress adds to many blocks) is given.
  • TODOs 1 to 4 in pairs (10m). TODO 1 is the registry call from the demo. TODOs 2 and 3 are one if/else on isset( $attr['source'] ); circulate for array_key_exists() (core/image's isDecorative defaults to false, and isset() would miss a false default). Before TODO 4, ask for a prediction: will the image's src be in the attrs?
  • Expected when done:
core/heading content: in the HTML (rich-text, h1,h2,h3,h4,h5,h6)
core/heading level: in the comment (default 2)
core/quote value: in the HTML (html, blockquote)
core/quote citation: in the HTML (rich-text, cite)
core/button tagName: in the comment (default "a")
core/button type: in the comment (default "button")
core/button url: in the HTML (attribute, a @href)
core/button title: in the HTML (attribute, a,button @title)
core/button text: in the HTML (rich-text, a,button)
core/button linkTarget: in the HTML (attribute, a @target)
core/button rel: in the HTML (attribute, a @rel)
parse_blocks() sees:
core/heading {"level":3}
core/image {"id":42,"sizeSlug":"large"}
  • Debrief (3m): "Core uses a fourth source the lesson did not list: rich-text. Where does it store?" (In the HTML, like html.) "Why is the button's tagName in the comment?" (It is a setting, not text.) "The image's src is not in the attrs: who reads it back?" (The editor, through the selector.)
  • Fast finishers: the folder lab labs/module-12/l6_2-static-blocks/card_price_starter/ (a must-use plugin that reads a static card's link with the HTML API and adds the live price after it; test with labs/module-12/l6_2-static-blocks/test_card_price.sh), then labs/module-12/l6_2-static-blocks/debug_card_report.php.
Start the lesson project

The lesson project is A Staff Pick on the Staff Picks Post: the finished card for The Hobbit under Lesson 2.1's list. It needs the block as the lesson's sections leave it (badge, deprecation and all): laptops whose card is at that point start it; the others finish the sections at home first.

  • Step 1 (12 minutes in the lesson): insert a Book Card after the list, type the title, author and recommendation ("everyone" in italics), set the link, H3 and the badge in Card settings, Sage in Styles. Update the post.
  • Done in the room = the Code editor shows the card's comment with only {"backgroundColor":"sage"} (the lesson prints the whole post). Ask why headingLevel and showBadge are not there. (Both are at their defaults.)
  • Goes home: Step 2 (the front end), Step 3 (the comparison table with Lesson 1.3's helper, deleting Card test, the parse_blocks check) and the pagesco-plan.txt line.
Checks for understanding

Ask these out loud during the demo and the lab:

  • Where is a card's title stored, and where is its heading level? Answer: the title in the HTML (inside the selector's element); the level in the comment, and only when it is not 3.
  • Which hook gives a block's wrapper the supports' classes and styles? Answer: useBlockProps() in edit and useBlockProps.save() in save (Quiz Q3 of the lesson).
  • What happens to the front end when a card turns invalid in the editor? Answer: nothing: the front end prints the stored HTML.
  • What three things does a deprecated entry repeat? Answer: the old attributes, the old supports and the old save (plus an optional migrate).

Workbook self-check, items Q1 to Q6 (learners do them at the end of the block or at home).

Answers: Q1 C) In the saved HTML: the href of the first <a> inside the block; Q2 {"showBadge":false}; Q3 C) Wrapping the author in a <cite> in save(); Q4 A) Inside <BlockControls> in edit; Q5 B) The class has-sage-background-color in the HTML and "backgroundColor":"sage" in the comment; Q6 save() must return the same HTML for the same attributes in every language: a translated string makes cards invalid as soon as someone edits in another locale. Full set with explanations in the Answer Key.

Differentiation

Support: learners new to React read edit.js and save.js side by side with the lesson's explanation and type only the attribute names; pair them with someone who has written JSX. For the lab, write the isset( $attr['source'] ) branch on the board.

Stretch: the card_price folder lab and debug_card_report.php; then the lesson's Exercise 3 (a Plain style variation) and the Bonus Challenge (the heading level in the toolbar: does it need a deprecation?).

6.3

Dynamic Blocks & Block Bindings

85 min
Objectives (from the lesson page)
  • Explain when a block should be dynamic, and what a dynamic block stores in post_content
  • Render a block on the server with render.php: attributes, a WP_Query through get_posts(), get_block_wrapper_attributes(), and escaping
  • Preview a dynamic block in the editor with ServerSideRender, and fill its controls from the REST API through @wordpress/core-data
  • Offer ready-made versions of a block as variations, generated in PHP
  • Bind core blocks to post meta with core/post-meta, and write a custom binding source with register_block_bindings_source()
Timing in the room
10mFrame: the printed card and the departure board; what a dynamic block stores
20mLive demo A: stale prices, the Book List's files and build, a page of comments, the setting
20mGuided lab: the next_events_starter/ plugin
15mLive demo B: what can be bound, core/post-meta's raw values, pagesco/book
20mStart the lesson project: single-book.html, Steps 1 and 2
Mental model to say

"A static block is a printed card: the shop prints it once, and it says the same thing until someone reprints it. A dynamic block is a station's departure board: what is stored is only 'show the next trains from platform 2', and the board looks up the timetable whenever someone glances at it. The post keeps the instruction, the comment; your render.php is the board."

Then the comparison on the board, from the lesson's table: stored = comment + HTML vs comment only; HTML made by save(), once vs render.php, every view; changing markup = a deprecation vs edit render.php; plugin off = HTML stays vs nothing shows.

Before demo B, the third picture: "A bound block is a shelf label with an empty slot. The design is fixed in the template; the slot says 'price of the book on this shelf', and a clerk, the source, fills it every time someone looks."

Three mistakes to expect, and how to coach each
  • Reading an attribute that has no default ($attributes['count']): a Warning INSIDE the page content, with curly quotes, naming build/.../render.php. Coach: "Which attributes get a default from block.json? Only the ones that declare one." (The lab's TODO 1, the debug handout.)
  • Fixing the file the message names, build/blocks/book-list/render.php. Coach: "What does the next build do to build/?" It empties it and copies src/ again. Edit src/, build (or keep npm start running).
  • A binding that shows its fallback. Coach with three questions: is the key exactly one of BookMeta::fields()? Is it registered with show_in_rest and without an underscore? Does a custom source declare uses_context? (Self-check Q10, Q11; the core_sources lab.)
Guided lab

Folder: labs/module-12/l6_3-dynamic-blocks/next_events_starter/, a small plugin whose block pagesco/next-events lists the next events from Lesson 5.5's table; your reference is labs/module-12/l6_3-dynamic-blocks/next_events_solution/. It practices render.php on data the lesson did not use: an attribute without a default that falls back to a setting (Events to show), a clamp, a query through the plugin's own class, get_block_wrapper_attributes() and escaping. It registers block.json from PHP and has no editor script, so it needs no build: the test renders it with do_blocks(), exactly as a page view would.

Checks for understanding

Ask these out loud during the demos and the lab:

  • What does a page with a Book List store? Answer: only the comment with the attributes; the HTML is made on every view.
  • Why does render.php use get_posts() and not a Loop with the_post()? Answer: it leaves the global $post alone, so a block in the middle of someone else's Loop breaks nothing; and it loads the meta in one query.
  • core/post-meta or pagesco/book for the price? Answer: pagesco/book: core/post-meta prints the raw 8.99; the shop's source formats it.
  • When does variations.php run? Answer: only when something asks for the variations (the editor, through REST), not on page views (lesson quiz Q5).

Workbook self-check, items Q7 to Q12 (learners do them at the end of the block or at home).

Answers: Q7 C) Run npm run build (render.php is copied into build/), then nothing: every page follows on its next view; Q8 4; Q9 D) get_block_wrapper_attributes() returns attributes that are already escaped (class and style from the supports); Q10 D) Nothing: an empty list item; Q11 A) Its fallback text, with no error; Q12 First published in 1945. Full set with explanations in the Answer Key.

Differentiation

Support: learners who did not reach the Book List type only render.php and copy the rest; in the lab, give them the solution's line for TODO 1 and let them do TODOs 2 to 4. For the bindings demo, the board table: source → args → value or null.

Stretch: core_sources_starter.php and debug_genre_counts.php; the lesson's Exercise 2 (an ISBN field that stays quiet) and Exercise 3 (only books in stock); the Bonus Challenge (registerBlockBindingsSource() in the editor).

Closing

Exit ticket (3 questions, no notes, 4 minutes)

Put the three questions on the slide. Learners answer in the workbook's Exit Ticket box or on a sticky note. Sort them before Session 13: question 2's pile tells you whether the checkpoint's Part C (blocks) needs a five-minute review in the warm-up.

  1. A static block's title and heading level: where is each stored? Answer: the title in the saved HTML (found by its selector), the heading level in the block comment (only when it differs from its default).
  2. Name two things a dynamic block's render.php must do with its attributes. Answer: treat them as input (isset or a default for optional ones, cast, clamp, sanitize) and escape everything it prints; plus starting the wrapper with get_block_wrapper_attributes().
  3. A bound paragraph shows its fallback text on a book page. Name two causes. Answer: the meta key is wrong, not registered with show_in_rest or protected (core/post-meta), or a custom source lacks uses_context or returns null.

If You Run Long or Short

Running long: what to protect and what to cut first
  • Protect: the empty array () from PHP; the validation error and its deprecation; render.php with the setting; core/post-meta next to pagesco/book.
  • Cut first (saves 5m): the supports step of the 6.2 demo; the workbook's worked example shows the supports and the style engine.
  • Cut second (saves 15m): the 6.2 project start: Step 1 goes home with Steps 2 and 3.
  • Cut third (saves 4m): the stale-price step of the 6.3 demo: tell the story, show the lesson's output.
Running short: what to add
  • Lesson 6.2's Exercise 1 live: the HTML API reads the Hobbit card's title and link (WP_HTML_Processor::create_fragment(), next_token()).
  • Lesson 6.3's ServerSideRender request with curl as admin: the block-renderer route returns render.php's HTML as JSON; then an orderBy outside the enum gets a 400.
  • Run debug_genre_counts.php for everyone and fix it together; the silent bug (a reversed clamp) is the best discussion.
Instructor Kit · Facilitator Guide

Session 13: The Interactivity API and Using the REST API

How to teach the session where the shop's pages react without reloading and its data answers over HTTP: the Interactivity API's server-first model (directives the server already evaluates, a small store that takes over), then the REST API's routes, headers, authentication and errors, and Checkpoint 2 on Modules 5 and 6.

2 lessons 3 hrs session Lessons 6.4–7.1 Checkpoint 2 Session 13 of 18 · Part 2

How to Use This Guide

  • Same rhythm for both lessons: frame (the goal and one mental model) → live demo (you type, they type along) → guided lab (a kit lab, new practice on the lesson's ideas) → start the lesson's own project. Today ends with Checkpoint 2 at 2:20: 30 minutes, scored, open notes, on Modules 5 and 6. The lesson exercises, quiz and journal are homework.
  • Every command below was run on WordPress 7.1.3 / PHP 8.5 to produce the output printed under it: Lesson 6.4's demo on the site after Lesson 6.3 (after:lesson_21), Lesson 7.1's on the site after Lesson 6.4 (after:lesson_22). Browser recordings (the filter's clicks, fetch() without a nonce) are the lesson's own, made with Playwright on a 7.1 site. REST requests shown as curl --user "maria:$PASS" were sent with a real application password; yours prints its own password once.
  • Labs live in labs/module-13/: _starter files are handouts, _solution files are yours, and the whole checkpoint-2/ folder stays with you until 2:20. The 6.4 labs need no browser and no build: wp_interactivity_process_directives() runs the server half of the Interactivity API on any HTML.
  • Part 2, Session 5 of 10. Teal blocks are hands-on, amber blocks are watch-outs. Lesson codes (6.4, 7.1) match the course site.
The #1 risk of Session 13: two big lessons squeeze the checkpoint

Lessons 6.4 and 7.1 are written for 140 and 140 minutes; the room has 115 for both, and Checkpoint 2 needs its full 30. A demo that runs ten minutes over eats the checkpoint, and a checkpoint started at 2:30 is unfair to the slow, careful learners it should reward. Start the checkpoint at 2:20 whatever happens. The cuts are listed under If You Run Long; the first is the 6.4 project start (5 minutes), then the browser step of the 6.4 demo, then the apiFetch step of the 7.1 demo. Both lessons' projects mostly go home anyway: say so at 0:00.

Before the Session

  • ☐ Projector site at after:lesson_21 (the end of Lesson 6.3, a working build). Rehearse 6.4's files and build once on a scratch copy; then put the projector site at after:lesson_22 for 7.1, or keep going on the same site (the 6.4 demo creates the Book Filter, which 7.1 does not need).
  • ☐ Two terminals: the project folder (wp shortcut, the build) and the WP-CLI container shell (docker compose run --rm wpcli sh) for curl. Keep PASS and DEVON_PASS in the shell once created; never in a file under wordpress/.
  • ☐ Files to hand out: labs/module-13/ WITHOUT the *_solution.* files and WITHOUT the checkpoint-2/ folder. At 2:20 hand out checkpoint-2/checkpoint_starter.php only (shared folder or USB stick), and the printed Part D page.
  • ☐ Run the kit check once: python3 labs/check_labs.py module-13 (14 results, about two minutes), and run checkpoint_solution.php on your site so you know the four lines it prints.
  • ☐ Print: the workbook's Checkpoint 2 page for every learner, and one rubric per learner (answer key, "Checkpoint 2: Rubric and Model Answer").
  • ☐ Board, before learners arrive: state · derived state · context; the status table 400 the request · 401 who are you? · 403 you may not · 404 no such route or item.

Questions and answers
  1. W1 (Lesson 6.2). The Hobbit card on the Staff picks post: which of its attributes does PHP's parse_blocks() see? Answer: Only the comment's: {"backgroundColor":"sage"}. Title, author, recommendation and link are in the HTML; headingLevel and showBadge are at their defaults.
  2. W2 (Lesson 6.2). You changed the card's save(). When do you need a deprecated entry, and when not? Answer: When content with the old HTML exists that must stay editable (a client's posts): always. While the block exists only on a test site: delete the test posts instead.
  3. W3 (Lesson 6.3). The Book List stores only <!-- wp:pagesco/book-list /-->. Who decides how many books it shows? Answer: render.php, on every view: no count means the Books per list setting (6), clamped to 1 to 24.
  4. W4 (Lesson 6.3). Which line makes WordPress pass the book's ID to a paragraph bound to pagesco/book? Answer: 'uses_context' => array( 'postId', 'postType' ) in register_block_bindings_source(); without it the fallback stays, silently.
  5. W5 (Lesson 6.3). What does the Hobbit's page show as its price, and where does the value come from? Answer: $10.99: the large paragraph is bound to pagesco/book's price field, which formats pagesco_price on every view.

Lesson Plans

6.4

The Interactivity API

55 min
Objectives (from the lesson page)
  • Explain how the Interactivity API splits the work: server-rendered HTML with directives, then hydration by a store in a script module
  • Scaffold an interactive block into the plugin, and build its viewScriptModule with --experimental-modules
  • Set state and per-element context in PHP with wp_interactivity_state() and wp_interactivity_data_wp_context(), including derived state the server can compute
  • Write a store with store(), state getters, getContext() and actions, and connect it with data-wp-on, bind, class and text
  • Build interactive features that stay accessible and keep working without JavaScript
Timing in the room
10mFrame: the stage and the lighting desk; server first, then hydration; state, derived state, context
25mLive demo: the module build, render.php, the store, what the server already did, the browser
15mGuided lab: open_today_starter.php
5mStart the lesson project: the Find a Book page
Mental model to say

"The server builds the stage: every book is on it, every genre link, finished and visible. Directives are cables from each light to a fader on the lighting desk: 'this book is lit while isVisible is true'. The store is the desk: move the genre fader and every light wired to it changes at once. You only ever touch the faders; the cables do the rest."

Then the two consequences on the board: the server evaluates directives too (the page is right before any JavaScript) and one shared runtime, loaded as a module only where an interactive block is. Then the design question before any code: "What is the ONE thing that changes when a customer clicks?" (the genre). "Everything else is derived. What does each element need to know about itself?" (its slug, its genres: context).

Live demo (you type, they follow)

From the site as Lesson 6.3 left it. The JavaScript and JSON files are pasted from the lesson; render.php is read aloud; the outputs are what curl, the build and the page really return.

  1. The module build (4m). "Interactive blocks are built a second way." The scaffold (--template @wordpress/create-block-interactive-template) downloads its template, so in the room create src/blocks/book-filter/ by hand. First the plugin's package.json: both scripts gain --experimental-modules: 
    "build": "wp-scripts build --webpack-src-dir=src/blocks --output-path=build/blocks --blocks-manifest --experimental-modules",
		"start": "wp-scripts start --webpack-src-dir=src/blocks --output-path=build/blocks --blocks-manifest --experimental-modules"
    "Without it, view.js is silently not built" (Common Mistake 1). Then the lesson's block.json: "interactivity": true and "viewScriptModule": "file:./view.js".
  2. render.php: state, derived state, context, directives (8m). Paste the lesson's render.php and read it in four parts with the room: the data (books, genres, each book's genre slugs); ?genre= validated against the real slugs; wp_interactivity_state() with two values and three CLOSURES; the HTML with data-wp-interactive, wp_interactivity_data_wp_context() and the directives. Write on the board: state = genre · derived = isVisible, isSelected, visibleCount · context = slug, genres.
  3. The store (4m). Paste view.js: the same three derived values as getters, and one action, selectGenre, wrapped in withSyncEvent() because it calls preventDefault(). Then style.scss, index.js, edit.js (ServerSideRender) and build:

                         visible: Brave New World, Dune, Fahrenheit 451
Clicked All books        Showing 11 of 11 books current: All books        address: /find-a-book/
                         visible: all 11
Page loads: 1
Console: (empty)
    "Three filters, one page load, an empty Console." With JavaScript switched off the same click reloads the page and the server filters it: progressive enhancement, almost for free.
Three mistakes to expect, and how to coach each
  • No --experimental-modules: "compiled successfully", no view.js, and a filter that reloads the page. Coach: "Is view.js in build/? Does the page load on every click?" (Lesson quiz Q1.)
  • A JavaScript getter that disagrees with its PHP closure: the page changes on hydration (a flash). Coach: "Write the closure and the getter side by side; same inputs, same answer." (Self-check Q2, the guided lab.)
  • Per-element data in the state, or a typo in the namespace. Coach: "Is this the same for every element (state) or one element's own (context)? Is the namespace spelled the same in render.php and view.js?" (Self-check Q4, the debug handout.)
Guided lab

File: labs/module-13/l6_4-interactivity-api/open_today_starter.php; your reference is labs/module-13/l6_4-interactivity-api/open_today_solution.php. An opening-hours box with a folded week: the learner writes two derived-state closures and the directives, and wp_interactivity_process_directives() does on the server exactly what WordPress does for a block with interactivity: true. It practices the server half of the lesson, which is the half PHP developers own, with no build and no browser.

  • Run it as shipped (2m): the paragraph says TODO, and the three days carry only their context.
  • TODOs 1 to 4 in pairs (9m). Before each run, predict which <li> gets hidden, aria-current and the class. Circulate for wp_interactivity_state( 'pagesco/hours' ) inside the closures (it works, but the namespace is already known: no argument needed) and for a forgotten !.
  • Expected when done:
<div data-wp-interactive="pagesco/hours"><p data-wp-text="state.todayText">Today (Saturday): 10:00-16:00</p>
<button aria-expanded="false" data-wp-on--click="actions.toggleWeek" data-wp-bind--aria-expanded="state.showWeek">The whole week</button><ul>
<li aria-current="false" hidden data-wp-context='{"day":"Friday"}' data-wp-bind--hidden="state.isHidden" data-wp-bind--aria-current="state.isToday" data-wp-class--is-today="state.isToday">Friday: 9:00-18:00</li>
<li aria-current="true" class="is-today" data-wp-context='{"day":"Saturday"}' data-wp-bind--hidden="state.isHidden" data-wp-bind--aria-current="state.isToday" data-wp-class--is-today="state.isToday">Saturday: 10:00-16:00</li>
<li aria-current="false" hidden data-wp-context='{"day":"Sunday"}' data-wp-bind--hidden="state.isHidden" data-wp-bind--aria-current="state.isToday" data-wp-class--is-today="state.isToday">Sunday: closed</li>
</ul></div>
  • Debrief (4m): "aria-current says false on Friday: why not simply absent?" (aria- attributes get the words true and false.) "Which directive did the server NOT touch?" (data-wp-on--click.) "What would the browser's store need?" (A getter for each closure and the toggleWeek action: the lesson's view.js pattern; optional at home.)
  • Fast finishers: labs/module-13/l6_4-interactivity-api/event_list_starter.php (data-wp-each repeats a template from a list in the state), then labs/module-13/l6_4-interactivity-api/debug_stock_badges.php.
Start the lesson project

The lesson project is A Find a Book Page: the Book Filter on its own page, which the header menu picks up by itself. In the room only Step 1 (5 minutes), on laptops whose build has view.js.

  • Step 1: a page "Find a Book" with the lesson's paragraph and the Book Filter. Then ask the server for the dystopian books, as text:
http://localhost:8080/find-a-book/?genre=dystopian   (the count, as text)
Showing 3 of 11 books

Checks for understanding

Ask these out loud during the demo and the lab:

  • What is the state of the Book Filter, and what is derived? Answer: the state is the genre (and the books' genres); isVisible, isSelected and visibleCount are derived.
  • Why are the genres links and not buttons? Answer: without JavaScript the link is followed and the server renders the filtered page; with it, the action prevents the navigation.
  • Which directives does the server process? Answer: interactive, context, bind, class, style, text, each; not on, watch, init, run.
  • What does the page load only where the block is? Answer: the view.js script module (and the import map entry for @wordpress/interactivity).

Workbook self-check, items Q1 to Q6 (learners do them at the end of the block or at home).

Answers: Q1 B) From the state JSON that render.php's wp_interactivity_state() put into the page; Q2 D) data-wp-on--click="actions.selectGenre"; Q3 8; Q4 A) In the element's context, wp_interactivity_data_wp_context( array( 'slug' => $slug ) ); Q5 C) Wrapping the action in withSyncEvent(); Q6 The link is followed (a page load) and the server renders the filtered page: the links are real ?genre= links and render.php reads the address. Full set with explanations in the Answer Key.

Differentiation

Support: learners new to JavaScript stores read view.js next to the render.php closures (the board's three columns) and type only render.php. In the lab, give TODO 1's closure on the board; TODO 2 is the same shape.

Stretch: event_list_starter.php and debug_stock_badges.php; the lesson's Exercise 3 (a heading that follows the filter) and the Bonus Challenge (hide sold-out books, with a no-JavaScript fallback).

7.1

Using the REST API

65 min
Objectives (from the lesson page)
  • Explain routes, endpoints, methods, JSON responses and status codes, and list the routes your site offers
  • Read the catalog from core endpoints and shape the answer with _fields, _embed, context, filters and the pagination headers
  • Authenticate the right way: cookie plus nonce for logged-in JavaScript, application passwords for other programs
  • Call the REST API from JavaScript with apiFetch, and handle its errors
  • Read REST errors (400, 401, 403, 404) and tell "who are you?" from "you may not"
Timing in the room
10mFrame: the service counter; base, namespace, route, endpoint, response; the request's trip
30mLive demo: the index and routes, headers and pages, 401, cookie and nonce, an application password, 400, 403, 404, apiFetch
15mGuided lab: catalog_queries_starter.sh
10mStart the lesson project: the inventory script sells the last copy
Mental model to say

"The shop floor is the website: customers browse the shelves, which is HTML. At the back is a service counter with a list of what it handles: 'ask for a book by its number', 'change a price'. Anyone may ask the counter for public information. For anything that changes the shop, the clerk first checks who you are, authentication, and then whether your role allows it, permission. What you get back is a neat package, JSON, with a slip stapled to it: the status code and the headers."

Then the five words on the board with the site's examples: base /wp-json/ · namespace wp/v2 · route /wp/v2/books/(?P<id>[\d]+) · endpoint GET or POST on a route · response JSON + status + headers. And the trip: authentication → route and method → arguments validated → permission → callback → JSON. "Lesson 7.2 builds counters of the shop's own."

Live demo (you type, they follow)

From the site as Lesson 6.4 left it, in the WP-CLI container shell (curl is there, http://localhost:8080 is the site). Learners type every curl: that is the skill.

  1. Ask the API about itself (4m). "Every site has a service counter at /wp-json/." Three fields of the index: 
    curl -s http://localhost:8080/wp-json/   (the fields name, url and namespaces)
    {
  "name": "Pages &amp; Co.",
  "url": "http://localhost:8080",
  "namespaces": [
    "oembed/1.0",
    "wp/v2",
    "wp-site-health/v1",
    "wp-block-editor/v1",
    "wp-abilities/v1"
  ]
}
    Then the routes Lesson 5.2's show_in_rest built for books and genres: 
    wp eval 'foreach ( array_keys( rest_get_server()->get_routes() ) as $route ) { if ( str_contains( $route, "books" ) || str_contains( $route, "genres" ) ) { echo $route, "\n"; } }'
    /wp/v2/books
/wp/v2/books/(?P<id>[\d]+)
/wp/v2/books/(?P<id>[\d]+)/autosaves
/wp/v2/books/(?P<parent>[\d]+)/autosaves/(?P<id>[\d]+)
/wp/v2/genres
/wp/v2/genres/(?P<id>[\d]+)
  2. The catalog, and its headers (5m). "Ten books, and the totals travel in headers." 
    curl -s -D - -o books.json http://localhost:8080/wp-json/wp/v2/books | grep -E '^(HTTP|Link|X-WP-)'
wc -c < books.json
rm books.json
    HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Link: <http://localhost:8080/wp-json/wp/v2/books?page=2>; rel="next"
X-WP-Total: 11
X-WP-TotalPages: 2
13202
    13202 bytes for ten books. Ask for less with _fields, and for a page with per_page and page: 
    curl -s 'http://localhost:8080/wp-json/wp/v2/books?_fields=id,title.rendered,meta.pagesco_price&per_page=3'
    [{"id":40,"title":{"rendered":"Animal Farm"},"meta":{"pagesco_price":8.49}},{"id":39,"title":{"rendered":"Fahrenheit 451"},"meta":{"pagesco_price":10.49}},{"id":38,"title":{"rendered":"Lord of the Rings"},"meta":{"pagesco_price":15.99}}]
    curl -s -i 'http://localhost:8080/wp-json/wp/v2/books?per_page=4&page=2&_fields=id'   (status line, three headers, body)
    HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Link: <http://localhost:8080/wp-json/wp/v2/books?per_page=4&page=1&_fields=id>; rel="prev", <http://localhost:8080/wp-json/wp/v2/books?per_page=4&page=3&_fields=id>; rel="next"
X-WP-Total: 11
X-WP-TotalPages: 3

[{"id":36},{"id":35},{"id":34},{"id":33}]
  3. Who is asking? 401 (3m). "Now change something, anonymously." 
    curl -s -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"meta":{"pagesco_price":12.99}}' http://localhost:8080/wp-json/wp/v2/books/30
    {"code":"rest_cannot_edit","message":"Sorry, you are not allowed to edit this post.","data":{"status":401}}
    401: "who are you?" Then the cookie and the nonce, from the container (the lesson's block: a cookie file for Maria, then users/me without, with and with a made-up nonce): 
    curl -s -o /dev/null -c jar.txt http://localhost:8080/wp-login.php
curl -s -o /dev/null -b jar.txt -c jar.txt --data-urlencode log=maria --data-urlencode pwd=maria-pass -d testcookie=1 http://localhost:8080/wp-login.php
curl -s -b jar.txt 'http://localhost:8080/wp-json/wp/v2/users/me?_fields=id,name'; echo
NONCE=$(curl -s -b jar.txt 'http://localhost:8080/wp-admin/admin-ajax.php?action=rest-nonce')
curl -s -b jar.txt -H "X-WP-Nonce: $NONCE" 'http://localhost:8080/wp-json/wp/v2/users/me?_fields=id,name'; echo
curl -s -b jar.txt -H 'X-WP-Nonce: 0123456789' 'http://localhost:8080/wp-json/wp/v2/users/me?_fields=id,name'; echo
rm jar.txt
    {"code":"rest_not_logged_in","message":"You are not currently logged in.","data":{"status":401}}
{"id":2,"name":"Maria Lopez"}
{"code":"rest_cookie_invalid_nonce","message":"Cookie check failed","data":{"status":403}}
  4. An application password (6m). "A program has no cookie and must never know Maria's real password." Create one for the inventory script (your 24 characters will differ; put them in PASS in the container shell): 
    wp user application-password create maria "Inventory script" --porcelain
    PeVINOjKoM7cd6O2FzYsnzqd
    Who am I, the sale that was refused a minute ago, and the book page that follows at once through Lesson 6.3's binding: 
    curl -s --user "maria:$PASS" 'http://localhost:8080/wp-json/wp/v2/users/me?_fields=id,name'
    {"id":2,"name":"Maria Lopez"}
    curl -s --user "maria:$PASS" -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"meta":{"pagesco_price":12.99}}' 'http://localhost:8080/wp-json/wp/v2/books/30?_fields=id,meta.pagesco_price'
    {"id":30,"meta":{"pagesco_price":12.99}}
    curl -s http://localhost:8080/books/dune/ | grep -o 'has-large-font-size wp-block-paragraph">[^<]*'
    has-large-font-size wp-block-paragraph">$12.99
    Put the price back (the lesson's next command, 14.99). "Basic authentication only encodes: HTTPS, or the local environment, as here."
  5. When the answer is no (7m). "Every error has the same shape: a code, a message, a status." Too many books: 
    curl -s -i 'http://localhost:8080/wp-json/wp/v2/books?per_page=500'
    HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request

{"code":"rest_invalid_param","message":"Invalid parameter(s): per_page","data":{"status":400,"params":{"per_page":"per_page must be between 1 (inclusive) and 100 (inclusive)"},"details":{"per_page":{"code":"rest_out_of_bounds","message":"per_page must be between 1 (inclusive) and 100 (inclusive)","data":null}}}}
    Devon, an author, with his own application password, on Maria's book: 
    curl -s --user "devon:$DEVON_PASS" -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"meta":{"pagesco_price":1}}' http://localhost:8080/wp-json/wp/v2/books/30
    {"code":"rest_cannot_edit","message":"Sorry, you are not allowed to edit this post.","data":{"status":403}}
    The same code as the anonymous POST, but 403: "I know you, and no." Two 404s and a context only editors get: 
    curl -s http://localhost:8080/wp-json/wp/v2/bookz; echo
curl -s http://localhost:8080/wp-json/wp/v2/books/99; echo
    {"code":"rest_no_route","message":"No route was found matching the URL and request method.","data":{"status":404}}
{"code":"rest_post_invalid_id","message":"Invalid post ID.","data":{"status":404}}
    curl -s 'http://localhost:8080/wp-json/wp/v2/books/30?context=edit'; echo
    {"code":"rest_forbidden_context","message":"Sorry, you are not allowed to edit this post.","data":{"status":401}}
  6. apiFetch, on the board (5m). Show the lesson's apiFetch fragment (read, write, catch) and the recording of Common Mistake 2: a plain fetch() on Maria's Dashboard is anonymous, wp.apiFetch() sends the nonce. 
    > await ( await fetch( '/wp-json/wp/v2/users/me?_fields=id,name' ) ).json()
{"code":"rest_not_logged_in","message":"You are not currently logged in.","data":{"status":401}}
> await wp.apiFetch( { path: '/wp/v2/users/me?_fields=id,name' } )
{"id":2,"name":"Maria Lopez"}

Network:  GET /wp-json/wp/v2/users/me?_fields=id,name                        no X-WP-Nonce header   401
          GET /wp-json/wp/v2/users/me?_fields=id%2Cname&_locale=user          X-WP-Nonce header      200
    "When an API says 'not logged in' while you are, check the nonce first."
Three mistakes to expect, and how to coach each
  • _fields without _links, so _embed embeds nothing. No error, no genres. Coach: "What does _embed follow? Is it still in the answer?" (Self-check Q10.)
  • fetch() without the nonce: "not logged in" on a screen where Maria plainly is. Coach: "Which header proves the request comes from your own page?" (Self-check Q12; lesson quiz Q2.)
  • The account password with --user: 401 rest_not_logged_in, indistinguishable from a typo in an application password. Coach: "Which password did you create for this program? Users > Profile: was it ever used?"

Checks for understanding

Ask these out loud during the demo and the lab:

  • Where do the totals of a collection travel? Answer: in the headers X-WP-Total and X-WP-TotalPages (and Link for the neighbors), so the body stays a plain list.
  • Cookie without a nonce, cookie with a wrong nonce: what does each get? Answer: treated as anonymous (401 for anything protected); 403 rest_cookie_invalid_nonce.
  • Devon gets rest_cannot_edit. 401 or 403, and what does it mean? Answer: 403: WordPress knows him and his role says no.
  • Why one application password per program? Answer: revoking one (a lost laptop, a retired script) cuts off exactly that program.

Workbook self-check, items Q7 to Q12 (learners do them at the end of the block or at home).

Answers: Q7 C) 401 rest_forbidden_context; Q8 X-WP-TotalPages: 2; Q9 A) 403 rest_cookie_invalid_nonce: the page must fetch a fresh nonce; Q10 D) _fields removed _links, so there was nothing to follow, and _embedded is cut off too; Q11 B) WP_ENVIRONMENT_TYPE is local; elsewhere WordPress offers them only on HTTPS; Q12 The REST nonce (X-WP-Nonce) for the logged-in user, and the API's root URL (also _locale=user, a JSON body and the server's error object on failure). Full set with explanations in the Answer Key.

Differentiation

Support: a card with the three request shapes: curl -s URL (read), curl -s -I URL (headers only), curl -s --user "maria:$PASS" -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{...}' URL (write). For the lab, TODO 1 and 2 together on the projector.

Stretch: who_may_starter.sh and debug_stock_list.php; the lesson's Exercise 3 (batch/v1) and Exercise 4 (register_rest_field); the Bonus Challenge (a search box with a debounce and AbortController).

Rules and scoring
  • Open notes: the lesson pages, their own plugin and pagesco-plan.txt; no neighbor, no AI assistant. Questions about the wording only.
  • Score with the rubric in the Answer Key: five rows, 0 to 2 points each. Run each learner's file once on your projector site (it changes nothing); compare with the model output line by line.
  • 8 to 10: on track for Session 14. 5 to 7: name the weakest row in your feedback and point to its lesson. Under 5: a one-to-one before Session 15; Module 7 builds directly on 5.3 and 5.5.
  • A learner whose site is not at the end of Lesson 6.3 (no Book List): score Part C from the code, and say so on the sheet.

Closing

Exit ticket (3 questions, no notes, 4 minutes)

Right after the checkpoint, so keep it short: three questions on today's lessons, on a sticky note.

  1. In the Book Filter, name the state and one piece of derived state. Answer: the state is the selected genre (and the books' genres); derived: isVisible, isSelected or visibleCount.
  2. 401 or 403: which means "who are you?" Answer: 401 (not authenticated); 403 is "I know you, and no".
  3. Which credential does a partner's nightly price script use? Answer: an application password of a user whose role can edit books, over HTTPS.
Homework (about 3 hours)
  • Finish both lesson projects. 6.4: Steps 2 and 3 (test it like a customer, with JavaScript off; clean up). 7.1: Steps 2 to 4, the Stock at a glance widget, and the checks.
  • Lesson exercises. 6.4: Exercises 1 and 2 (every filter from the server, the state registry); Exercise 3 is a stretch. 7.1: Exercises 1 and 2 (the catalog page by page, a draft round trip with a throwaway password); 3 and 4 are stretches.
  • Both Quick Quizzes on the lesson pages (answers are in the Answer Key).
  • Journal: both entries (state, derived state and context for the filter; every program that might talk to the site).
  • Before the Next Lesson (7.1): the widget works for Maria, Fahrenheit 451 is in stock; keep the "Inventory script" password (in $PASS, never in wordpress/) and create Devon's "Test" password for Lesson 7.2; reread Lesson 5.3's sanitize and validate and Lesson 5.5's EventsTable::find() and add().
  • Optional: labs/module-13/l6_4-interactivity-api/event_list_starter.php, labs/module-13/l7_1-rest-api/who_may_starter.sh and both debug handouts.
Bring list for Session 14
  • A site at the end of Lesson 7.1 (the widget, fifteen features) and Maria's "Inventory script" and Devon's "Test" application passwords in your password manager.
  • The project folder with labs/; Session 14's labs call the site's own REST API over HTTP, no internet needed.

If You Run Long or Short

Running long: what to protect and what to cut first
  • Protect: the checkpoint's 30 minutes (start at 2:20 even if a lab is unfinished); what the server already did for ?genre=fantasy; 401 versus 403 and the application password.
  • Cut first (saves 5m): the 6.4 project start: the Find a Book page is one paste at home.
  • Cut second (saves 4m): the browser step of the 6.4 demo: the workbook and the lesson have the recording.
  • Cut third (saves 5m): the apiFetch step of the 7.1 demo: the project's widget at home teaches it.
Running short: what to add
  • Lesson 6.4's Exercise 1 live: the count for every genre, romance and an encoded <script>, from curl.
  • Lesson 7.1's Exercise 3: restock two books in one batch request, read the answer's per-request status, undo it.
  • Run who_may_starter.sh for everyone and fill in the table together before running the solution.
Instructor Kit · Facilitator Guide

Session 14: Custom Endpoints, External APIs and Cron

How to teach the session where the shop opens API counters of its own and starts calling another company's: routes with arguments, schemas, errors and permission checks, then a careful HTTP client, transients that survive a broken supplier, WP-Cron jobs scheduled once, and an ability for assistants.

2 lessons 3 hrs session Lessons 7.2–7.3 Session 14 of 18 · Part 2

How to Use This Guide

  • Same rhythm for both lessons: frame (the goal and one mental model) → live demo (you type, they type along) → guided lab (a kit lab, new practice on the lesson's ideas) → start the lesson's own project. The lesson exercises, quiz and journal are homework.
  • Every command below was run on WordPress 7.1.3 / PHP 8.5 to produce the output printed under it: Lesson 7.2's demo on the site after Lesson 7.1 (after:lesson_23), Lesson 7.3's on the site after Lesson 7.2 (after:lesson_24). REST requests shown as curl --user "maria:$PASS" were sent with a real application password. Timing outputs (the timeout demo) differ by a few milliseconds on every run.
  • No internet is needed: the supplier is the course's sandbox inside the site, and the kit's 7.3 labs call the site's own pagesco/v1 API over HTTP, as if it were another company's. Only the lesson's last exercise (Open Library) needs a connection.
  • Labs live in labs/module-14/: _starter files and folders are handouts, _solution files and folders are yours.
  • Part 2, Session 6 of 10. Teal blocks are hands-on, amber blocks are watch-outs. Lesson codes (7.2, 7.3) match the course site.
The #1 risk of Session 14: two long lessons of PHP classes

Lessons 7.2 and 7.3 are written for 145 and 150 minutes and are the plugin's longest files so far (BooksEndpoint, EventsEndpoint, Client, Availability, DailySync, Abilities). Typing them in the room would take the whole session. Paste the classes, read them aloud, and type only the commands and the curl requests: the skill is reading answers and errors, not typing arrays. Both projects' later steps go home (7.2 Steps 3 and 4, 7.3 Steps 3 and 4); say so at 0:00.

Before the Session

  • ☐ Projector site at after:lesson_23 (the end of Lesson 7.1, the Stock at a glance widget). Keep Maria's "Inventory script" password in PASS and Devon's "Test" password in DEVON_PASS in the WP-CLI container shell (docker compose run --rm wpcli sh), never in a file under wordpress/.
  • ☐ Rehearse 7.2's two versions of BooksEndpoint and the EventsEndpoint, and 7.3's sandbox, Client and Availability, on a scratch copy; have the lesson pages open to paste from.
  • ☐ Files to hand out: labs/module-14/ WITHOUT the *_solution.* files and the opening_hours_solution/ folder. Run the kit check once: python3 labs/check_labs.py module-14 (15 results, about two minutes).
  • ☐ Checkpoint 2: bring the scored rubrics and give each learner a minute in the warm-up with their weakest row.
  • ☐ Board, before learners arrive: the four desks validate → sanitize → permission → callback; phone = wp_remote_get · sticky note = transient · closing checklist = WP-Cron.
Known traps of this session
SymptomCauseFix
A route answers, but X-WP-DoingItWrong in the headersNo permission_callbackAlways write the key; __return_true only for public reads (Mistake 1).
per_page=500 acceptedA custom sanitize_callback replaced the schema's checksKeep 'validate_callback' => 'rest_validate_request_arg' next to it (Mistake 2).
500 Internal Server Error with "data":nullA WP_Error without a statusarray( 'status' => 404 ) on every WP_Error a callback returns (Mistake 3).
"REST API routes must be registered on the rest_api_init action"register_rest_route() on initHook rest_api_init.
Trying to access array offset on null after a remote callOnly is_wp_error() was checked; the body was HTML or an errorCheck the status and the decoded shape too (Lesson 7.3, Mistake 1).
Pages hang for secondsA remote call on page views, with the default 5-second timeoutRead a transient; call from a cron job; set a short timeout.
The job ran four timeswp_schedule_event() on every requestSchedule on activation, guarded with wp_next_scheduled() (Mistake 2).
The job "ran" but did nothingThe callback was added only inside is_admin()Add cron callbacks unconditionally (Mistake 3).

Questions and answers
  1. W1 (Lesson 6.4). curl asks /find-a-book/?genre=fantasy. How many books does the server send with the hidden attribute? Answer: 9 of eleven: the server evaluated data-wp-bind--hidden for each book (two fantasy books stay visible).
  2. W2 (Lesson 6.4). Why does selectGenre need withSyncEvent()? Answer: It calls event.preventDefault(); since 6.8 actions may run after the event, too late to stop the link.
  3. W3 (Lesson 7.1). A client gets 403 rest_cannot_edit. Fix the request, the credentials or the role? Answer: The role: 403 means "I know you, and no" (Devon on Maria's book). 401 would be the credentials.
  4. W4 (Lesson 7.1). How does a client learn how many pages the catalog has at per_page=5, without reading the books? Answer: A HEAD request (curl -I) and the header: X-WP-TotalPages: 3 on the projector site.
  5. W5 (Lesson 7.1). Why can the Stock at a glance widget POST to /wp/v2/books with plain apiFetch, and an outside script cannot? Answer: apiFetch sends Maria's cookie AND the page's wp_rest nonce; a script has neither, so it needs an application password.

The projector site's answers to W1 and W4:

Lesson Plans

7.2

Custom REST Endpoints

70 min
Objectives (from the lesson page)
  • Register routes with register_rest_route() on rest_api_init, as a feature class of the plugin
  • Declare arguments with types, defaults, limits and enums, and add your own validate_callback and sanitize_callback without losing the built-in checks
  • Describe responses with a JSON Schema, and return WP_REST_Response objects with headers and status codes
  • Return errors as WP_Error with the right status, and know what WordPress does with one that has none
  • Write a real permission_callback for every route, and explain why __return_true is only for public reads
Timing in the room
10mFrame: a window with a printed menu; route, arguments, schema, permission; the four desks
25mLive demo: a first route, OPTIONS, fantasy by price, four 400s, 400 and 404, Mistake 1
20mGuided lab: the opening_hours_starter/ plugin
15mStart the lesson project: the events route, Steps 1 and 2
Mental model to say

"Core's counter handles everything for everyone, so its menu is long and its packages are big. The shop opens a window of its own with a short printed menu: 'books, by genre or stock, sorted three ways, ten details each' and 'events: read them, or add one if you work here'. The menu is the route and its arguments; the card describing each package is the schema; the sign 'staff only' on the second item is the permission callback. A window without such a sign serves anyone who walks up."

Then the four desks on the board, in order: validate (types, ranges, enums, your validate_callback) → sanitize (strings become integers, defaults fill in) → permission (may this user?) → callback (gets clean, typed values). "A request that fails at a desk never reaches the next."

Three mistakes to expect, and how to coach each
  • No permission_callback, or __return_true on a write. Coach: "Who may call this, and what stops everyone else?" Look at the response headers of your own routes. (Self-check Q5.)
  • A sanitize_callback that switches the schema off (absint on per_page). Coach: "Which function checks the maximum now?" Keep rest_validate_request_arg as the validate_callback. (The debug handout.)
  • A WP_Error without a status, or an error that leaks existence. Coach: "What status does a client see? What does the message tell a stranger?" (Self-check Q6.)

Checks for understanding

Ask these out loud during the demo and the lab:

  • In which order do the desks run? Answer: validate, sanitize, permission, callback.
  • Why WP_Query and not get_posts() in get_books()? Answer: found_posts and max_num_pages for the X-WP-Total headers.
  • What does rest_authorization_required_code() return? Answer: 401 when nobody is logged in, 403 when someone is.
  • What does a WP_Error without a status become? Answer: a 500 with "data":null (lesson quiz Q5).

Workbook self-check, items Q1 to Q6 (learners do them at the end of the block or at home).

Answers: Q1 B) POST; Q2 200 6 2; Q3 A) 400 rest_missing_callback_param: arguments are validated before the permission check; Q4 D) validate_callbacks run first; the schema checks of the other arguments run in the sanitizing step, which a failed validation never reaches; Q5 C) A check of current_user_can( 'edit_others_posts' ) that returns a WP_Error with rest_authorization_required_code(); Q6 An endpoint must not tell visitors what exists behind an ID they may not see: drafts, private books and other post types all get the same 404. Full set with explanations in the Answer Key.

7.3

External APIs, Transients & WP-Cron

80 min
Objectives (from the lesson page)
  • Call an external API with wp_remote_get() and wp_remote_post(), and handle each way it can fail: no answer, an error status, or an answer that is not what you expected
  • Keep API keys in wp-config.php and choose wp_safe_remote_get() when a URL comes from a user
  • Cache answers in transients, explain where they are stored and how a persistent object cache changes that, and cache failures briefly too
  • Schedule recurring work with WP-Cron, start and stop it on activation and deactivation, and inspect and run it with WP-CLI
  • Register an ability with the Abilities API and run it over the REST API
Timing in the room
10mFrame: the phone, the sticky note, the closing checklist
30mLive demo: the sandbox, three ways to fail, transients, WP-Cron, abilities
20mGuided lab: remote_answers_starter.php
20mStart the lesson project: Steps 1 and 2
Mental model to say

"When a bookseller wants to know whether the distributor has more copies of The Great Gatsby, she calls. Sometimes the line is busy, sometimes nobody answers, sometimes the person reads the wrong list. A good bookseller writes the answer on a sticky note with the time, so the next colleague does not call again, and at closing time somebody works through a checklist."

Then the three pieces on the board: the phone = wp_remote_get() and friends; the sticky note = a transient, which may fall off the wall early, so you always check; the closing checklist = WP-Cron, which WordPress works through when the next visitor walks in after closing time. "A page that shows supplier data never waits for the supplier when a fresh note exists, and the nightly job keeps the note fresh."

Live demo (you type, they follow)

From the site as Lesson 7.2 left it. Scratch scripts are saved in wordpress/ and run with wp eval-file; delete them at the end of the demo (the lesson's rm line).

  1. A supplier to call (5m). "Riverside Books is fictional, so the course gives you its sandbox: three files in wordpress/supplier-sandbox/, plain PHP." Paste the lesson's .htaccess, availability.php and orders.php; then the key and the address go into wp-config.php, never into code:

    <?php
$response = wp_remote_get(
	'http://localhost:8080/supplier-sandbox/v1/availability?isbns=9780743273565',
	array(
		'timeout' => 5,
		'headers' => array( 'X-Api-Key' => PAGESCO_BOOKS_SUPPLIER_KEY ),
	)
);

if ( is_wp_error( $response ) ) {
	echo 'No answer: ', $response->get_error_message(), "\n";
	return;
}

echo implode( ', ', array_keys( $response ) ), "\n";
echo wp_remote_retrieve_response_code( $response ), ' ', wp_remote_retrieve_response_message( $response ), "\n";
echo wp_remote_retrieve_header( $response, 'content-type' ), "\n";

$data = json_decode( wp_remote_retrieve_body( $response ), true );
print_r( $data['items'][0] );
    headers, body, response, cookies, filename, http_response
200 OK
application/json; charset=utf-8
Array
(
    [isbn] => 9780743273565
    [available] => 0
    [next_delivery] => 2027-11-15
)
    An array, read with the wp_remote_retrieve_*() helpers; the body is a string you decode and check.
  3. Three ways to fail (6m). "The supplier will have bad days. Provoke all three." The lesson's supplier-failures.php: 
    Wrong key:  response 401 {"error":"invalid_api_key","message":"Send a valid API key in the X-Api-Key header."}
Down:       503, Retry-After 120, JSON: NULL
No host:    WP_Error http_request_failed: cURL error 6: Could not resolve host: supplier.invalid (Domain name not found)
    A 401 and a 503 are normal responses, not WP_Errors; the 503 is HTML, so json_decode() gives NULL; only the missing host is a WP_Error. Then the slow cousin (supplier-slow.php, a 2-second timeout against a 4-second answer): cURL error 28: Operation timed out after 2066 milliseconds (your milliseconds differ) and 1.9 seconds lost for nothing. Pages read caches; jobs call.
  4. Transients (6m). "A sticky note with an expiry date." With WP-CLI, see where it lives: 
    wp transient set pagesco_books_demo 'Gatsby: back November 15' 600
wp transient get pagesco_books_demo
wp db query "SELECT option_name, autoload FROM wp_options WHERE option_name LIKE '%pagesco_books_demo'"
wp transient delete pagesco_books_demo
wp transient get pagesco_books_demo
    Success: Transient added.
Gatsby: back November 15
option_name	autoload
_transient_timeout_pagesco_books_demo	off
_transient_pagesco_books_demo	off

Success: Transient deleted.
Warning: Transient with key "pagesco_books_demo" is not set.
    Two rows in wp_options, not autoloaded; the last command warns on purpose. No persistent object cache here (wp_using_ext_object_cache() prints NULL), so transients live in the database; with Redis they would live in memory and could vanish early. Then the read-through: the lesson's cache-demo.php makes one request for three views: 
    View 1: next delivery 2027-11-15, HTTP requests so far: 1
View 2: next delivery 2027-11-15, HTTP requests so far: 1
View 3: next delivery 2027-11-15, HTTP requests so far: 1
    "Cache failures too, briefly, and never store false."
  5. WP-Cron (6m). "The closing checklist, worked through by the next visitor." Core's events, sorted by recurrence (WP-CLI lists them by next run, which changes): 
    wp cron event list --fields=recurrence,hook --format=csv | sed 1d | sort
wp cron schedule list
wp cron test
    "1 day",delete_expired_transients
"1 day",recovery_mode_clean_expired_keys
"1 day",wp_privacy_personal_data_cleanup_requests
"1 day",wp_scheduled_auto_draft_delete
"1 day",wp_scheduled_delete
"1 hour",wp_privacy_delete_old_export_files
"1 week",wp_delete_temp_updater_backups
"1 week",wp_site_health_scheduled_check
"12 hours",wp_update_plugins
"12 hours",wp_update_themes
"12 hours",wp_update_user_counts
"12 hours",wp_version_check
+------------+-------------+----------+
| name       | display     | interval |
+------------+-------------+----------+
| hourly     | Once Hourly | 3600     |
| twicedaily | Twice Daily | 43200    |
| daily      | Once Daily  | 86400    |
| weekly     | Once Weekly | 604800   |
+------------+-------------+----------+
Success: WP-Cron spawning is working as expected.
    Three rules on the board: times are earliest times · no visitors, no jobs (system cron in 8.4) · jobs run without a user. And the warning: wp cron event run moves a recurring event; fire the hook with do_action() instead.
  6. The Abilities API, in one look (3m). "A third way to open the shop to programs, for assistants." Core's three: 
    wp eval 'foreach ( wp_get_abilities() as $ability ) { echo $ability->get_name(), ": ", $ability->get_label(), "\n"; }'
    core/get-site-info: Get Site Information
core/get-user-info: Get User Information
core/get-environment-info: Get Environment Info
    The project adds pagesco/check-stock (Step 4, at home).
Three mistakes to expect, and how to coach each
  • Trusting the answer: only is_wp_error() checked, then $data['items'] on a maintenance page: two Warnings and a confident "0 copies". Coach: "Which of the three failures does this line handle?" (The guided lab, the debug handout.)
  • Scheduling on every request: four daily events after three commands. Coach: "Where does a plugin do things exactly once?" Activation, guarded by wp_next_scheduled(). (The cron lab.)
  • A cache that never hits: storing false, or checking if ( $cached ) for a value that can be 0. Coach: "What does get_transient() return when nothing is there?" (Self-check Q8, the debug handout.)
Guided lab

File: labs/module-14/l7_3-external-apis-cron/remote_answers_starter.php; your reference is labs/module-14/l7_3-external-apis-cron/remote_answers_solution.php. One careful client function, pagesco_lab_ask(), against five answers: the shop's own pagesco/v1 (Lesson 7.2) called over HTTP like a stranger's API (data, a 400, a 404), a web page that is not JSON, and a host that does not exist. It is the lesson's Client::decode() written by the learner, on an API they know inside out.

  • Run it as shipped (2m): five lines of pagesco_todo.
  • TODOs 1 to 4 (14m). Circulate for the status check written as !== 200 (fine here) and for the message taken from the JSON only (the HTML page has none: fall back to wp_remote_retrieve_response_message()).
  • Expected when done:
genre=fantasy     2 books: The Hobbit, Lord of the Rings
genre=romance     pagesco_remote_http_error (400): Invalid parameter(s): genre
books/99          pagesco_remote_http_error (404): No book was found with that ID.
a web page        pagesco_remote_bad_response: The answer is not JSON.
shop.invalid      http_request_failed: cURL error 6: Could not resolve host: shop.invalid (Domain name not found)
  • Debrief (4m): "Which of the five is a WP_Error before your code touches it?" (Only shop.invalid.) "Which would a page view wait longest for?" (A timeout: 3 seconds here.)
  • Fast finishers: labs/module-14/l7_3-external-apis-cron/events_cache_starter.php (a read-through transient that also caches a failure), labs/module-14/l7_3-external-apis-cron/cron_plan_starter.sh, then labs/module-14/l7_3-external-apis-cron/debug_event_counts.php.

The lesson project is The Supplier Sync: ISBNs, a client, a cached Supplier column, a nightly job and an ability. In the room: Steps 1 and 2 (20 minutes).

  • Step 2: paste src/Supplier/Client.php and src/Supplier/Availability.php, register Availability, ask the supplier once (the lesson's refresh() command), then the Books screen as Maria. The Supplier cells, in title order:

Checks for understanding

Ask these out loud during the demo and the lab:

  • A 503 from the supplier: WP_Error or array? Answer: an array; only no answer at all is a WP_Error (lesson quiz Q1).
  • Where does a transient live on this site, and on one with Redis? Answer: two non-autoloaded rows in wp_options; in the object cache, where it may be evicted early.
  • A job due at 3:00 on a shop without night visitors: when does it run? Answer: with the first request after 3:00.
  • Why does the cron callback check no capability? Answer: cron runs without a user, and nobody can trigger it with input of their own.

Workbook self-check, items Q7 to Q12 (learners do them at the end of the block or at home).

Answers: Q7 D) An empty string; Q8 bool(false); Q9 A) wp_safe_remote_get(): it refuses private networks and odd ports; Q10 B) wp eval 'do_action( "pagesco_books_daily_sync" );'; Q11 C) In wp-config.php (or an environment variable it reads), on each site; Q12 | pagesco_books_daily_sync | 1 day |. Full set with explanations in the Answer Key.

Differentiation

Support: a card with the three checks in order (is_wp_error, the status, the shape) and the three transient functions. In the lab, TODO 2 and 3 on the projector.

Stretch: events_cache_starter.php, cron_plan_starter.sh, debug_event_counts.php; the lesson's Exercise 2 (invalidate the note when an ISBN changes) and Exercise 3 (a six-hour recurrence); the Bonus Challenge (a Reorder row action).

Closing

Exit ticket (3 questions, no notes, 4 minutes)

Learners answer in the workbook's Exit Ticket box or on a sticky note.

  1. Name the four desks a REST request passes, in order. Answer: validate, sanitize, permission, callback.
  2. Name the three ways a call to another server can fail. Answer: no answer (WP_Error: DNS, refused, timeout); an error status (a normal response); a body that is not the data you expect.
  3. Where does a plugin schedule its daily job, and what guards it? Answer: in the activation callback, guarded by wp_next_scheduled(); cleared on deactivation.

  • Finish both lesson projects. 7.2: Steps 3 and 4 (event 7 through the API). 7.3: Steps 3 and 4 (the daily sync, the check-stock ability) and the checks.
  • Lesson exercises. 7.2: Exercises 1 and 2 (rest_do_request, the schema check); Exercise 3 is a stretch. 7.3: Exercises 1 to 3 (an order through the client, invalidation, a six-hour recurrence); Exercise 4 needs the internet.
  • Both Quick Quizzes on the lesson pages (answers are in the Answer Key).
  • Journal: both entries (an endpoint the shop does not have yet; a real service for a client's site).
  • Before the Next Lesson (7.3): the Supplier column and one daily event; no scratch scripts or must-use plugins left (ls wordpress wordpress/wp-content/mu-plugins); Node 22.13 or newer for wp-env in Lesson 8.1 (node --version).
  • Optional: labs/module-14/l7_2-custom-endpoints/schema_rules_starter.php, labs/module-14/l7_3-external-apis-cron/events_cache_starter.php, labs/module-14/l7_3-external-apis-cron/cron_plan_starter.sh and both debug handouts.

Running short: what to add

Instructor Kit · Facilitator Guide

Session 15: Debugging, Testing and Performance

How to teach Lessons 8.1 and 8.2: debugging with evidence instead of guesses (the debug log, a hook that logs, a backtrace, recovery mode, --skip-plugins), checks that machines run (PHPUnit in wp-env, shown as recorded; PHPCS to zero findings), and performance work that starts with a number: the query report, the object cache, N+1, and the Core Web Vitals of the front page.

2 lessons 3 hrs session Lessons 8.1–8.2 Session 15 of 18 · Part 2

How to Use This Guide

  • Same rhythm for both lessons: frame (the goal and one mental model) → live demo (you type, they type along) → guided lab (a kit lab, new practice on the lesson's ideas) → start the lesson's own project. The lesson exercises, quiz and journal are homework.
  • Type, do not paste. Every command below was run to produce the output printed under it, on WordPress 7.1.3, PHP 8.5, MySQL 9.7 and WP-CLI 2.12: Lesson 8.1's demos on the site as Lesson 7.3 leaves it, Lesson 8.2's on the site as Lesson 8.1 leaves it, which is what your projector site has at that point. Four kinds of output are recordings quoted from the lessons, and say so: the PHPUnit runs in wp-env, the SQLite Object Cache, the browser measurements (LCP, CLS, INP) and the PHPCS reports of the project.
  • The lessons are the reference. Keep lesson_26.html and lesson_27.html open in browser tabs. Labs live in labs/module-15/ (learners keep the folder in their project folder, next to compose.yaml): _starter files and next_event_starter/ are handouts, _solution files and next_event_solution/ are yours.
  • Each lesson was written for 150 minutes of work alone (Lesson 8.2: 150); the room has 130 minutes for both. The room does the mental models, the demos, two labs and the first three steps of each project; the tests in wp-env (8.1 Step 4), the browser measurements (8.2 Step 4) and the exercises go home. The Agenda says exactly what.
  • Part 2 (Sessions 9 to 18) builds on the site each lesson leaves; a learner who is a lesson behind does the guided labs from their own state and catches up on the projects at home. Teal blocks are hands-on, amber blocks are watch-outs. Lesson codes (8.1, 8.2) match the course site.
The #1 risk of Session 15: the tooling eats the session

Lesson 8.1's project installs 34 Composer packages (PHPUnit, PHPCS, the WordPress Coding Standards) from the internet, and its tests need Node.js 22.13 or newer for wp-env, which downloads images and WordPress on its first start. Lesson 8.2 installs a plugin from WordPress.org. On venue Wi-Fi, all of it at once is half an hour of progress bars. Before: ask learners to run composer update in the plugin folder at home (Step 1 of Lesson 8.1, with the alias), and to start wp-env once (npx @wordpress/env start, then stop). In the room: the 8.1 project starts with composer show --direct on every machine; whoever has no packages yet runs composer update during the demo, not during the project. wp-env runs at home only. Instead of installing in the room: Query Monitor and the SQLite Object Cache are shown from the lesson's recorded cards; nothing later depends on either.

Before the Session

  • ☐ A week before: remind learners that Lesson 8.1's Step 1 (composer update) and a first npx @wordpress/env start need the internet and Node.js 24 (Session 9's Part 2 check); ask them to do both at home and to bring the site as Lesson 7.3 leaves it (the 7.3 project finished, wp cron event list shows pagesco_books_daily_sync).
  • ☐ Run the kit check once: python3 labs/check_labs.py module-15 from this kit's folder (every line PASS; 14 results in about two minutes). With your own course project: WP_LABS_COMPOSE=~/pagesco-dev python3 labs/check_labs.py module-15 (labs/README.md); labs/module-15/l8_1-debugging-testing/test_next_event.sh needs the site after Lesson 8.1's Step 2.
  • ☐ Projector machine: the course site as Lesson 7.3 leaves it, a copy of it (or a database export) as Lesson 8.1 leaves it for the second half (wp db export ~/s15-after-8-1.sql after your own run-through of 8.1's project, and its plugin folder), the wp and composer shortcuts, VS Code on the plugin folder, two terminals (one for commands, one for tail -f wordpress/wp-content/debug.log), a browser with the Books screen as Maria, http://localhost:8025 (Mailpit) and Chrome's DevTools, plus lesson_26.html and lesson_27.html.
  • ☐ Rehearse the crash once: activating pagesco-crash takes the whole site down for WP-CLI; know the --skip-plugins line by heart before you do it in front of the room, and delete the two recovery-mode options afterwards so the next run sends a fresh email.
  • ☐ Board, before learners arrive: "symptom → suspects → evidence"; the debug constants table (local | production); the three piles of PHPCS findings (fix · auto-fix · document); the measuring loop "measure, change one thing, measure again"; and the request with its three places where time goes (server, network, browser).
  • ☐ Print or share: the workbook (Session 15), sticky notes for help flags and the exit ticket.

Opening Segment

0:00

Warm-up and Homework Check

10 min
Timing
6mFive retrieval questions on Lessons 7.2 and 7.3 (workbook, Warm-up), pairs compare
4mHomework check: the 7.3 project's checkpoint (wp cron event list, the Supplier column), the APIs note in pagesco-plan.txt
Questions and answers
  1. W1 (Lesson 7.3). Name the three ways a call to the supplier can go wrong, and what wp_remote_get() returns for each. Answer: No answer at all (a WP_Error: DNS, refused, timeout); an answer that is not a success (an array with a 401 or 503 status); a success whose body is not the JSON you expect. Only the first is a WP_Error.
  2. W2 (Lesson 7.3). The Supplier column reads a transient. What happens when the transient has vanished? Answer: Availability::get() reads through: it calls the supplier, stores the answer again (12 hours, 5 minutes after an error) and returns it. A transient may vanish at any time, so code never relies on it being there.
  3. W3 (Lesson 7.3). Why does the lesson run the daily job with wp eval 'do_action( "pagesco_books_daily_sync" );' instead of wp cron event run? Answer: wp cron event run on a recurring event reschedules it to now plus the interval: the 03:00 job would move to whenever you ran it.
  4. W4 (Lesson 7.2). Your REST route returns a WP_Error without a status. What does the client get? Answer: A 500. The route's callback should give its WP_Error array( 'status' => 404 ) (or the right code); permission callbacks use rest_authorization_required_code().
  5. W5 (Lesson 7.3). Where do the supplier's address and key live on your site, and why there? Answer: In wp-config.php (PAGESCO_BOOKS_SUPPLIER_URL and _KEY, set with wp config set): configuration per environment, never in the plugin's code. Lesson 8.4 moves them to the server's environment.
Watch-outs
  • A learner without the 7.3 state (no supplier sandbox, no daily job): Lesson 8.1's case cannot be reproduced on their site. Pair them for the demo; their guided lab works anyway (fake_supplier fakes the supplier), and the 7.3 project is the first homework item.
  • W2 and W3 come back in today's demos: the transient holds the evidence of the 8.1 case, and the 8.2 project's invalidation proof runs the daily job with do_action().

Lesson Plans

8.1

Debugging & Testing

65 min
Objectives (from the lesson page)
  • Configure WP_DEBUG, the debug log and error display for development and production, and keep the log private
  • Trace a problem with error_log(), hooks such as http_api_debug and doing_it_wrong_run, and wp_debug_backtrace_summary()
  • Recover from a fatal error with recovery mode and WP-CLI's --skip-plugins, and use Query Monitor to look inside a request
  • Write PHPUnit integration tests with WP_UnitTestCase, factories and pre_http_request, and run them in a wp-env test environment
  • Set up PHPCS with the WordPress Coding Standards for a plugin, fix what it finds, and justify the exceptions with a ruleset or phpcs:ignore
Timing in the room
10mFrame: the detective (symptom, suspects, evidence); the debug constants; unit and integration tests, and why tests never use the network
20mLive demo: the supplier case from the log, a backtrace, a crash and recovery mode, --skip-plugins, the public log, the recorded PHPUnit run
15mGuided lab: fake_supplier_starter.php
20mStart the lesson project: Steps 1 to 3 (composer update, phpcs.xml.dist, fix, auto-fix, document, 0 findings)
Mental model to say

"Debugging is detective work. A symptom: the Supplier column says 'not reachable'. Suspects: the network, the address, the key, the code. Evidence rules them out, one by one. The worst habit is changing code until the symptom goes away. The best is making the program tell you what it is doing." Write symptom → suspects → evidence on the board.

Then the two professional habits in one sentence each: "When something goes wrong, find out why with evidence: the log, a hook that logs, a backtrace, recovery mode. Before anything goes wrong, let machines check the code: tests that run the plugin inside a real WordPress, and PHPCS, which reads every line for what tests rarely catch."

Then the testing picture: unit tests run one function without WordPress (fakes for WordPress), integration tests run your code in a freshly installed WordPress with a test database: WP_UnitTestCase, a rollback after each test, factories for data. "And one rule: tests never use the network. pre_http_request answers instead, so a test decides exactly what the supplier says, including its bad days."

Live demo (you type, they follow)

In the WP-CLI container shell (docker compose run --rm wpcli sh) and the browser, on the site as Lesson 7.3 leaves it. The outputs below come from that site; on yours the time stamps differ and everything else matches.

  1. The debug constants (2m). "Since Lesson 1.2 your site runs with debugging on. Here is all of it, from the WP-CLI container." 
    wp eval 'foreach ( array( "WP_DEBUG", "WP_DEBUG_LOG", "WP_DEBUG_DISPLAY", "SCRIPT_DEBUG" ) as $name ) { printf( "%-17s %s\n", $name, var_export( constant( $name ), true ) ); } printf( "%-17s %s\n%-17s %s\n", "environment", wp_get_environment_type(), "error_log", ini_get( "error_log" ) );'

WP_DEBUG_LOG      true

  2. A case: "Supplier not reachable" (5m). "A colleague edited wp-config.php. A few minutes later Maria's Books screen says the supplier is not reachable. No guessing: evidence." Break the key by one character, then look as Maria: 
    wp config set PAGESCO_BOOKS_SUPPLIER_KEY 'sandbox-7f3a9d'
wp transient delete pagesco_books_supplier_availability
    Success: Updated the constant 'PAGESCO_BOOKS_SUPPLIER_KEY' in the 'wp-config.php' file with the value 'sandbox-7f3a9d'.
Success: Transient deleted.
Supplier not reachable
    Evidence 1, what the code already recorded (Availability keeps the error in its transient): 
    wp eval 'echo get_transient( "pagesco_books_supplier_availability" )["error"], "\n";'
    The supplier answered 401: Send a valid API key in the X-Api-Key header.
    Evidence 2, make the code talk: save the lesson's temporary logger as wordpress/wp-content/mu-plugins/pagesco-debug-http.php, delete the cached failure, reload the Books screen, and read the new line of debug.log: 
    <?php
/**
 * Plugin Name: Pages & Co. Debug: HTTP requests (temporary)
 */

add_action(
	'http_api_debug',
	function ( $response, $context, $transport, $args, $url ) {
		$key = $args['headers']['X-Api-Key'] ?? '';
		error_log(
			sprintf(
				'HTTP %s %s, key %s, answer %s',
				$args['method'],
				strtok( $url, '?' ),
				'' === $key ? 'none' : substr( $key, 0, 8 ) . '…',
				is_wp_error( $response ) ? $response->get_error_message() : wp_remote_retrieve_response_code( $response )
			)
		);
	},
	10,

Three mistakes to expect, and how to coach each
  • Changing code until the symptom disappears. A learner edits Client.php to "fix" the 401. Coach: "What is your evidence? What did the transient say, what did the log say?" The answer was in wp-config.php all along. (Self-check Q2, the debug handout.)
  • Logging secrets. The quick logger writes the whole API key, or the whole request. Coach: "Who reads this log, and for how long does it live?" Eight characters are enough to compare. (The debug handout's silent bug.)
  • Making PHPCS quiet instead of making the code right. A plugin-wide exclude, or // phpcs:ignore without a rule and a reason. Coach with the three piles on the board: fix, auto-fix, document; every exception names its rule and says why. (Self-check Q5, the lesson quiz Q4.)

It practices the lesson's central testing idea on the learner's own site, without wp-env: each check fakes one answer of the supplier with pre_http_request and asserts the exact error code the client returns.
