Checks for understanding

Ask these out loud during the demo and the lab:

  • The Books screen says "Supplier not reachable". Where do you look first? Answer: at what the code already recorded: the transient's error (the 401 message), then make the code talk with an http_api_debug logger.
  • Which page triggers the recovery email: the home page or wp-login.php? Answer: a protected page such as wp-login.php or wp-admin; and at most once a day per error.
  • Why does a test fake the supplier instead of calling the sandbox? Answer: so the test controls the answer, bad days included, and passes or fails because of your code only (lesson quiz Q3).
  • PHPCS flags echo get_block_wrapper_attributes();. Wrap it in esc_html()? Answer: no: core escapes it; a phpcs:ignore for that rule on that line, with the reason (lesson quiz Q4).

Workbook self-check, items Q1 to Q6 (learners do them at the end of the block or at home).

Answers: Q1 B) A file outside the web root, such as /home/pagesco/logs/wordpress.log; Q2 pagesco_supplier_http_error 503; Q3 D) wp --skip-plugins=pagesco-crash plugin deactivate pagesco-crash; Q4 A) Must-use plugins load in alphabetical order: it must be there before the plugin that asks too early; Q5 C) Excluded that rule for those two file patterns in phpcs.xml.dist, with a comment: WordPress includes them inside a function, so the variables are local; Q6 npx @wordpress/env run cli --env-cwd=wp-content/plugins/pagesco-books vendor/bin/phpunit: the plugin's own PHPUnit 9.6; the container's global phpunit is 10.5, which the WordPress 7.1 test library does not support. Full set with explanations in the Answer Key.

Differentiation

Support: learners new to testing do the guided lab with the lesson's SupplierClientTest open next to it: each pagesco_lab_check() is one assertSame(). For PHPCS, hand out the decision table as the only reference: every finding goes into one of three piles.

Stretch: debug_supplier_log.php and the PHPCS folder lab; the lesson's Exercise 1 (SettingsTest) and Exercise 3 (what PHPCS sees in insecure code); the Bonus Challenge (PHPCompatibilityWP and a render_block() test).

8.2

Performance & Caching

70 min
Objectives (from the lesson page)
  • Measure what a request costs with SAVEQUERIES and $wpdb->queries, read an EXPLAIN of a meta query, and recognize missing options and N+1 queries
  • Explain the object cache, its persistent version and transients, choose between them, and cache your own query with a key that is invalidated when the data changes
  • Describe how WordPress 7.1 loads block CSS, script modules and classic scripts, and use wp_preload_resources and fetchpriority where they help
  • Explain srcset, sizes, lazy loading and why block templates get no automatic image optimization
  • Measure LCP, CLS and interaction timing in a browser, and say honestly what a local lab measurement can and cannot tell you
Timing in the room
10mFrame: the line at the register; three places where time goes; object cache, persistent cache, transients
20mLive demo: first byte, SAVEQUERIES and the query report, the object cache, N+1, the lazy hero image, the recorded numbers
15mGuided lab: query_count_starter.php
25mStart the lesson project: Steps 1 to 3 (the events cache, the settings row, update_postmeta_cache)
Mental model to say

"A busy Saturday at Pages & Co., a long line at the register. You could hire a second cashier, buy a faster card reader or move the gift wrapping. A good manager first stands next to the register for ten minutes with a notepad: if the time goes into wrapping, the card reader money is wasted." Then the rule on the board: measure, change one thing, measure again.

Then the three places, each with its tool: "The server builds the HTML (SAVEQUERIES, the query report). The network carries it and every file it names (View Source, the Network panel). The browser turns it into pixels (Core Web Vitals: LCP, INP, CLS)."

Then the caches, as a table on the board: the object cache remembers within one request; a persistent object cache (an object-cache.php drop-in: Redis, Memcached) keeps it between requests; a transient outlives the request on any site, in wp_options or in the persistent cache. "And every cache needs an invalidation plan: a key that knows when the data changed."

Live demo (you type, they follow)

From the project folder and the WP-CLI container, on the site as Lesson 8.1 leaves it. Recorded cards (the persistent cache, the browser numbers) are marked as such.

  1. How long until the first byte? (2m). "Before any idea, a number." Three pages, the server's share of the time (yours differ, and differ between two runs: run it twice): 
    for page in / /books/dune/ /find-a-book/; do
  curl -s -o /dev/null -w "$page  %{http_code}  %{size_download} bytes  first byte after %{time_starttransfer} s\n" "http://localhost:8080$page"
done

  5. Mistake 3: lazy-loading the image that matters most (4m). "The hero image, as the theme's pattern wrote it:" 
    <img src="http://localhost:8080/wp-content/themes/pagesco/assets/images/book-image.webp" alt="A hardcover book with a black-and-white photo on its cover" style="width:280px"/>
    No width, no height, no fetchpriority: WordPress skips block templates. Then the lesson's "lazy-load everything" must-use plugin, mistake-lazy.php: 
    <?php
/**
 * Plugin Name: Mistake: Lazy-Load Every Image
 */

add_filter(
	'render_block_core/image',
	function ( $html ) {
		$image = new WP_HTML_Tag_Processor( $html );
		if ( $image->next_tag( 'img' ) ) {
			$image->set_attribute( 'loading', 'lazy' );
		}
		return $image->get_updated_html();
	}
);
    <img loading="lazy" src="http://localhost:8080/wp-content/themes/pagesco/assets/images/book-image.webp" alt="A hardcover book with a black-and-white photo on its cover" style="width:280px"/>
    In the lesson's lab measurement (Chromium, Slow 4G) LCP went from about 1480 ms to about 2012 ms: "no message tells you". Then rm pagesco-count-isbns.php wp-content/mu-plugins/mistake-lazy.php wp-content/mu-plugins/pagesco-query-report.php; wp config delete SAVEQUERIES.
  6. Core Web Vitals, honestly (2m). Show the lesson's console snippet and its recorded numbers: LCP about 1480 ms with the hero image as the LCP element, CLS 0.101 (over 0.1), interactions on the Book Filter 16 ms. Say: "Lab numbers compare a change on one machine. Field data from real visitors, after the launch, decides the rest."
Three mistakes to expect, and how to coach each
  • Optimizing without a number. "I added a cache, it feels faster." Coach: "What was the count before, and after? Same page, same machine, twice." (The guided lab, self-check Q7.)
  • A cache nobody clears. A learner caches the shortcode's HTML for a day. Coach: "Add an event. When does the page show it?" Then the last-changed pattern: the key changes when the data does. (Lesson Mistake 1, self-check Q10, the debug handout.)
  • Trusting a warm cache. N+1 disappears behind a persistent cache and comes back after wp cache flush. Coach: "Measure with an empty cache." (Self-check Q9.)
Guided lab

File: labs/module-15/l8_2-performance-caching/query_count_starter.php; your reference is labs/module-15/l8_2-performance-caching/query_count_solution.php. It practices the lesson's measuring habit on five calls learners already write every day: each row runs a call twice and prints its queries, so the object cache becomes visible. The rule of the lab: write the prediction in the comment before you run.

  • Run it as shipped (2m). cp labs/module-15/l8_2-performance-caching/query_count_starter.php wordpress/, wp eval-file --use-include query_count_starter.php: row 1 (an autoloaded option: 0 and 0), then TODO.
  • Rows 2 to 6 in pairs (10m). Predict, then write the pagesco_lab_row() call. Circulate for row 5: pagesco_lab_forget_meta() first, or row 4's WP_Query has already cached some of the meta and the count is lower.
  • Expected when done:
call                                                                     first     again
get_option( 'blogname' )                                                     0         0
get_option( 'pagesco_lab_missing' )                                          1         0
get_post_meta( 33, 'pagesco_price' ) and 'pagesco_author'                    1         0
WP_Query: the three cheapest books                                           6         0
get_post_meta() over 11 books, one by one                                   11         0
get_post_meta() over 11 books, after update_postmeta_cache()                 1         0
  • Debrief (3m): "Which predictions were wrong?" (Usually row 2: a missing option costs one query, then none; and row 4's six.) "Which row is the supplier feature's lookup before the project, and which after?" (Rows 5 and 6.)
  • Fast finishers: labs/module-15/l8_2-performance-caching/cheapest_cache_starter.php (the last-changed pattern on a query of their own), labs/module-15/l8_2-performance-caching/page_weight_starter.sh (what the pages download), then labs/module-15/l8_2-performance-caching/debug_events_cache.php.
Start the lesson project

The lesson project is A Faster Shop, with Numbers: four improvements, each measured. In the room: Steps 1 to 3 (25 minutes); the hero image (Step 4) needs a browser with DevTools and time, and goes home with Step 5.

  • Before Step 1: the query report and SAVEQUERIES from the demo stay on (the lesson says so). Learners who skipped the demo create both now.
  • Step 1: the new EventsTable.php (type it: the key, is_array(), flush_cache() in install, add and delete_before), the measurement, and the invalidation proof with the past event and do_action( "pagesco_books_daily_sync" ). Learners without the SQLite Object Cache (no internet) skip its rounds: the proof works without it.
  • Step 2: the new Activator.php, deactivate and activate, the empty autoloaded row (a:0:{}, auto), the five addresses again: one query fewer each.
  • Step 3: Mistake 2's script, the two lines with sed (or by hand), 12 queries to 2, refresh() still finds 11 books.
  • Done in the room = the settings row exists and pagesco-count-isbns.php says 2 queries. Goes home: Step 4 (pattern edit, pagesco_preload_hero_image(), measured with the console snippet and Slow 4G) and Step 5 (the table, the instruments removed, composer lint 0).
Checks for understanding

Ask these out loud during the demo and the lab:

  • The report lists pagesco_books_settings under missing options on every request. What does it cost? Answer: one query per request; an autoloaded row removes it (lesson quiz Q1).
  • A value stored with wp_cache_set(), no persistent cache: how long does it live? Answer: until the end of the request (lesson quiz Q2, self-check Q8).
  • Why the group's last-changed value in the key? Answer: every write renews it, so every older cached result becomes unreachable without anyone deleting it (lesson quiz Q3).
  • A laptop measurement says LCP 1.4 s. What do you know? Answer: a baseline to compare a change against on the same machine; field data decides the rest (lesson quiz Q5).

Workbook self-check, items Q7 to Q12 (learners do them at the end of the block or at home).

Answers: Q7 1; Q8 B) bool(false); Q9 C) 501 queries; the fix is update_postmeta_cache( $ids ) before the loop: 2 queries; Q10 B) A cached empty result, array(), would count as a miss: a location without events would query the database on every call; Q11 D) The hero image had no reserved space; the Image block's aspectRatio attribute fixed it; Q12 wp_preload_resources, with 'fetchpriority' => 'high' (and 'as' => 'image'). Full set with explanations in the Answer Key.

Differentiation

Support: a learner who is lost in the numbers gets one question per row: "first time, second time, why the difference?" The table in the lesson's Step 5 is the map; every row of it is one step.

Stretch: cheapest_cache_starter.php and debug_events_cache.php; the lesson's Exercise 3 (the price query at two thousand books) and the Bonus Challenge (caching the catalog route, and the case its key misses).

Debrief

2:35

Before and After: What the Checks Prove

15 min
Sequence
  • Two numbers per lesson (5m). Ask pairs for their before and after: PHPCS 58 findings to 0 (or how far they got); pagesco-count-isbns.php 12 queries to 2; the missing option gone. Write them on the board next to the morning's "measure, change one thing, measure again".
  • What each check proves, and what it cannot (5m). composer lint: the code follows the standard and escapes, prepares, checks nonces where it can see it; not that it works. The tests: the behaviors they name, on a fresh WordPress; not the browser, not the theme. The query report: the server's work; not what the visitor feels. Lab Web Vitals: a comparison on one machine; not the field. "Which of these would have caught the 401 of this morning?" (None: the log did. Debugging and testing are two different habits.)
  • The notes (5m). Learners write the Quality and Performance headings into pagesco-plan.txt now, with today's numbers. Lesson 9.1's final project asks for exactly this kind of proof ("composer lint clean, the PHPUnit suite green in wp-env, the numbers before and after").

Closing

Exit ticket (3 questions, no notes, 4 minutes)

Put the three questions on the slide. Learners answer in the workbook's Exit Ticket box or on a sticky note and leave it on the way out. Question 2's pile tells you whether Session 16's warm-up repeats the last-changed pattern.

  1. A live site shows "There has been a critical error on this website." Name two places to look, and one command that still works when a plugin is the cause. Answer: the server's error log (or debug.log on development), the recovery mode email; wp --skip-plugins=<plugin> plugin deactivate <plugin>.
  2. Why does EventsTable::find() put wp_cache_get_last_changed( 'pagesco_events' ) into its cache key? Answer: every change to the table renews it (flush_cache()), so after a write every old key is unreachable and no stale list is ever read.
  3. Name one thing a lab measurement on your laptop can tell you, and one it cannot. Answer: whether a change made the page better or worse on the same machine; not what real visitors on their phones experience (field data, after the launch).

  • Lesson exercises. 8.1: Exercises 1 and 3 (SettingsTest; what PHPCS sees in insecure code); Exercise 2 is a stretch. 8.2: Exercises 1 and 2 (the emoji script; the inline CSS budget); Exercise 3 is a stretch. Remove the exercise test files afterwards if you want your counts to match the later lessons.
  • Both Quick Quizzes on the lesson pages (five questions each; answers are in the Answer Key).
  • Journal: both entries. The 8.1 prompt asks about the last bug you chased; the 8.2 prompt asks you to measure a slow site before you guess.
  • Before the Next Lesson (from 8.2): wp config get SAVEQUERIES says it is not defined, wp plugin list --status=dropin is empty, and the twelve tests pass once more in wp-env.
  • Optional: the labs not reached in class: labs/module-15/l8_1-debugging-testing/debug_supplier_log.php, the PHPCS folder lab next_event_starter/, labs/module-15/l8_2-performance-caching/cheapest_cache_starter.php, labs/module-15/l8_2-performance-caching/page_weight_starter.sh (run it before and after your Step 4) and labs/module-15/l8_2-performance-caching/debug_events_cache.php.

Instructor Kit · Facilitator Guide

Session 16: Distribution and Deployment

How to teach Lessons 8.3 and 8.4 and hand out the final project: translator-friendly strings, accessibility checks that are honest about their limits and a release ZIP that ships only what runs; then the shop's code in Git, release builds from a tag, a migration previewed and the production configuration, rehearsed on a second WordPress; and the Reserve & Pick Up brief, milestones and rubric.

2 lessons 3 hrs session Lessons 8.3–8.4 Session 16 of 18 · Part 2

How to Use This Guide

  • Same rhythm for both lessons: frame → live demo → guided lab → start the lesson's own project; exercises, quiz and journal are homework. Then a third block: the final project's brief, handed out today so that learners arrive at Session 17 with a plan.
  • Type, do not paste. Every command below was run to produce the output under it on WordPress 7.1.3, PHP 8.5, MySQL 9.7 and WP-CLI 2.12: Lesson 8.3's demos on the site as Lesson 8.2 leaves it, Lesson 8.4's on the site as Lesson 8.3 leaves it. Recordings quoted from the lessons say so: Plugin Check and the Spanish front end (they need the internet), the keyboard walk and axe audits (a browser), and everything on the pagesco-live rehearsal server.
  • The lessons are the reference: keep lesson_28.html, lesson_29.html and lesson_30.html open. Labs live in labs/module-16/: _starter files are handouts, _solution files are yours. Each lesson was written for 150 minutes of work alone (Lesson 8.4: 150); the room has 120 for both, plus 25 for the brief.
  • Git, the release builds and the rehearsal server run on the learner's own computer (the WP-CLI container has no git); the kit's labs practice the server-side half (WP-CLI, wp db, cron) on the development site.
The #1 risk of Session 16: the launch needs the earlier release

Lesson 8.4's project commits and tags "Pages & Co. Books 1.1.0": it needs Lesson 8.3's release finished (Steps 3 to 5: the Spanish files, the accessibility fixes, the readme and the ZIP), which does not fit in the room. So the room starts Lesson 8.4's project at Step 3 (the rehearsal server: download, .env, docker compose up -d), which needs nothing from 8.3; Steps 1 and 2 go home after 8.3's Step 5. Before: learners download pagesco-live.zip at home (Session 15's bring list) and check git --version. In the room: nobody types git commit before wp plugin list shows pagesco-books 1.1.0.

Before the Session

  • ☐ A week before: remind learners of the bring list (the site as Lesson 8.2 leaves it, pagesco-live.zip downloaded, Git, Node.js 24, internet at home for es_ES and Plugin Check).
  • ☐ Run the kit check once: python3 labs/check_labs.py module-16 (every line PASS; 14 results in about two minutes); with your project, WP_LABS_COMPOSE=~/pagesco-dev ... (labs/README.md). Lesson 8.4's labs need the site after Lesson 8.3.
  • ☐ Projector machine: the site as Lesson 8.2 leaves it, and a copy as Lesson 8.3 leaves it (a database export and the plugin folder) for the second half; pagesco-live unzipped next to pagesco-dev, its .env made and its images pulled (docker compose pull in its folder) so that up -d takes seconds; Git configured; lesson_30.html printed or on screen for the brief.
  • ☐ Print: the workbook (Session 16), and one copy of Lesson 9.1's brief, milestones table, security checklist and rubric per pair (or the final project part of final-assessment.html).
  • ☐ Board: the publisher's three jobs (i18n · l10n · a11y); "code goes up · content comes down · configuration stays"; the release recipe (tag → git archive → composer install --no-dev → npm ci, build, plugin-zip).

Opening Segment

0:00

Warm-up and Homework Check

10 min
Timing
6mFive retrieval questions on Lessons 8.1 and 8.2 (workbook, Warm-up), pairs compare
4mHomework check: composer lint 0, the twelve tests green, the Performance table in pagesco-plan.txt
Questions and answers
  1. W1 (Lesson 8.1). On a live site, where do PHP's messages go, and why not to wp-content/debug.log? Answer: To a log outside the web root (or the server's log), display always off: wp-content/debug.log is a public download (200 for anyone).
  2. W2 (Lesson 8.1). Which command runs the plugin's tests, and in which site? Answer: npx @wordpress/env run cli --env-cwd=wp-content/plugins/pagesco-books vendor/bin/phpunit, in the plugin's own wp-env test site on port 8889, never in the site you develop on.
  3. W3 (Lesson 8.2). get_posts() with 'fields' => 'ids', then get_post_meta() for each ID: what is that called, and the fix? Answer: N+1 queries; update_postmeta_cache( $ids ) before the loop loads all the meta in one query.
  4. W4 (Lesson 8.2). What makes a cached result of EventsTable::find() unreachable after a new event is added? Answer: add() calls flush_cache(), which renews wp_cache_get_last_changed( 'pagesco_events' ), and that value is part of every key.
  5. W5 (Lesson 8.2). The theme's hero image got two fixes. Which, and what did each change? Answer: The Image block's aspectRatio (CLS 0.101 to 0.001: the space is reserved) and a preload with fetchpriority high in wp_preload_resources (LCP a little earlier).
Watch-outs
  • No tests run yet (wp-env did not start at home): fine for today; they must be green before Session 17, because Lesson 9.1's Milestone 7 adds five.
  • A learner still on 8.1's project: the 8.3 labs run on the 8.2 state; they finish 8.2's Steps 4 and 5 before 8.3's Step 5.

Lesson Plans

8.3

Internationalization, Accessibility & Distribution

60 min
Objectives (from the lesson page)
  • Generate a POT file with wp i18n make-pot, write translator-friendly strings, and produce .mo, .l10n.php and JavaScript .json translations with WP-CLI
  • Explain how WordPress 7.1 finds a plugin's translations, for PHP (Domain Path) and for scripts (wp_set_script_translations() and block.json)
  • Check a theme and its blocks for accessibility with contrast ratios, a keyboard walk and an automated axe audit, and say what automated checks miss
  • Prepare a plugin for distribution: a valid readme.txt, version numbers, the directory guidelines, a release ZIP without development files, and a clean Plugin Check report
  • Write an uninstall routine that removes content only when an administrator has opted in
Timing in the room
10mFrame: manuscript, translations, editions for every reader
20mLive demo: make-pot, the JSON hashes, untranslatable strings, contrast, the uninstall without its taxonomy, the ZIP's autoloader, Plugin Check as recorded
15mGuided lab: plural_strings_starter.php
15mStart the lesson project: Steps 1 and 2
Mental model to say

"A publisher who buys a novel does three things before every reader can have it. The manuscript is prepared for translators: nothing that only works in English. Translators produce the Spanish edition. And there are editions for readers who read differently: large print, an audiobook." On the board: i18n = your code, every string through a translation function with the text domain, in a form a translator can work with; l10n = translation files, from anyone, later; a11y = a quality of every page.

Then distribution in one sentence: "Pages & Co. Books is installed on one site, and it is still distributed: to staging, to the live site, to the next developer, as a ZIP with a version number. Building it to the directory's standard is the professional baseline."

Live demo (you type, they follow)

In the WP-CLI container, on the site as Lesson 8.2 leaves it.

  1. Strings to a POT file (4m). "A translator never reads your code: they get a POT file." From the WP-CLI container: 
    wp i18n make-pot wp-content/plugins/pagesco-books /tmp/pagesco-books.pot --exclude=src/blocks,tests
grep -c '^msgid ' /tmp/pagesco-books.pot
grep -B3 -A4 '^msgid "%d seat"' /tmp/pagesco-books.pot
    Plugin file detected.
Success: POT file successfully generated.
132
#. translators: %d: number of seats.
#: src/Shortcodes/EventsShortcode.php:65
#, php-format
msgid "%d seat"
msgid_plural "%d seats"
msgstr[0] ""
msgstr[1] ""
    Read the entry from the top: the translators comment you wrote in Lesson 5.5, the file and line, php-format, singular and plural. Then why --exclude=src/blocks,tests: JavaScript translations are matched to the script the browser loads, so the POT points at build/. The names those JSON files will need: 
    for script in assets/js/stock-widget.js build/blocks/book-list/index.js; do
  echo "$(printf '%s' "$script" | md5sum | cut -d' ' -f1)  $script"
done
    cfe2bc3ef2a0800531dc26491d4caca6  assets/js/stock-widget.js
1ef6e759fb00b1b9d64a64056a083f27  build/blocks/book-list/index.js
  2. Mistake 1: strings a translator cannot translate (4m). "Four typical mistakes in a scratch file, wordpress/pagesco-strings-test/strings.php. Count what make-pot notices." 
    <?php
/**
 * Plugin Name: Strings Test
 * Text Domain: pagesco-books
 */

$shown = 3;
$total = 11;
$genre = 'Fantasy';

echo sprintf( __( 'Showing %s of %s books', 'pagesco-books' ), $shown, $total );
echo __( 'Books in ', 'pagesco-books' ) . $genre;
echo sprintf( __( '%d books', 'pagesco-books' ), $shown );
echo __( $genre, 'pagesco-books' );
    wp i18n make-pot pagesco-strings-test /tmp/strings.pot
grep '^msgid' /tmp/strings.pot
    Plugin file detected.
Warning: The string "Showing %s of %s books" contains placeholders but has no "translators:" comment to clarify their meaning. (strings.php:11)
Warning: Multiple placeholders should be ordered. (strings.php:11)
Warning: The string "%d books" contains placeholders but has no "translators:" comment to clarify their meaning. (strings.php:13)
Success: POT file successfully generated.
msgid ""
msgid "Strings Test"
msgid "Showing %s of %s books"
msgid "Books in "
msgid "%d books"
    Two warnings for four mistakes, and exit 0. The silent two are worse: "Books in " is a fragment, and __( $genre ) produced no entry at all. Then rm -r pagesco-strings-test /tmp/strings.pot.
  3. Contrast, computed (3m). "Accessibility check one: numbers, not taste." Save the lesson's wordpress/pagesco-contrast.php: 
    wp eval-file pagesco-contrast.php
    ink      on paper     13.9:1  AAA   body text
oxblood  on paper      8.8:1  AAA   links
slate    on paper      5.8:1  AA    dates, small text
ink      on sage      12.0:1  AAA   header band
paper    on ink       13.9:1  AAA   notice bar, footer
paper    on oxblood    8.8:1  AAA   buttons
    4.5:1 for normal text, 3:1 for large text and control outlines. Then the two checks no script does: the keyboard walk and an axe audit, recorded in the lesson (show its cards): the selected genre's focus is invisible, the Navigation nests a list, the notice is outside any landmark.
  4. Mistake 2: an uninstall that cannot find the genres (3m). "uninstall.php runs with the plugin NOT loaded. Reproduce that with --skip-plugins:" 
    wp --skip-plugins=pagesco-books eval '$genres = get_terms( array( "taxonomy" => "genre", "hide_empty" => false ) ); echo is_wp_error( $genres ) ? $genres->get_error_code() . ": " . $genres->get_error_message() : count( $genres ) . " genres", "\n";'
wp --skip-plugins=pagesco-books eval 'echo count( get_posts( array( "post_type" => "book", "numberposts" => -1 ) ) ), " books\n";'
    invalid_taxonomy: Invalid taxonomy.
11 books
    Books found (WP_Query just compares a column), genres not (an unregistered taxonomy is a WP_Error): an uninstall that loops over that deletes nothing, silently. The project's uninstall.php registers the taxonomy first.
  5. Mistake 3: the development autoloader in a ZIP (3m). "Copy what a careful ZIP would contain, and load it as WordPress would." 
    mkdir -p /tmp/zip-test/vendor

8.4

Deployment & Maintenance

65 min
Objectives (from the lesson page)
  • Choose a hosting type for a WordPress project by what it needs, and explain how code, content and configuration move between development, staging and production
  • Keep a WordPress project's own code in Git with a .gitignore, and build release files from a tagged commit with composer install --no-dev, npm ci, npm run build and the plugin ZIP
  • Move a database with wp db export, wp db import and wp search-replace, including serialized values and a plugin's own tables
  • Configure WordPress for production: debugging and development mode off, the environment type, secrets outside the code, a real cron job, file editing disabled and a least-privilege database account
  • Back up a site and prove the backup with a restore, deploy an update, and keep a maintenance checklist
Timing in the room
10mFrame: code goes up, content comes down, configuration stays
20mLive demo: the configuration, development mode, secrets, Git, a dry run, serialized data, what the web root hands out, the recorded rehearsal
15mGuided lab: migration_preview_starter.sh
20mStart the lesson project: Step 3, the rehearsal server
Mental model to say

"Pages & Co. moves into a bigger store. The carpenter builds the shelves in the workshop and carries them in finished. The books come along once, on moving day, and from then on the booksellers add and sell them in the store. The alarm code is set for the new building and never painted on a shelf." On the board: code goes up (Git, a release build, a deploy) · content comes down (the database moves once, then only copies from live) · configuration stays (written per environment).

Then the consequence that surprises everyone once: "An edit in the live Site Editor is content. Deploy a new header.html and Maria's header stays." (Self-check Q7.)

Checks for understanding
  • A bug fix after a month live: what do you deploy? Answer: only the plugin ZIP built from the release tag (lesson quiz Q1).
  • Export without --all-tables-with-prefix: what is missing? Answer: the plugin's events table (lesson quiz Q2).

Workbook self-check, items Q7 to Q12.

Answers: Q7 B) Maria's header: Site Editor changes are saved in the database, and they win over the theme's files; Q8 12 13: wp_pagesco_events, the plugin's own table, which WordPress does not register; Q9 A) The GUID is an identifier feed readers use to recognize posts, not a link: it must not change; Q10 D) Git cannot let a file back in when its folder is ignored: the folder is let in, its contents ignored again, then the one subfolder let in; Q11 composer install --no-dev --optimize-autoloader: the development packages (PHPUnit, PHPCS), so vendor/composer has no autoload_files.php that requires them; Q12 C) It fails with error 1044, and leaves a small header-only file under the backup's name. Full set with explanations in the Answer Key.

Differentiation

Support: one card with the release recipe in order (tag, git archive, composer install --no-dev -o, npm ci, build, plugin-zip) and the launch in order (code first, then the database).

Stretch: the lesson's three exercises (launch check as code, nightly backup script, smoke test), and the Bonus Challenge (a CI workflow on release-* tags).

The Final Project

2:25

The Final-Project Brief: Reserve & Pick Up

25 min
Timing
8mThe brief: Maria's requirements, read aloud, and what learners hand in
7mThe ten milestones, the security checklist and the rubric
8mFirst plan, in pairs: nouns and verbs, requirements to layers
2mWhat Session 17 starts with, and what to plan tonight
Objectives (from the lesson page)
  • Turn a client's brief into data, rules, routes, blocks and screens, and decide where each rule is enforced
  • Build a feature through every layer of the course: a custom table, settings, a service class with a custom hook, REST routes with real permission callbacks, form handlers, a staff screen, a dynamic and an interactive block, and a theme pattern with live data
  • Make it secure and private by default: nonces and capabilities on every change, ownership in every query, escaping, and personal data kept no longer than needed
  • Prove the feature with coding standards, PHPUnit tests, a smoke test from outside, accessibility checks and a performance measurement
  • Release it from a tagged commit and deploy it as code only, then present your work against a rubric
Sequence and talking points
  • The brief (8m). Hand out the brief (lesson_30.html, "The Brief"; or the final project part of final-assessment.html). Read Maria's eight requirements aloud and ask after each: "Which layer handles that?" Then the hand-in: the Git repository with tag release-3 (plugin and theme 1.2.0), both ZIPs, the proof (composer lint, PHPUnit, the smoke test on both sites, the performance numbers), RESERVE-AND-PICKUP.md, a five-minute showcase. The lesson estimates 300 minutes; Sessions 17 and 18 give it studio time, the rest is homework.
  • Milestones and assessment (7m). Put the milestones table on the slide (read from the lesson) and say: "Each ends with something you can check and commit. Three sittings: 1 to 4, 5 to 7, 8 to 10." Then the security checklist (it carries the most points) and the rubric: 80 of 100 is portfolio-ready.
  • First plan (8m). In pairs, the From Requirements to Code habit: underline the nouns (the data: a hold, a customer, a book, a pickup date), the verbs (reserve, cancel, collect, email), and fill a requirements-to-layers table: rule, door (form, REST, block), screen. Pairs share one decision each: why a custom table, why "expired" is computed.
  • What comes next (2m). "Session 17 starts at Milestone 1 with your plan in your hands, on the site and server as Lesson 8.4 leaves them. Tonight: finish 8.3 and 8.4 first, then read the brief again and write your plan." Read the bring list.

Watch-outs
  • Do not start building today. A learner who types code for holds tonight on a site still at 8.2 builds on the wrong state; the plan is tonight's work.
  • The reference solution (downloads/pagesco-final, and each milestone's "Reference solution" panel) exists: say so, and say how to use it: try first, then compare.
  • Privacy is a requirement, not a nice-to-have: holds name customers (requirement 8, the checklist's last row).

Closing

Exit ticket (3 questions, no notes, 4 minutes)
  1. Give one example each of code, content and configuration on the Pages & Co. site, and how each moves to the live site. Answer: the plugin (Git, release ZIP, deploy); the books (the database, once at launch, then created live); the supplier key (written on the server, never copied).
  2. Name two translator-friendly rules for strings. Answer: whole sentences with placeholders; numbered placeholders with a translators comment; _n() for counts; _x() for ambiguous words; literal strings only.
  3. Which two Reserve & Pick Up requirements do you expect to be the hardest, and which layer handles each? Answer: any honest pair; for example "nobody can see anyone else's holds" (the user ID in the SQL WHERE, "not found") and "works without JavaScript" (forms to admin-post.php under the block's store).
Homework (about 2 to 3 hours)
  • Finish Lesson 8.3's project first: Steps 3 to 5 (Spanish, the accessibility fixes, version 1.1.0 with readme, ZIP and Plugin Check) and the Release note.
  • Then Lesson 8.4's project: Steps 1 and 2, then 4 to 7 on the rehearsal server you started today, and the Deployment note. The final project deploys to that server.
  • Lesson exercises. 8.3: Exercises 1 and 2 (3 is a stretch). 8.4: Exercises 1 and 2 (3 is a stretch).
  • Both Quick Quizzes and both journal entries; both "Before the Next Lesson" lists.
  • The final project's plan: read Lesson 9.1's Brief, From Requirements to Code, the Security and Privacy Checklist and How Your Work Is Assessed; write your requirements-to-layers table and three questions. Do not build yet.
  • Optional: the labs not reached: labs/module-16/l8_3-i18n-a11y-distribution/a11y_scan_starter.sh (before and after your Step 4), labs/module-16/l8_3-i18n-a11y-distribution/release_check_starter.sh (after Step 5), labs/module-16/l8_3-i18n-a11y-distribution/debug_seats_spanish.php, labs/module-16/l8_4-deployment-maintenance/restore_drill_starter.sh, labs/module-16/l8_4-deployment-maintenance/cron_audit_starter.php, labs/module-16/l8_4-deployment-maintenance/debug_launch_check.sh.
Bring list for Session 17
  • The site as Lesson 8.4 leaves it: wordpress/wp-content is a Git repository with a clean working copy and the tags release-1 and release-2 (git status, git tag -n), plugin and theme 1.1.1, composer lint exits 0.
  • The rehearsal server ~/pagesco-live launched, with plugin and theme 1.1.1, its new passwords in your password manager, LOCK TABLES granted, and one backup in backups/ (Lesson 8.4, Steps 3 to 7). docker compose up -d in its folder before the session.
  • The test environment works: npx @wordpress/env start in the plugin's folder, the twelve tests green (Node.js 24; the node:24 and composer:2 images pulled).

If You Run Long or Short

Running long: what to protect and what to cut first
  • Protect: the 8.4 frame and Git; the final-project brief (at least 15 minutes); the 8.3 uninstall test.
  • Cut first (saves 3m): the Plugin Check recordings (they are in the Answer Key).
  • Cut second (saves 4m): the 8.4 pattern-cache step: tell it with the self-check's numbers.
  • Cut third (saves 8m): the brief's first plan in pairs goes home with the reading.
Running short: what to add
  • restore_drill_solution.sh on the projector: the drill read line by line.
  • Lesson 8.4's Exercise 3 (the smoke test) live against the development site and a wrong address.
  • Longer planning for the final project: pairs swap tables and review each other's against the security checklist.
Instructor Kit · Facilitator Guide

Session 17: Final Project Kickoff and Studio I

How to run the first studio of the final project: turn Maria's brief for Reserve & Pick Up into data, rules and doors, meet the three most expensive mistakes on purpose, measure before building, then let learners build Milestones 1 to 4 (the plan, the holds table and settings, the rules and the email, the first doors) with real done-when outputs for every milestone and a check-in for every learner.

1 lesson (first studio) 3 hrs session Lesson 9.1 · Milestones 1–4 Session 17 of 18 · Part 2

How to Use This Guide

  • Session 17 is the first of two studios for the final project, Lesson 9.1's Reserve & Pick Up, the course's capstone. There is no new lesson content to present: the room turns Maria's brief into a design, then learners build Milestones 1 to 4 with you circulating. Session 18 finishes Milestones 7 to 9, holds the showcase and teaches Lesson 9.2.
  • The lesson is 300 minutes for a learner working alone, 250 of them for the ten milestones. Where they happen: Milestones 1 to 3 and the start of 4 in this room; the rest of 4, then 5 (the two blocks) and 6 (live prices) at home; 7 (quality), 8 (release 1.2.0) and 9 (the code-only deploy) in the Session 18 studio; 10 (the write-up) at home. Submission: one week after Session 18. The rubric, the scoring guidance, the grading run and the reference numbers are in final-assessment.html at the kit's root.
  • Learners met the brief at the end of Session 16 (the brief, the milestones table, the security and privacy checklist and the rubric were the reading). Today they need their site exactly as Lesson 8.4 left it: the wp-content Git repository with release-1 and release-2, plugin and theme 1.1.1, and the pagesco-live rehearsal server. The warm-up checks it.
  • Every command and file below is the lesson's own, run on a site at the end of Lesson 8.4 (WordPress 7.1.3, PHP 8.5, MySQL 9.7, WP-CLI 2.12); the outputs are real and each one matches the lesson's own output card line for line. Each milestone has a "done when" with the output learners compare; the lesson hides a reference solution behind each one. The rule for the room, as the lesson says: try first, then open the reference and compare; different names are fine when the brief, the checklist and the checks are met.
  • The kit's labs for this session (labs/module-17/l9_1-final-project/) are short practice on the same habits for the guided lab and for stuck learners, never the project. Teal blocks are hands-on, amber blocks are watch-outs.
The #1 risk of Session 17: building on the wrong site

Reserve & Pick Up is built on the site Lesson 8.4 left: Git in wp-content, release-2, the rehearsal server. A learner who skipped Lesson 8.4's Git steps or whose pagesco-live is broken can build Milestones 1 to 7 on their development site, but cannot release or deploy in Session 18 without it. In the warm-up: git tag -n in wordpress/wp-content (release-1 and release-2) and docker compose ps in pagesco-live, for everyone. Fix now or plan: a missing repository is five minutes (Lesson 8.4's .gitignore, git init, commit, tag release-2) and is done before Milestone 1; a broken pagesco-live is rebuilt at home with Lesson 8.4's launch steps and checked at the start of Session 18. Nobody starts Milestone 2 on a site that is not at 1.1.1.

Before the Session

  • ☐ At the end of Session 16 (or by email): learners read The Brief, Milestones and Timeline, From Requirements to Code, the Security and Privacy Checklist and How Your Work Is Assessed on lesson_30.html, and run docker pull node:24 and composer:2 at home if they have not since Lesson 8.4. Ask each to bring one question about the brief.
  • ☐ Your own reference site: a copy of the course site at the end of Lesson 8.4 on the projector (the demo changes nothing that lasts except the query report file, which Milestone 1 keeps). Have lesson_30.html open at the brief, and final-assessment.html for the rubric questions.
  • ☐ Run the kit check once: python3 labs/check_labs.py module-17 (9 results, about a minute and a half). With your own course project at the end of Lesson 8.4: WP_LABS_COMPOSE=~/pagesco-dev python3 labs/check_labs.py module-17.
  • ☐ Board, before learners arrive: the counter drawing (shelf = data, house rules = rules, three doors: form, REST, block), the eight requirements as eight short lines, the milestone timeline (S17: 1 to 4 · home: 4 to 6 · S18: 7 to 9 · home: 10 · due one week after S18), and an empty check-in board with a column per milestone.
  • ☐ Print or share: the workbook pages for Session 17 (milestone tracker, requirement map, the predict items), the rubric from final-assessment.html (one per learner: they score themselves at the end), sticky notes.
Known project traps
SymptomCauseFix
Every page: "There has been a critical error"; WP-CLI tooA line in Plugin::feature_classes() for a class whose file does not exist yet (or a typo in its namespace)Read the end of debug.log (Class "PagesCo\Books\..." not found). Add each line together with its file; remove the line to get the site back.
The sed command adds nothing, or adds a line with spacesThe lesson's sed ... a\ has three TABS after the backslash; a copy from some terminals turns them into spacesAdd the line in the editor instead; grep -c '::class,' must say 21, then 22, then 25.
holds_tables 0 even after a page viewmaybe_upgrade() is not hooked (the feature line is missing) or the version option already says 1 from an earlier trygrep -c '::class,'; wp option get pagesco_books_holds_db_version; delete the option and reload once.
holds-check.php: pagesco_hold_duplicate on the FIRST lineHolds from an earlier try are still in the tablewp db query "TRUNCATE TABLE wp_pagesco_holds" and run it again (Milestone 4 truncates too).
holds-check.php: Uncaught Error: Call to a member function ... on falsejordan or priya do not exist yetMilestone 3's two wp user create lines first.
No email in Mailpit, or the wrong oneHoldMail's feature line missing; or another learner's newest message (shared Mailpit in some setups)grep -c '::class,' says 22; Mailpit's search box: to:jordan@example.com.
curl --user "jordan:$JORDAN" answers 401 rest_forbiddenThe shell variable is empty: a new terminal, or the JORDAN=$(...) line ran in another oneCreate the application password again in this terminal (echo $JORDAN must print it).
Books > Holds missing for MariaThe menu needs edit_others_posts, or the HoldsPage line is missingMaria is an editor: check the feature line, then the capability constant.
The forged POST returns 303 instead of 403The handler skipped check_admin_referer()That is a real security bug: the smoke test of Milestone 5 would flag it too.

In the room. Lesson 9.1 is 300 minutes for a solo learner; the room has 150 after the warm-up, the break and the wrap-up. The frame and the demo take 35 (the brief, the requirement map, the checklist, the rubric, the three Common Mistakes and the baseline), the guided lab 15, and the studio 100: Milestones 1 to 3 completely (the lesson's estimate: 70 minutes) and the start of Milestone 4.

Goes home (about 2 to 3 hours). The rest of Milestone 4 (the REST checks with application passwords, the staff screen, the forged request, the truncate and the commit), Milestone 5 (the two blocks: about 45 minutes, and npx @wordpress/create-block needs the internet) and Milestone 6 (live prices, 15 minutes). The optional kit labs. The exercises, the lesson's quiz and the journal wait until after Session 18, when the feature is complete.

Protect, in this order: the readiness check (nobody builds on a site that is not at 1.1.1 with Git); the requirement map (learners leave knowing which layer handles each line of the brief); Milestone 2's done-when (the table created by maybe_upgrade(), the pattern every later milestone and the live deploy depend on); Milestone 3's holds-check run. Cut first: the third demo step (the $title sniff: point at the lesson), then the guided lab (send ownership_sql home; Milestone 3 practices the same), then Milestone 4 in the room (it starts at home instead).

Lesson Plan

9.1

Final Project: Launch the Pages & Co. Website

160 min
Objectives (from the lesson page)
  • Turn a client's brief into data, rules, routes, blocks and screens, and decide where each rule is enforced
  • Build a feature through every layer of the course: a custom table, settings, a service class with a custom hook, REST routes with real permission callbacks, form handlers, a staff screen, a dynamic and an interactive block, and a theme pattern with live data
  • Make it secure and private by default: nonces and capabilities on every change, ownership in every query, escaping, and personal data kept no longer than needed
  • Prove the feature with coding standards, PHPUnit tests, a smoke test from outside, accessibility checks and a performance measurement
  • Release it from a tagged commit and deploy it as code only, then present your work against a rubric
Timing in the room
20mFrame: the brief, data/rules/doors, the requirement map, the checklist, the rubric, the timeline
15mLive demo: Common Mistakes 2, 1 and 3, then the Milestone 1 baseline
15mStudio: Milestone 1
25mStudio: Milestone 2
15mGuided lab: ownership_sql_starter.php
35mStudio: Milestone 3
25mStudio: Milestone 4, the start
Frame: from Maria's brief to layers (20m)

Read the brief aloud, one requirement at a time, and underline on the board as the lesson says: nouns are data (customer, book, hold, three days, the counter's list), verbs are actions (reserve, cancel, collect, email), and each rule gets sorted by where WordPress lets you enforce it. Then the mental model, in the lesson's words:

Think of the counter at Pages & Co. The shelf behind it holds the books (the data). The house rules hang on the wall: three days, three books, no sold-out books (the rules). Customers can ask at the counter, phone, or use the website (the doors: a form, the REST API, a block). Whoever answers, they read the same house rules on the same wall. In code: one table class that only stores, one service class that only decides, and several thin doors that only check who is asking and pass the question on. When a rule changes, you change it in one place, and every door follows.

Then the requirement map, the lesson's table, as a check: for each line, ask the room which layer handles it before you show the answer.

RequirementHandled byMilestone
1. Reserve; three days; expiredHolds::place() computes pickup_by from the setting; Holds::status() computes "expired"2, 3
2. Limits; no duplicates; not sold out; settingsHolds::place(); settings hold_days and max_holds on Settings > Pages & Co. Books2, 3
3. My holds; cancel; only your ownthe My Holds block; HoldsTable::finish() with the user ID in its WHERE; a "not found" for anyone else's hold3, 4, 5
4. Staff list and "collected"Books > Holds (Admin\HoldsPage), the collect handler, capability edit_others_posts4
5. Emailthe plugin's own action pagesco_books_hold_placed, and Holds\HoldMail listening to it3
6. No JavaScript, screen readers, no reloadforms that post to admin-post.php; an Interactivity API store that sends the same form to the REST API; role="status" messages4, 5, 7
7. Live prices on the home pagethe pagesco/book binding source learns a book's slug; the theme's staff picks pattern binds its prices6
8. Personal data; tested; safe deploysthe daily job deletes holds 30 days after their pickup date; uninstall drops the table; lint, tests, smoke test; a code-only deploy with a backup first7, 8, 9

Then the two tables learners will be scored against: the Security and Privacy Checklist (the rubric's biggest area with Features: 20 points each) and the rubric itself. Read the checklist's "Proven by" column: several lines are proven from outside by the smoke test of Milestone 5, the rest by Milestone 3's checks, PHPUnit and code review.

ThreatThe rule in Reserve & Pick UpProven by
Cross-site request forgeryEvery form carries a nonce for its action and its ID (pagesco_books_place_hold_30); the REST API needs the wp_rest nonce with cookies; nothing changes on GETSmoke test: a form without a nonce gets 403
Broken access controlCustomers need to be logged in (read); staff actions need edit_others_posts, checked in the handler and in the menu; every REST route has a permission_callback that returns a WP_Error with rest_authorization_required_code()Smoke test: visitors get 401, customers cannot collect; Books > Holds refuses an author
Someone else's hold (IDOR)The user ID comes from the login, never from a form; cancelling puts it in the SQL WHERE; another customer's hold is "not found", not "forbidden", so it does not even confirm that it existsMilestone 3's checks, PHPUnit
Cross-site scriptingEscape late in every template (esc_html, esc_attr, esc_url); messages chosen from a fixed list by a code in the address, never text from the address; data-wp-text sets text, not HTMLCode review, composer lint
SQL injectionEvery query through $wpdb->prepare() with %i, %d and %s, or $wpdb->insert()/update() with formatsCode review, composer lint
Open redirectsHandlers redirect with wp_safe_redirect() to addresses they build themselvesCode review
AbuseAt most max_holds waiting holds per customer; only logged-in customers, whose accounts the shop createsMilestone 3's checks, PHPUnit
Personal dataHolds name customers: they are deleted 30 days after their pickup date by the daily job, dropped on uninstall, never sent to the supplier, and listed in the readmeMilestone 2 and 8, readme.txt
AreaPointsMeets (half)Exceeds (full)
Features20Reserve, My holds, cancel, staff list and collect, the email and live prices all work in the browserEvery refusal has a clear message; expired holds show as expired; empty states are friendly; the settings change the rules without code
Data and rules15A table with keys created by dbDelta(); the rules in one placeIndexes for the real queries; "expired" computed, not stored; the table created on update by maybe_upgrade(), not only on activation; a custom hook others can use
Security and privacy20Nonces, capabilities, escaping and prepared queries everywhereEvery line of the checklist, with ownership in SQL, "not found" for other people's holds, and old holds deleted on schedule
Blocks and experience15Both blocks render the right state for visitors, customers and sold-out booksWorks without JavaScript; no reload with it; announced to screen readers; no duplicate IDs; a sensible editor preview
Code quality10composer lint is clean; the feature pattern of Lesson 5.1Every standards exception documented with a reason; every string translatable with translator comments; a new POT
Testing10You tested every rule by handPHPUnit tests for the rules and the REST door pass in wp-env, and the smoke test passes on both sites
Release and deploy5A tagged release deployed to the rehearsal serverVersions bumped everywhere they live, the ZIP checked before upload, a backup before the deploy, the database untouched
Write-up and showcase5A write-up that says what you builtThe write-up maps every requirement to code and names a decision you would defend; the showcase follows the checklist and fits five minutes

Score yourself, or swap with a classmate: each area earns 0 (missing), half (meets) or all of its points (exceeds). 80 or more out of 100 is a solid, portfolio-ready project. The reference solution is written to score full points; yours can get there with a different design. Finish with the timeline on the board, and the deal: "Each milestone ends with a check you can run. Commit after each group. Try first, then open the reference."

From the project folder with the wp shortcut; the Node and Composer steps in the plugin's folder (wordpress/wp-content/plugins/pagesco-books) as in Lessons 6.1 and 8.1. "Holds are not posts, so WordPress has no meta capability for them: the owner goes into the query. That is Milestone 3."

Three mistakes to expect, and how to coach each
  • Building the doors first. A learner starts with the REST route or the block because that is what shows. Coach with the counter: "Which rule does this door enforce? Then it is in the wrong layer." The order of the milestones is the order of the layers. (Self-check Q12.)
  • Ownership in PHP, after the query. $hold = HoldsTable::get( $id ); if ( $hold->user_id !== $user ) ... works, but tells a stranger that hold 12 exists (403 instead of 404) and is one forgotten if away from the IDOR. Coach: "Put the owner in the WHERE and let a miss be not found." (Self-check Q5, the guided lab.)
  • Copying the reference without reading it. The reference panels are complete; a learner can paste ten files in ten minutes and learn nothing. Coach: "Close the panel. Tell me what waiting() does with a 0." (Q10.) Pasting is allowed after trying; the showcase's "one decision you would defend" and the write-up are where it shows.

Check-in board

Tick each learner's milestones during the studio; it tells you who needs a 15-minute check-in before Session 18 and who may help others next time.

LearnerM1 plan + 3 numbersM2 six columns, version 1M3 holds-check: 10 linesM4 routes + 401Note for Session 18
Checks for understanding

Ask these out loud during the studio:

  • Which layer enforces "at most three books"? Answer: the rules, in Holds::place(); every door calls it (the lesson's quiz Q2).
  • Why does cancel() answer "not found" for another customer's hold? Answer: so a stranger cannot even learn that the hold exists; the owner is in the WHERE.
  • Who creates the holds table on the live site in Milestone 9? Answer: HoldsTable::maybe_upgrade() on the first request that loads the new code.
  • Where do the user's ID and the hold's ID come from in the cancel handler? Answer: the user from the login (get_current_user_id()), the hold from the form, checked by the nonce for its action and that ID.

Workbook self-check, items Q1 to Q12 (learners do them at the end of the studio or at home).

Answers: Q1 B) A hold is one customer, one book, a status and a date: typed columns with indexes answer "this customer's holds" and "what is waiting" directly, and old rows can be deleted cleanly; Q2 D) Nowhere: Holds::status() computes it from pickup_by and today's date every time a hold is shown; Q3 20 (twenty features); 25 after Milestone 4 (five new features, one line each); Q4 A) On the next request that loads WordPress: maybe_upgrade() runs on init, finds no version option and installs it; Q5 C) Cancel ANY customer's waiting hold by sending its ID; Q6 B) The request is well formed and the customer is allowed to ask; the shop's current state says no (Conflict); Q7 bool(true) then bool(false): the meta capability with the ID, delete_post, 15; Q8 D) The rules class knows nothing about email: others (an SMS, a staff notice in Exercise 2) attach to the same moment without changing the rules; Q9 A) wp_date( 'Y-m-d', time() + $days * DAY_IN_SECONDS ); Q10 WHERE ( 0 = 0 OR user_id = 0 ): always true, so the user filter is switched off (all customers); with 4 it becomes ( 4 = 0 OR user_id = 4 ); Q11 C) 403 with The link you followed has expired.; Q12 the data (a table class that only stores), the rules (one class, Holds, that only decides), the doors (REST routes, forms, blocks that only check who is asking and pass the question on). Full set with explanations in the Answer Key.

Differentiation

Support: a learner who is behind after Milestone 2 pairs with a neighbor for Milestone 3 (one keyboard, the behind learner reads each rule aloud before it is typed) and types Milestone 4 at home from the reference with the lesson open. Book a 15-minute check-in before Session 18 for anyone not past Milestone 3. Learners who joined Part 2 without Part 1: the project needs no theme work until Milestone 5's template line.

Stretch: the kit's own_action folder lab and debug_trash_door.php; then the lesson's Going Further idea, the waitlist, as a plan only (Milestone 1's format: rules, doors, personal data and for how long), to defend in the showcase.

Closing

Exit ticket (3 questions, no notes, 4 minutes)

On the slide; learners answer in the workbook's Exit Ticket box or on a sticky note. Sort the notes before Session 18: question 2's "not yet" pile gets a word in the Session 18 warm-up, because the smoke test and the PHPUnit test both depend on it.

  1. Name the three layers of Reserve & Pick Up and one class in each. Answer: data (HoldsTable), rules (Holds), doors (HoldActions, HoldsEndpoint, the blocks; HoldsPage for staff).
  2. Priya sends DELETE /pagesco/v1/holds/5 for Jordan's hold. What does she get, and which line of code decides it? Answer: 404 pagesco_hold_not_found; HoldsTable::finish() with her user ID in the WHERE (called by Holds::cancel()).
  3. Which milestone is the next one you will finish, and what is its done-when? Answer: their own (Milestone 4: the REST checks and the forged request answered 403; or Milestone 5: the four states of the Reserve block and the smoke test's eight ok lines).
Homework (about 2 to 3 hours)
  • Finish Milestone 4 with the lesson's checks (the application passwords, the staff screen as Maria and Devon, the forged request), the truncate, revoking the test passwords and the commit.
  • Milestone 5: the Reserve for Pickup and My Holds blocks (scaffold with npx @wordpress/create-block: needs the internet), the template line, the My holds page, the four states, and holds-smoke.sh: eight ok lines on your development site. Try the JavaScript path in a private window.
  • Milestone 6: live prices in the staff picks (the binding learns a slug), with and without the plugin; commit.
  • Optional: the kit labs labs/module-17/l9_1-final-project/rsvp_rules_starter.php, the own_action folder lab and labs/module-17/l9_1-final-project/debug_trash_door.php.
  • Not yet: the lesson's exercises, quiz and journal come after Session 18, when the feature is complete.
  • Before Session 18 (it needs them): npx @wordpress/env start once in the plugin's folder (wp-env from Lesson 8.1; the first start downloads images: do it at home), then npx @wordpress/env stop; pagesco-live starts with docker compose up -d.
Bring list for Session 18
  • Your site at Milestone 6 (committed), holds-smoke.sh in the WordPress root, wp-env started once at home, pagesco-live working.
  • pagesco-plan.txt with the plan and the baseline numbers, the workbook, and a first idea for the showcase's "one decision you would defend".

If You Run Long or Short

Running long: what to protect and what to cut first
  • Protect: the readiness check; the requirement map; Milestone 2's done-when; Milestone 3's holds-check run.
  • Cut first (saves 3m): the third demo step (the $title sniff); point at Common Mistakes 3 on the page.
  • Cut second (saves 15m): the guided lab: ownership_sql goes home, Milestone 3 practices the same habit.
  • Cut third (saves 25m): Milestone 4 in the room; it starts at home with the lesson open.
Running short: what to add
  • Milestone 4's application-password checks together: Jordan's 409, Priya's 201, Jordan's DELETE of hold 5. Ask for a prediction of each status first.
  • A design review in threes: each learner explains their HoldsTable and one rule; the others look for the owner in every query.
  • Start Milestone 5's scaffold for everyone on a good connection (npx @wordpress/create-block ...), so the download is done before home.
Instructor Kit · Facilitator Guide

Session 18: Final Project Studio II, Showcase and Next Steps

How to run the course's last session: finish Reserve & Pick Up in the studio (standards, tests and numbers, release 1.2.0 with its ZIP check, the code-only deploy to the rehearsal server), hold a five-minute showcase for every learner, then teach Lesson 9.2 (headless and CORS, what WordPress 7.1 ships for AI, an ability answered for a model, a portfolio-ready repository) and close the course.

2 lessons (studio + 9.2) 3 hrs session Lessons 9.1–9.2 Session 18 of 18 · Part 2 · course close

How to Use This Guide

  • Session 18 is the course's last. Its first half finishes the final project (Lesson 9.1, 300 minutes for a solo learner): the studio does Milestones 7 (quality), 8 (release 1.2.0) and 9 (the code-only deploy), then every learner shows the feature in a five-minute showcase. Its second half teaches Lesson 9.2 (110 minutes): headless, AI in core, abilities as tools, contributing, careers.
  • Learners arrive with Milestones 4 to 6 done at home (Session 17's homework): both blocks, holds-smoke.sh with eight ok lines, live prices, committed. The warm-up checks that on every machine. Milestone 10, the write-up, goes home; the submission is due one week after today (the lesson's submission checklist, in the workbook). The rubric, the scoring guidance, the grading run and the reference numbers for scoring are in final-assessment.html at the kit's root.
  • Every command below is the lessons' own, run in page order: 9.1 from a site at the end of Lesson 8.4, 9.2 from the end of 9.1 (WordPress 7.1.3, PHP 8.5, MySQL 9.7, WP-CLI 2.12); every output equals the lesson's card. Two kinds of step cannot run that way, in the lesson either, and are QUOTED from the lesson's recorded cards and labelled: the PHPUnit run in wp-env, and Milestone 9 on the learners' rehearsal server.
  • The kit's labs: labs/module-18/l9_1-final-project/ (version places, the release file list, a smoke test, a release-check handout) for stuck or early learners in the studio, labs/module-18/l9_2-next-steps/ (the 9.2 guided lab and practice). Teal blocks are hands-on, amber blocks are watch-outs.
The #1 risk of Session 18: the studio eats the showcase and Lesson 9.2

Milestones 7 to 9 are 75 minutes in the lesson's estimate and the studio has 65; wp-env's first start and npm ci can take minutes on venue Wi-Fi. Protect the showcase: at 1:15 everyone stops, wherever they are; a learner who has not deployed shows the development site and the smoke test there, and deploys at home (the rehearsal-server proof goes into the submission). Before: wp-env started once at home (Session 17's bring list), the node:24 and composer:2 images pulled. In the room: a learner whose wp-env does not start records the rest of Milestone 7 and runs PHPUnit at home; nobody debugs Docker for ten minutes during the studio.

Before the Session

  • ☐ Two days before: remind learners to finish Milestones 4 to 6 (holds-smoke.sh: eight ok lines, exit status 0), to run npx @wordpress/env start once in the plugin's folder and stop it, and to start pagesco-live once (docker compose up -d in it).
  • ☐ Your projector site at the end of Lesson 9.1 for the 9.2 demo (or a copy you bring to that state), and your own Lesson 8.4 rehearsal server if you want to show Milestone 9 live. Tabs: lesson_30.html at Milestone 7, lesson_31.html, Mailpit, Books > Holds.
  • ☐ Run the kit check once: python3 labs/check_labs.py module-18 (14 results, about two minutes). On your own project: WP_LABS_COMPOSE=~/pagesco-dev python3 labs/check_labs.py module-18.
  • ☐ Showcase groups of three on paper, mixing strong and weaker projects; the showcase sheet below, one per group, and the rubric from final-assessment.html.
  • ☐ Course close: the evaluation form (link or paper), the submission checklist printed, certificates of completion if your program issues them (after the final project is scored).

Lesson Plans

9.1

Final Project: Launch the Pages & Co. Website

95 min
Objectives (from the lesson page)
  • Turn a client's brief into data, rules, routes, blocks and screens, and decide where each rule is enforced
  • Build a feature through every layer of the course: a custom table, settings, a service class with a custom hook, REST routes with real permission callbacks, form handlers, a staff screen, a dynamic and an interactive block, and a theme pattern with live data
  • Make it secure and private by default: nonces and capabilities on every change, ownership in every query, escaping, and personal data kept no longer than needed
  • Prove the feature with coding standards, PHPUnit tests, a smoke test from outside, accessibility checks and a performance measurement
  • Release it from a tagged commit and deploy it as code only, then present your work against a rubric
Timing in the room
30mStudio: Milestone 7, standards, tests, speed, accessibility
15mStudio: Milestone 8, release 1.2.0
20mStudio: Milestone 9, the code-only deploy
30mShowcase, in groups of three

Showcase (30m)

Groups of three, at one laptop each in turn: five minutes per learner with a timer, two minutes of questions, then the next. You rotate between the groups and fill the showcase line of the rubric (Write-up and showcase, 5 points: the showcase follows the checklist and fits five minutes; the write-up comes with the submission). The lesson's checklist, on the slide and in the workbook:

  1. The problem (30 seconds): the sticky notes, in one sentence each from the brief.
  2. A visitor opens a book: "Log in to reserve". Then a customer logs in and reserves it: no reload, the message is announced. Show the email in Mailpit.
  3. The rules: reserve the same book again, then a sold-out one, then one too many. Change "Holds per customer" in the settings and try again.
  4. My holds: the list, a cancel. Then turn JavaScript off in the browser and reserve again: it still works.
  5. The counter: Books > Holds as Maria, "Mark collected".
  6. The home page: change Dune's price in the editor, reload the home page.
  7. The proof: composer lint, the PHPUnit summary, the smoke test's output on the rehearsal server, git tag -n.
  8. One decision you would defend (why a custom table, why "not found" instead of "forbidden", why expired is computed) and one thing you would do next.

Learners who have not deployed show the development site and say what is left; the rehearsal server's smoke test goes into the submission. Peers note one strength and one question per showcase on the workbook page; the question goes into the presenter's write-up ("the one question they asked that you could not answer yet", Lesson 9.1's Before the Next Lesson).

LearnerChecklist steps shown (of 8)The decision they defendedFit 5 minutes?One strength for the feedback
Three mistakes to expect, and how to coach each
  • Fixing the proof instead of the code. A failing smoke test line "fixed" by changing the test's grep, a lint warning silenced for the whole plugin. Coach: "What does this line of the checklist protect? Make the code do that."
  • Importing the development database to make the live site match. The 404 on My holds tempts everyone. Coach: "Code goes up, content comes down, configuration stays. Which is a page?" (Q4.)
  • A showcase that is a code tour. Ten minutes of scrolling through classes. Coach with the checklist: the problem in one sentence, then the browser, then the proof, then ONE decision.
Checks for understanding

Ask during the studio:

  • Why does the theme get a new version although its PHP did not change? Answer: its template and pattern changed, and the live pattern cache only notices a new Version.
  • What would have caught a ZIP without src/Holds? Answer: listing the ZIP and loading a new class with its own autoloader before upload (the lesson's quiz Q5).
  • Which data does a deploy change on the live site? Answer: none but what the new code creates itself (the holds table); the page and the test customer are created by hand on live.

Workbook self-check, items Q1 to Q6.

Answers: Q1 C) Documents ONE exception in phpcs.xml.dist, for that file, with its reason: a custom table has no WordPress API, and holds are per user and change with every click, so a cache would mostly be invalidated before it is read; Q2 1.2.0 1.2.0: the theme's template and pattern changed, and without development mode the live site caches pattern files until the theme's Version changes (Lesson 8.4); Q3 A) wp plugin install ran with the OLD plugin in memory, and wp db query does not start WordPress: no new code has run init yet; Q4 D) Create the page ON the live site (it is content: it lives in the database), with wp post create, as the readme's upgrade notice says; Q5 three per staff pick (get_page_by_path() for the slug, then the book and its meta) for the live prices; indexed primary-key lookups under a millisecond each, the page has no per-user content so a page cache serves it, and an object cache keeps them; Q6 B) A screen reader would otherwise read "Cancel, Cancel, Cancel" with no way to tell which hold each one cancels. Full set with explanations in the Answer Key.

Differentiation

Support: a learner without a working rehearsal server releases (Milestone 8) and runs the smoke test of their development site in the showcase; the deploy is done at home with Lesson 8.4's launch steps first. A learner far behind shows Milestones 1 to 6 and gets a written plan with a check-in date inside the submission week.

Stretch: the lesson's Exercises 1 to 3 (collect over REST, the shop's email through the action, the personal data exporter) as must-use plugins; the waitlist of Going Further as a plan in the write-up's "Next".

9.2

Next Steps: Headless, AI in Core & Your Career

55 min
Objectives (from the lesson page)
  • Explain what "headless" WordPress means, when it is worth its costs, and build a small front end on your own REST routes that pages through results, handles HTML fields correctly and works across origins
  • Describe what WordPress 7.0 and 7.1 ship for AI (the AI client, wp_supports_ai(), the Connectors screen) and what they do not (a model, a provider, an AI feature), and write code that degrades gracefully when no provider is set up
  • Show how an ability such as pagesco/check-stock becomes a tool an AI model can call, and why its permission callback still decides
  • Find your way into contributing to WordPress: the Make teams, Trac and GitHub, Learn WordPress, meetups and WordCamps
  • Choose a career direction, turn the Pages & Co. project into a portfolio piece without leaking secrets, and keep up with WordPress releases
Timing in the room
10mFrame: where you are now, headless, AI as plumbing, contributing and careers
15mLive demo: CORS, AI in core, Connectors, a model's function call for Maria and Devon
15mGuided lab: cors_headers_starter.sh
15mStart the lesson project: step 4 and the start of step 5
Mental model to say

"A traditional WordPress site is a shop where the stockroom and the shop floor are one building: the theme is the shop floor. Headless keeps the stockroom, WordPress with the stock, the rules and the staff entrance, and sends goods out through a loading door, the API, to shop windows anywhere: a website built with another framework, a phone app, a kiosk." Then the trade, on the board: what the theme gave for free (templates, the Site Editor, previews, plugins' front ends, one deployment) has to be rebuilt in front. "It pays for apps and many front ends; it costs a second deployment and every preview."

Then AI in core in one sentence: "WordPress 7 ships plumbing: a client plugins can use, a screen for a provider's key, a switch to turn it off. No model, no provider, no AI feature." Then contributing (make.wordpress.org, a team, one meeting, evidence in every report) and careers (agency, freelance, in-house, a plugin business, headless) in one minute each: the lesson has the tables, the learners read them at home.

Lesson 9.2's model-check.php (project step 2) prints what a model is told about pagesco/check-stock and sends the call a model would send, through core's resolver. Save it in the WordPress root, then: 
    wp eval-file model-check.php --user=maria
    Tool: wpab__pagesco__check-stock
Description: Says whether the shop has a book in stock, how many copies the supplier has, and when the supplier's next delivery is.
Input schema: {"type":"object","properties":{"slug":{"type":"string","description":"The book's slug, such as the-great-gatsby.","minLength":1}},"required":["slug"],"additionalProperties":false}
Answer for maria: {"title":"The Great Gatsby","in_stock":false,"supplier_available":0,"next_delivery":"2027-11-15"}
    wp eval-file model-check.php --user=devon | tail -n 1
    Answer for devon: {"error":"Ability \"pagesco\/check-stock\" does not have necessary permission.","code":"ability_invalid_permissions","data":null}
    "A model can only ever do what the logged-in person may do, and only with the abilities the plugin listed for that prompt." rm model-check.php.
Three mistakes to expect, and how to coach each
  • Treating CORS as security. "I will restrict the origin and the API is safe." Coach: "curl sends no Origin and ignores CORS. Who refuses a visitor on /holds?" (The permission callback: the guided lab's last line.)
  • A generate_text() result printed as text. The lesson's Common Mistake 2: a WP_Error into esc_html() is a fatal error on every book page. Coach: "What does it return when no model exists? On every fresh site."
  • Reading only the first page. Six books, no error. Coach: "What does X-WP-TotalPages say?" (The kit's debug_headless_client.php.)
Guided lab

File: labs/module-18/l9_2-next-steps/cors_headers_starter.sh; your reference is labs/module-18/l9_2-next-steps/cors_headers_solution.sh. It asks the shop's API the way a browser on another origin would and prints, header by header, what that page may read, then a protected route: readable, refused.

  • Run it as shipped (2m). cp labs/module-18/l9_2-next-steps/cors_headers_starter.sh wordpress/ then docker compose run --rm wpcli sh cors_headers_starter.sh.
  • TODOs 1 to 4 (10m). The same grep and cut on another header each time; TODO 4 reads the status line with curl -i. Circulate for the carriage returns (tr -d '\r'), which make a value look right and compare wrong.
  • Expected when done:
== GET /pagesco/v1/books, from http://localhost:3000 ==
Allow-Origin: http://localhost:3000
Allow-Credentials: true
Expose-Headers: X-WP-Total, X-WP-TotalPages, Link
Books: 11 on 2 pages
holds as a visitor: 401, Allow-Origin: http://localhost:3000
  • Debrief (3m): "The holds route answered 401 and still sent Allow-Origin. Why is that fine?" (The page may read the refusal; it cannot get in.)
  • Fast finishers: labs/module-18/l9_2-next-steps/ai_readiness_starter.php (five honest lines for a client meeting about AI, and a helper that never breaks the page), then labs/module-18/l9_2-next-steps/debug_headless_client.php.
